Mr, dames Sketchley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, when Mr. T. C. Fowke, who for upwards of twenty years had been Solicitor to the Company, was requested by the Board to 811 up the vacaitcy, which we are pleased to say he consented to do, and he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- ate. Mr. Fowke is not a shareholder, but holds a Policy in the Company upon his own life for £l,OOO, and therefore may be looked upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders. The total Income of the Company for the year was £178,310 18s Bd, being an increase of £21,928 lie 9d. PHILOSOPHER BILL. Aw'm just gooin' deawn for a pipe an' a gill An' a haul an heawr's camp wi' Philosopher Bill; - He's the fausest owd chap that aw ever did see, WP a reet merry twinkle i' °ether blue e'e. Othetn e'en ov owd Bill's! they con look a mon through, Be can tell in a crack a wise chap fro' a foo : Id wer just through him readin' fooak's thowts wi' sich skill That he fost geet the name o' Philosopher BilL He's nod to co rich; but he's ne'er discontent, For his life, like his money, 's bin terble weel spent; His motto were awlus " Tek keer o' yore own • Melt yore childer do th' same; let your neighbour's alone; Dornd lock up yore heart when yo lock yore heawse door, But keep a warm lace in 't for t' wanderin' poor; For wi' some beggar an owd pair o' shoon Yo may find a new pair when yo're climbin' Aboon!" But the things he cries deawn we o t.' strength ov his lungs Are envious fooak an' their envious tongues ; " They're th' seawrdocks o' th' waurld "—so hersaid yes- terneet— " An' they cornd abide th' appos for tastin' so sweet. So they tittle an' tattle, an' poo a long face. Iv yo keep yorser wakken, an' lick urn i' th' race; An' though yo'd to walk. whol they rooade in a cart, They'll whimper like lads 'Tha'd to mich ov a start.'" "Iv yo're merry an' single, an' howds up yore yed, They'll say •Thad'il hey to be tamed when it's wed;' Iv yore wed, wi' two childer, whol they've a lot moor, They'll wish to the Lord yo were pown wi' a scoor ; Iv a chap an' his mate con keep thick o their life. They're sure to cry 'henpeck' at him or his wife; An' sooa they keep singin' wherever yo torn, 'One hauf o' this waurld doesn'd know as it's born!" " Heaw different," says Bill, "are the mates we've both known, 'At'll reek booath yore luck an' misfortunes their own; An' 11 awlus contrive to be somewheer abeawt When gore lamp o' good fortune hes welly gone eawt. 0, they'll feed the wake flame wi' a word- o' good cheer, An' rejoyce i' their hearts when id blazes eawt clear, Fbr they'n pity an' charity strong i' their breast, An' the angels keep guard when they lie deawn to rest." Aw've hearkened owd Bill till ml e'en were quite dim, An' aw've often thowt angels coom tokin' to him; For though sometimes he rages at wrong an'. disate. There's nubry th' waurld as lie knows heaw to hate! May he live to be moor than a hundred year' owd, • Wi' his cupboard weel packed, an' his hearth never cowd, An' his daicent owd dame to keep breetenin' still The last cheery days o' Philosopher Bill! Higher Walton, Sept. 1, 12:,88. GAORGA HULL.

From every good action there ought to be a double fruit—good to the object in contemplation, and good to the bystander by example. A Quaker's advice to his son on his wedding day: "When thee went a-courting I told thee,to keep thy eyes wide open; now that thee is married I tell thee to keep them half shut'? Love one human being purely, and you will love all. The heart in this heaven, like the wandering sun, sees nothing, from the dew drop to the ocean, but a mirror which it. warms and fills. PAT'a EXCUSE.—" See here, driver, I ordered a smart trap to take a drive in Phoenix Park, and you c-me around in rags not fit for a beggar !" Driver of jaunting- CST : "I knows it, ver honour, and I would like to wear fine clothes, but there's not a tailor in all Dublin can take rue measure, I'm that ticklish." Tramp (to citizen who has donated a sixpence for a night's lodging) : "If you Could give me one more six- pence, sir, I can get a bed all to myself." Citizen: "No, I can't do that, but here is a suggestion—You ask the gentlemen you are to sleep with for an additional coin. fie ought to be willing to give it gladly." A public building, which the proprietors boasted could be emptied of a large audience in case of fire in SIK minutes, beat the record the other night. At the clo.e of a " free " lecture, the Chairman announced that a col- lection would be taken to defray the cost of the hall. The large audience was outside on the pavement in less _

than four minutes. The execution of good resolutions and new purposes should be entered upon at the earliest practicable mo- ment. for, if unduly deferred, such purposes are a tor- ment and not the inspiration they might be. Those vitho win their battles in the world, as well as those who win their battles with the world, are those who strike

instantly and heavily, Who can tell the value of a sedle? It costs the giver nothing, but is beyond price to the erring and relenting, the sad and cheerless, the lost and forsaken. It disarms malice, subdues temper, turns hatred to love., revenge to kindness, and paves the darkest paths with items of sun- light. A smile on the brow betrays a kind heart, a pleasant friend, an affectionate brother, a dutiful son, a happy husband. It adds a charm to beauty; it decorates the face of the deformed, and makes a lovely woman resemble an angel in paradise. A Sum i ADDITION.—Binks was calling on the apple of ' his eye. He picked up a volume of "Lucille," and ran across an inscription on a Sly-leaf. " Ah. a present ?" he remarked. "Yes, from a clear friend, oh, ever so long age—seven or eight years." ." So long as that ?". "Oh, yes. I was quite a little girl." When three weeks had gone by without the regular every other day appearance of ilinkF, and it began to look as though he really meant it, she looked up the book and found the explanation .in the inscri-ation. It. read, "To Miss Clara, ins her twen- tieth birthday." That fly-leaf is torn out now. A very rare fish. Platy/minx (Alepiecures) ferox, has itist been caught in the Rarlssfjord in Iceland. It is five feet nine inches long, with small shark-like fins, thefee on the back being about a foot in length. The head is pointed, and the teeth long and sharp. It appeared to lie on the surface of the water, and a fisherman caught it by its tail, when it attempted to bite him. Prof. Lilt- ken states that hitherto only three specimens of this fish have been caught, viz., one at Madeira, one in Green- land, and one previously in Iceland. It is believed that this is the mysterious fish, the fax-cii, i.e., the eel with a mane, of which the Faroe fishermen stand in such awe. The other day, while a registrar sat warming his feet at the fire, a stranger opened his office door and inquired. "How much will you charge me to read over about 15 lines of printed matter from a book I have?" "Why? Can't you read them?" replied the official. "I can; but I want to hear how the lines sound when read aloud. I'll give you a shilling to read them to me." "Go ahead, then; I can't earn money any quicker." A woman at that moment stepped in, and the stranger put down the book on the desk, clasped he; hand, and said, "Begin at the pencil mark there, and read slowly." The registrar's chin dropped as he saw that the reading matter was the usual form of marriage; but he didn't withdraw from his word, for, as he said afterwards, "I am an upright man, and might have lost even the shilling by refusing." A REMAREAELE MENORY.—A remarkable instance of memory has just come to my notice, writes a correspon- dent of the Critic (New York). Its possessor is a lady member of Dr. Howard Crosby's church in New York. Without having taken a single note, she will when she goes home write out every word of her pastor's sermon, and he tells me she never makes a mistake of a "toe" or an "and "—that every sentence not only embodies his idea but gives it in his exact language. For 25 years this lady has been performing these feats of memory, and during that time she has written out some two thousand sermons. The manuscripts of some of them she has had bound and presented to Dr. Crosby. They make 40 lance volumes. But this is not all of her devoted labours; she has written out, also from memory, all of his lectures, and she has classified his opinions on all the subjects upon which he has spoken during these years, and has made an elaborate series of indexes to them. Not a word is omitted. Even when the preacher drops into Greek, Latin, or Hebrew, she follows him, for she is proficient in each of these languages. MODERN SCYLLA. THE EARTUQUAKB OF 1783. Modern Scylla possesses but few objects of:interest ; it is for it classical associations and the graceful beauty of its surroundings that it is most renowned. The earth- quake of 1783 destroyed nearly all the town. This ter- rible catastrophe took place early in the morning of February sth, after a succession of comparatively cold days. Suddenly a powerful shock agitated the west coast of Calabria. In a moment Scylla and its castle were in ruins. After the first shock the inhabitants in a body took refuge from their falling houses on the sea- shore, like the people of Pompeii when overwhelmed by the lava of Vesuvius. The aged Prince Ruffo of Scylla awaited the result before the crucifix in his chapel; but, being over-persuaded to fly to his great inland castle of . La Melia. was forced to retreat, as the road was blacked by the rocks which had been hurled from the mountain. ' Back to the shore he returned, and joined fervently in prayer with his people, who passed the night in deep anxiety. The sun sank beneath the horizon; no repeti- tion of shock being felt, thp people began to cherish the hope that they were saved. Half an hour before midnight. a second catastrophe occuiTed. A part of Monte Jaci, the next headland, thundered into the sea, which, with irresistible force and with angry rear, was driven on the other side of the Pam, a headland cpposite the Strait. Then rtturned the vast retiring wave, sweeping away in its fierce onrush the Prince and more than one thousand of his subjects. When the sun again cast his'rays upon the scene Scylla was no mote; but the shore far and wide was covered with the dead, and strewn with the ruins of the once-smiling town.—Stosclay Maga:ice. div.head: NORFOLK BROADS.
div.p: THE NORFOLK BROADS.
BY WALTE. D. C. COMMAND, MA., Oxort, To lovers of the rugged and grand the Nortolk Broads present nothing very remarkable. The tourist who has "done' Norway and Switzerland, or _ _ _ .
even the Scotch and Cumberland lakes, and who

looks To; ianything similar in the Broads, will be disappointed by their insipidity. Yet, althoug,h not the "biggest thing,' or even the best, in any particular line, these reaches of river, and widening stretches of water, possess in harmony with the surroundings a peculiar character and an individual beauty which is not lost on the true lover of na-

ture. - The impression is one of intense tranquility. An air of repose rests everywhere—on fen and dyke, on straggXng village, and lonely farmstead; the still- ness is broken only by the cry of a swan or water- fowl from the reeds, or by the sound of a voice from the shore. Where you come upon cultivation, everything proceeds so leisurely, so dreamily, that it leaves you undisturbed in your reverie ;. the wheat is standing in stacks—a certain sign of ac- tivity—yet for all the life that is visible, it might hate been reiped without hands, let alone ma- chinery.% On the green undulating meadows, cattle are browsing, and a few scattered smith downs, which gaze at the boat as it glides along, some fat Norfolk geese line the bank in array ias though re- sentful of the intrusion, but there sno noisy pro- test, as evidently against the rules. It is not till you reach/the comparatively animated village by the water-side,with its quaint old hostelry and land- ing staith, that the spell is broken by a ban 4of children, who beg for coppers and sing John Bar- leycorn." This species of mendicancy, rife enough i in modern places, has a special interest here, and s almost pardonable, linked with the word " lar- gesse," which, with many other old words, is still in vogue in these parts. The survivals in dialect and local customs are, it

may here be observed, as numerous and as interest- ing as the many architectural remains. Often in the names, as in the features of the people, you may trace their Norse or Danish origin. In the names, too, of one or more villages is embodied tht memory of Felix the Burgundian, Apostle of East Anglia. Then again, as you sail on your way to Horning Ferry along the Bene, in a bend of the , river a few miles above Ado, you come across the ruins of St. Benet's Abbey, 1 built by Canute for Black Benedictines. I The " Abbot" of the ruin is now, as his

Lordship's full title shows, the Bishop of Nor- wich. Thus the charm sif the Broads is heightened by various associations; historical, archaeological, kc., and theses, loci is certainly a spirit of the past. and has little to do with the prosaic side of the present any more than with its progress and its prosperity. The character of the county side is indeed that of the county accentuated. The county has only three considerable towns, Norwich with innumerable churches. Yarmouth with its plc- ture-rque, narrow "rows," and Kings Lynn, and has altogether a very sparse population. It is, of course, the exact contrary to Lancashire, and for this very reason, as a contrast, may recommend itself as a heliday resort. The Broads have been brought comparatively near to Cot tonopolis by the H.S. and L., and one may safely affirm, without speaking of the " maduing crowd" and of ignoble strife," that these still waters afford grateful relief from the smoke and stir of indttstrial centres. East Anglia, political critics say, is behind the times. To ' be sure it is. And herein lies its efficacy as a sum- mer retreat. What can be' better as a restorative than to step out, as it were, by a back door from the noisy present, from the very nineteenth cen- tury, which, according to nerve doctors, does the ' mischief? It is especially on the inner broads, aloeg the less accessible dykes, and the branch dykes, that you find the perfect repose. Such is a tiny broad between Horning and Ranworth. The place is scarcely ever visited, and lies covered with vegetation, clothed with varied beauty, divided into several smaller lakes, these separated from each other by groves of rushes and dotted with islands. The broads that lie along the water highway are stirred many times a day by the pleasure steamer. The tide of trippers and excursionists has risen of late years; and it is owing to the thoughtless folly and wilful dpredations of these people that riparian owners have been compelled to protect their property. The privileges accorded for years. to yachtsmen, anglers, naturalists, and to visitors generally, who knew how to behave, have in 8013113 instances been ungenerously turned against pro- prietOrs, and been brought forward as proving pre- scriptive right of way. This is at any rate the de- fence, whether right or wrong, in the recent dis- putes on South Walsham Broad, made much of in the "Times," and mentioned in the local'Press as the "Battle of the Broads." Looking at the two sides of the question, while nobody could sympa- thise with the highhanded attack on public righth, all are sorry to see either rights or privileges abused, and would be glad in the interests both of visitors and residents if the warning is accepted..hy those for whom it is meant. For the artist this level landscape, with its flat pastures and scattered farm-steads, stunted willows and banked up rivers, offers sober pictures of an English Holland. Not the least conspicuous feature is the turning windmill,which with sails above. and water-wheel below does double duty, grinding the corn, and draining the marsh. For the field naturalist, whether entomologist. omithOlogist, or botanist, the Broads are a paradise, more productive than the pool tit Frodsham, though that, too, has pleasant enough associations The birds shot, a scene on the " broads," and those which used to be' but are no more seen, is a fruitful topic for discuss- ion. The bustard, the crane, the spoon- bill, the ruff, the kingfisher, and golden oriole, are all instances of' species which have suffered from the zeal of specimen-hun- ters, and still more from the ignorance of peasants or self-styled sportsmen. The grebe still breeds upon the broads in tolerable numbers, and the redshank, lapwing, and common sandpiper, still, it is said, nest on the surrounding marshes. Certain forces, how- ever, are busy exterminating; the supply follows te demand; fancy prices are paid for rare birds shot in the locality. Then, too, it is Often those vt‘ho do not know and value a rarity who drop across the best specimens and consign them to the common stock pot, or worse. A countryman lately shot a bittern, and, dubbing it a "funny old hernsher" (heron), threw it on the dung-hill. Similar anec- dotes might be multiplied; but not to trespess too much on valuable space, the writer here closes .„e these random notes on the Norfolk Broads. again

div.head: PRESENTATION TO MR. JOB SWALE'S.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO MR. JOB SWALE'S.

1 On Saturday a number of members of the Primi- tive Methodist Chapel, Legh-st., met to do honour to out of their late colleagues, Mr. Job Swales, who heS recently 'removed to Manchester, having been offered and accepted an important appointment in that city. A substantial tea was provided and thoroughly enjoyed by those present. The after proceedings were opened by singing and prayer; led by the minister, the Rev. Walter Graham, who subsequently called upon Mr. J. Bissell, the super- intendent of the Sunday school, to occupy the chair, as the oldest member connected with Primi- tive Methodism in Warrington. Mr. Bissell joined the society before the present chapel was erected, and has been a co-worker with Mr. Swaltis for more than 20 years.—ln an interesting and sympathetic address the Chairman referred to the rise and pro- gress ,of Primitive Methodism in Warrington, touch- ing more particularly upon the various departments of Christian work in which Mr. Smiles flad been engaged as steward, local preacher, class leader, and Sunday school superintendent. In all these depart- ments he had gained an ,unimpeachable reputation for consistency of character, faithful , service, and untiring zeal tor the welfare of Zion, and was de- servedly loved and esteemed, both in the church and outside, for his excellent qualifications and genial disposition. After addresses by the Rev. X. Gra- ham, Mr. Wm. Crampton (trustee). and Mr:Richard Bridge (secretary). the Chairman called Upon Mr. Joseph Titchett to make the presentation which, duty that gentleman performed in a very suitable menner, The Present comisted of an illuminated address, admirable in design and finish, and bore the following inscription To Mr. Job Swales.—Dear Sir,-:-We, the trustees, teachers, scholars, and members of the Primitive Metho- dist Church, Legh-st., Warrington, cannot permit your connection with us to terminate without expressing our high appreciation of the valuable and faithful services you have rendered to this church for a period of more than thirty years, during which period you have, at various times, held the offices of teacher and superin- tendent of the Sunday school, local preacher, class leader, and trustee. We deeply regret your removal ' from our midst, and trust your future career will be as distinguished for zeal for the church of Christ as the past has been.---Signed, on behalf of the above,W. Crampton, trustee; Joseph Bissell, superintendent of Sunday school; Rd. Bridge, secretary; Joseph Titchett, class leader; Walter Graham, minister.-Bth September, 1886.

Mr. Swales, who was_visibly affected during the proceedings, in returning thanks for the gift, com- menced by singing the well-known hymn " Prain ye the Lord, 'tis good to raise, your hearts and voices in His pritise," in which the audience heartily joined. Afterwards, he dwelt upon his long con- nection with Primitive Methodism, ths,happy and refreshing seasons he had' enjoyed with the brethren, and the many battles they had together fought and won in the name of their common Saviour, who had made them more than con- querors. His concluding remarks were especially addressed to,the young people present, whom he exhorted to enter vigorously upon Christian work, to rally round their minister, and to spend and be spent, with him, in the ever-blessed service of God. The interest manifested in the meeting was sus- tained to the close, and will long be remembered by all who took part in the ceremony. The Address, it may be added, is on view at Messrs. Jesper's shop, in Sankey-at. We learn that the Senior Class of Females, as a token of esteem for Mr. Swales as their teacher, have presented him with a large pho- tograph of the members of the class.

A BURGLAR CAUGHT AT RAINHILL.

, At Widnes Police Court on W ednesday, a labourer named Patrick Finn (33), who lives in Victoria-et., Rainhill, was charged with having burglariously entered the house of John Blackham, collier, Rain-

hill, with intent to commit a robbery. From th. evidence adduced it appeared that on Tuesday night Blackham was at work, and, in order that he could gain admittance early in the morning without arousing the occupants, the parlour window was left unfastened, so that he could lift it-and get the key of the door. The prisoner was aware of this arrangement. At about ten minutes past eleven o'clock at night on Tuesday, when Mrs. Blackham and her mother were in bed, the prisoner was alleged to have gone to the house, opened the window, and effected an entrance. The banging of the window awakened Mrs. Blackham, who shouted—" Is that you, John?' Prisoner made answer in the affirmative, and Mrs. Blackham thereupon said "Why Rayon home so soon?" He replied "There is no work. From his voice the women now perceived that it was not Blackham who was in the house, and they opened the bedroom window and shouted for help. Prisoner then made an attempt to escape, but Police Constable Walsh, who was passing at the time, caught him without difficulty. The magis- trates sent prisoner to take his trial at the next Liver- pool Assizes.

ODE ON THE OPENING OF ST. EDWARD'S NEW CATHOLIC CHURCH, RUNCORN. Br W. H. LBATHWOOD. Sister of Heaven! Jesu's Immortal Bride! Truth's only Daughter! Virgin pure and bright! When thy beloved came at eventide, Wet with cold droppings from the falling night How was thy heart awakened with delight. Yet sleep oppress'd thee—earth's deluding 514ep. He knock'd, but knock'd in vain—Oh Shularnite ! What bitter yearnings made thine eyes to weep, Ere, yet again, his face did through thy lattice peep! , But with the morn's soft breaking he returned; He came 'neath paling stars, and thy sweet eyes, Which up the mountain pathway vainly yearn'd, Dropp'd joyous tears. A King from Paradise ,Re softly came, nor roebuck swifter flies, Glancing o'er Lebanon, through loneliness Of cedar, spreading darkly to the skies: His smiles fell on thine eyes of deep distress, ' And words of love unto thy soul his tones address : "Come, my beloved, from the leopard's mountains! In Hermon, Shenir, and Amana's hills. The lion couches, watching by the fountains— He stoops to drink the wave of Gilead's rills! Come to the plain *here summer dew distils; Where fig-leaves burst beneath the quickening ray; Joy's warbling ev'ry scented vineyard fills, And cries the turtle's mate at close of day, Arise, my love, my dm, my fair one one, come away !" Stich was thy call, Heiress and Bride of heaven! A. 4 wildly-beating heart gave back reply— • " Set me a seal upon thine arm and riven Life's life shall be, ere passion sinks to die! (For love is strong as death, and blazes high With power Immortal, that the waves profound Of ocean may not quench its ecstasy.) And, my beloved !. by thy sacred wound, I e'en shall bit on high thy heavenly consort crowned ! " Hail, holy Church! for whom the cross of shame Was borne, and death with an Immortal's woe! Didst thou not look upon that pierced frame, That head so beauteous, hanging cold and law! Could deadlier drops of agony e'er flow Than Jam shed when death and torturing gloom Wrung with a thousand pangs His hallow'd brow? That thou shouldst blossom in eternal bloom, A Deity saw death and sank into the tomb! And thou hast bloomed triumphant o'er the earth, A lamp of living light through mighty ages Miming all; thy heav'n-born ray call'd forth To truth transcendent earth's.most gloomy pages. And at thy fount philosphers and sages Drank of that stream, only on earth divine Lacking the tzhich man's thirsty spirit rages. And had raged e'er it found this gift of thine, For lasting peace with life that portion cloth combine. Thou did'at renew the seat of mighty Rome! And e'en west mightier, for the tribes whose tread Trampled her form, fed suppliant Iteath thy dome. They saw the holy crown upon thine head Its sacred right, and when the harvest spread Of potent nations basking in the smiles, Their monarchs sued prerogatives in dread; Thine Empire sat enthroned in classic piles. And the rough Saxon rais'd to thee his barbarous aisles! Yet aast thou nurst in Tribulation's breast! And being purest, Hell's concentred ire I Hung'hotly o'er thee, asit were, to wrest From out thy soul its spark of living fire. . In vain! in vain! thine eyelids' deep desire Was fixed on heaven, in ev'ry rapturous close Of saintly life, whose joy death chuld not tire. And not with slaught'ring sword thy power arose, But Martyr's blood, it walls, its strength, thy spirit woes!

Now let me turn to thee, meek edifice! Whose humble aspect asked this tribute song; Not thine the Dome which rises to the abyss Of heaven, at eve the brightening stars among, So lofty that the adoring heart unstrung, Dashes the eye with Feeling's tend'rest tear. Thou lackest soaring arches, which prolong Sweet music, I'et is stained window here Whence holy light from Angel forms falls soft and olear ! I watched thee when the tender-eyed twilight Dream'd dim in he.av'n, and watching saw thee blest; Methought those spotless spirits dress'd in white, Night's sparkling stars through the blue pathways pressed, To gaze on thee; and softly from the west A holiness seemed spreading through the deeps. :Was it but fancy that my soul confess'd, Or, did all heaven declare the He. who sleeps Nor slumbers, o'er thy form a special vigil keeps? _ Rises in splendour's pride, St. Peter's fane, Where master-minds have wrought, each spirit dreams As though a thought of Godhead to attain. In Wry stone embellishment, high gleams Each golden lamp, whence melting sunlight streams', O'er saint and angel, column arch and sin hie, And ev'ry ray and ev'ry shadow seems • ' Soft breathing of a Presence all divine As the Unseen our thought in feelings would define! But thou, St. Edward's! lacking ornament Of art, halt yet that presence of the Dove, The indwelling tight from heav'nly regions sent With glance of joyous eyes from forms above, Etre doth the shade of the Almighty move To us unseen, and here shall souls partake With thee the mystic comfort of His lore Whom, on thy breast when endless day cloth break At last, the Lamb shall see and pity for thy sa4ce !

WAVrilirdSMN SVEDAK —The letter of President Cleve- and fo2eeaW aceepting the Democratic candidaty for the Idetaty has been published. It is devoted almost ' I%re Cxelretevserte..the tariff, and makes no mention of the fishelleas question. After an elaborate argument in fa ,vf the reduction of the existing customs deities, _'-oe President says :—" We have entered upon no "vmade of Free Trade; the reform we seek to inaugu- is predicted upon the utmost care for estab- lished industries and enterprises, a jealous regard for the interests of American labour, and a sincere desire to relieve the country from the injustice and danger el a condition which threatens evil to all the People 'of the land." e The Democratic patty," oon- tinuesethe President, "regards trusts with unalterable hatred, and counts upon the checking of their baleful ePerations as among the good resnits promised by re- vente reform." He asserts that while the Democratic maiarity were attempting with extreme moderation to redeem the tariff pledges common to both parties, they Were met by determined opposition and obstruction, litcl the minority, refusing to co-operate with tile Democrats in the House of the Representatives or to propose another remedy, have remitted the redemp- tion of their party pledges to the douleteul power of the Senate. President Cleveland then proceeds to endorse the pledges of the National Dem )cratic platform, among which are protection for American citizens at home and abroad, the regulation of a sound financial system, the construction of coast defence, the preservation of public lands for settlers, the limitation or checking of monopo- listic tendencies, the proper recognition of American labour., a generous regard for ex-soldiers, their widows, , aad orphans, protection against senile immigration, a strict adherence to the principle of civil service re- form, the euananteeing to coloured people of their rights of citizenship, and a humane Indian policy." The letter proceeds :—The Democratic party proposes to re- duce taxation by freeing from duty imported raw materials used in home manufacture, and thus to stimu- late our domestic industrial enterprises. It intends to do this with due regard to the interests of working men, bat in this connection the President is of opinion that the labourer can be better protected by additional and lucre direct legislation to restrict the immigration of Unintelligent labour, which is crowdine out American working men by working at wages which ought not to satisfy those who claim American citizenship. NEW YORK, MONDAY NIGEM—At the meeting of the Dominion Cabinet, on Saturday, Mr. Langevin and Mr. Thompson agreed that Canada must prepare for retalia- tion, and Mr. Thompson said the contingency of war must be considered. The Premier, Sir John Macdonald, said the talk about war was moonshine. Retaliation, if it should be becun, would scarcely survive the United States presidential election. Sir Adolphe Caron argued that President Cleveland could not retrocede from the Position he has taken. up. The majority of the Ministers agreed that the Dominion should be put into a thoroughly defensive state immediately. Mr. Langevin's Proposal to demand a prompt recognition of Canada's Jurisdiction over the Lake St. Clair Canal was postponed. Toecerro, MONDAY.—Lord Stanley of Preston, Governor- General, arrived here to-day, and was cordially.cheered. A deputation, headed by the Mayor, escorted him to the hotel, where he received addresses from the Toronto Synod and various societies. He paid a visit to the Board of Trade, where he received another address. In 'replying, referring to the remarks of President Cleve- land on the fisheries question, he complimented the Canadians on their calm, dignified, while firm attitude at the present crisis. To-night there will be a torch- light procession in the Horticultural Gardens, where the 'civic address will be presented to his Excellency, and -afterwards he will hold a reception of Lancashire lads and lasses. DISASTER TO A FISHING FLEET.-137 LIVES, LOST. A Gloucester, Massachusetts, 'despatch, dated Sept. 8, brings a terrible tale of the sea, told by Captain Ryan, of the schooner A. D. Story. He arrived on the 7th inst., from Iceland, having sailed on March 29. Off the south °oast of Iceland he reports that a large fleet of French fishing vessels had gathered to fish, when a heavy gale came on, causing great destruction among the fleet and scattering it in all directions. Six vessels were lost with their crews. One had her decks swept, toeing her cap.'taM and eleven men, another her captain and three men, and a third her captain and two men. Thetetal lose, as far as ascertained, is 137 men. Many of the vessels were so badly damaged that they had to be abandoned, causing 300 men to be left in Iceland in a destitute con- dition until a steamer arrived to carry them away. The IPPPI7 or toed was lirniteA. There were few natives lving there, and the men endured great hardships.

CARLIST AGITATION IN SPAIN. MADILID, MONDAY .NIGHT.—It is reported to-day that the Carlists have been victorious in a large number of districts in the elections for the provincial Wards, par: ticularly in the northern provinces of Biscay and Gui- puzcoa. The struß7to has been more animated than any since the Civil War. The Carlists have, however, during the contest given evidence of a strength and an -enthusiasm that has alarmed the Government not a little, and there is already some talk of replying to this manifestation by suppressing the privileges that have hitherto been enjoyed by the provincial boards of the Northern Provinces. The most serious side of the agitation has been the part played by the-clergy, who are C.arlist to a man, and are said to have menaced those efectors credited with the intention of voting for the Liberals with a refusal of the secranlents. They -are even stated to have declared from the pulpit that • there would be no redemption in after life for those voting for the "heretical" Liberals. The Bishop„, Vittoria, who has been a prime mover in the Caflist agitation, has been warned.

TERRIBLE -FLOODS IN SPAIN. MADRID, TUFSDAT MORNlNG.—lntelligenee has reached here from the province of Granada, to the effect that the rivers Xenil and Guadalfeo, swollen by the recent rains have risen to an enormous height, overflowing their banks, and flooding the whole district. The damage done in the valleys is enormous. A number of villages have been swept away, leaving not a trace behind, and the rush -Of water was so great that many bridges have likewise been destroyed. A panic seized the population in alt the low- lying regions, and hundreds sought refuge from the advancing floods by ascending the mountains. It is feared that the loss Of lire will be great. though no estimate of the number.of victims can yet be -Tormed. Twelve dead bodies have already been recovered. A fire breice out in the coal bunker of the•mail steamer, Pembroke'Castle, -and ten coolies were suffocated before help couldreaeh -thern. Three of the ere w and three officers while trying 10 effect the mime of themolies, were overcorne'hy the fumes, and are now lyingin -a precarious condition. The :damage to the ship and cargo is not extensive. AU tondo was awakened on Saturday merti- ingl .to the 'painful and awful fact that another murder:fo'r more diabolical and fiendish than those Viet have preceded it, had been perpetrated on a wornam flf the same 'bless as the poor wretch who was found In Buck's-row on Friday week. The victim in this caeowas discovered about a quarter to six o'clock in the morning lying fa a back yard at the foot of a passage leading bite a lodging-house„ No. 29, Hanbury-street, formerly Bro Wes-lane, Spitalfields. The house is occupied by a Mtn. Emelia Richareson. who lets it out to various t, lodgers; and it seems that the doer which admits into;' this passage, at the foot of which Iles the yard, where the body was found, is always open, for tbe convenience 61 the lodgers. A Mr. and Mrs. Davis occupy the upper storey (The house consisting of Three storeys), and us Mr. Davis was going to work at the time 'mentioned he found a woman lying oft her back, close top to the flight of steps leading Into the yard. Her thror:t was eutepen in a fearful manner—so deep, in fact, that thelnutderer, thinking he lied severed the tread from the body,tied handkerchief round it. so asto keep item. It Voss also found that her abdomen laid been completely 'ripped open, and the bowels, hart, and entrails were lying at 'tier side. Tim arm on which she Was lying was covered with clots of thiak blood, roost horrible to look at. Davis immediately cortimunitereed with the pollee atthe Cone- neercial-stesat station, and Inspector Chandler and several constables arrived on the Scene in a.ihort time. • when they fottral the woman in the condition described.; Even at That 'early hem. the ' nos spread ,euickly, and great exeltement pr evailed amoug the occupants of the adjoining houses; and an excited crOwd gathered in front of Mrs. Richardson's house, and 'alslo around the ..mortureiyin'Old"Mentagueestreet, whither the body was quickly removed. As the corpselay in The rough coffin in whieh'it was placed in theatortuary—the same coffin in reihieh 'the -unfortunate 'Mrs. Nicholls was put— it an appearance Which could not but eke pity forthe-srickini and indietation at The brutal murder , ern' eXtretrso degree. Two teeth had been knockedout of thetlewer' jaw, the third-finger of The left hand bore siestrseef iings'baving been wrenched off it; and the hands and-arms were considerably bruised. The exeitoment in the' vicinity was intense, and innti- enerible ma:tours were 'flying about. One report had it that's leatheriapron and a long knife had been 'found near ahe place where the body lay, beVineing, it was said, ton man 'Whose name is unknOwsi, but who was nick- niaraed-"•Leather Apron" and 'evidently known 'in the 'district. 'There-est be Uttle doriht now'tlatt this latesteraurder is -toe Of The series of-fiendish 'atrocities ore women Which Moe been goint 'on during the past few- months, ' this.miting the fourth case--eaill in the same district. 'Looking 'at the corpse, no one, could thinkbtherwise "tinui that the murder had been :committed bvsn maniac ''-er'sereteb of the lowest type of 'humanity.- Indeed, we 'should have to go to MP wilds of fltingery, or search the records of the French lower peasant :lift, before a. mere sickening andetescoltinc tragedy coulerbe found. A grave responsibility rests with Kite police in the district. -- THE DECEASED'IDENTITTMD.

A' woman, named Amelia Farmer, on Saturday gave trifOrmation that she bad been a fellow lodger with the 'deceased, and had 'knOwn her for some considerable , ' time. She stated that thd deceased women was Annie thapman. the wife of a yeterinarY gurgeon, who had (bid at Windsorabhut 18 months ago. She CLIIS accord- , ingly taken to the mortuary at half-pastlll o'clock and immediately recognised her friend. apparently being 7nauch touched at the clreadfel spectacle. . Litter on she ' made a statement di what' She knew of the history, ef the Ismurdered woman. Arinie Chapman had for a long time been separated from her husband, a veterinary **eargeon at Windsor; by neuttea,l agreement, and had :been allowed lOs. Yveek' by him for her maintenance. , The money had 'teen sent by Post:Office order, made payable at the Caramerchil-strent Post, office, and had ' always come regularly. 'Abut 18 Months ago the instal- menis suddenly-ceased, ail& upon iteToiry being made, it , was found thatehe husband had died. Annie Chapman. : had two children, butelothere they were she could not say. The deceased had a mother and sister, who were ! living in the neighbottritood of Brampton or Fultrani. Farmer had been in the hebit of writing letters for her friend, but couldenot remember the raact address of the ; mother or sister.'but thorght it was near the Bremerton , I Hospital. Last-vreek Chapman het intimated her in- tention of communicating with her-sister, saying, "If can get a pair .of bootbirom my sister, I shall go hop- picking." Another relation, a brother-in-law of the de- eeased, lived somewtreee in or near Oxford-street. Farmer asserted that dier murdered friend was epee- rently a sober, steady4going sort of woman, and one who seldom todle any drink.,'' For some time pest she had 'been 'living occasionally with a men named Ted ‘Stotiley;,Who had (been in the militia, but, was Bow working at some neigbbrraring brewery. Ted 'Sterile-7 was a good-tempered man. rather tall, about rsfiftllOin., fair, and of florid com- plexion. He was •the last man in the world to have quarrelled with Channean, nor would he have injured ' her in any way. At the beginning of the week the , deceased had been-rather severely knocked about on 'file hi-east and face bef,.. another WCKE24u in the locality through jealousy in 'connection with Ted Stonley, and, had been olgigedto got° the casual ward. As a regular: :neans of livelthood she had not been in the habit nf ,requenting the streets, but had made antimacassars for sale. Sometimes-she would buy flowers or matches with which to pick up a' Irving. Farmer was perfectly certain 'fiat on Friday night the murdered woman had worn three rings, which were not genuine, but were halts.; tions, otherwise she would net have troubled to go out to find money forlier lodgings. The police, on the state- ment of Farmer, made a vigilant search for the mot:here sister, and brotbeMineiave, but without success: A man named Chapman, from. Oxford-street, was found, but' proved to be no reletive. ARRESTS AND DISCHARGES. Although two or three men ha' been apprehended during Saturday and Sunday on . suspicion, they gave ,atisfactory amounts -of their tnevements, and were liberated. -

A man was arrestetl.a Gravesend on Monday morning. Supt. Berry, between eight and nine p.m. on Sunday, received a communication that there was a suspicious- looking individual let the Pope's Head pulabc- i house, West-street, .and the Officer at once de- snatched a sergeant, to the house, and had the man apprehended. ' It was noticed that his hand bad been wounded, -find, ,cn examining, it, -the superintendent leasad pat • it shad evidently been tOitten. In answer to the supftrintendent, prisoner stated vhat he was going down' Brick-lane, Spitalfields. at 4 al -via-Saturday morning, when a. Woman fell down in a fit. tie stooped to pick her up, whereupon she bit him through the hand. Two policemen, then came up, and ha ran away. Dr. 'Whitcombe, the police surgeon, ex- . smined the man's clothing, and diseovered blood spots eV, two shirts which bewas .carrying in a bundle. He vms also of opinion that blood had been wiped off his boots. The woman,. the prisoner said, was in the stwet, not at the bark of-a lodging-house.. The prisoner added that on Friday be WU walking about Whitechapoi all-night The prisoner gave his name as Wm. Henry 'Pigott, and is about 40 years of age. • The police has:e aseertained that he sleptata common ledgine-house in 'Whiteehapel 'on Friday 'night. He was subsequently handed over to the charge of Sergeant Abberline, of Scotland Yard, and they arrived at Conaraereial-street Pollee Station in the afternoon. The prisoner stands barely five feet high. He thas along dark beard, and wears dark clothes. He Issas -without ,waistcoat, and tlierf., were several blood-stains on his clothes, and apparently he had been drinking-heavily, his condition indicating a recent recoveny from dS'lixisavt tremenA. Several witnesses were called 'to see , the prisoner, but failed to identify him. This %,74.S particularly the Case with' Mrs. Fiddymont, who hos.a distinct recollection of the suspected man. The prissoner was suffering from shivering fits, and, having beets-examined by Dr: Phillips, divisional surgeon, was 'pmws,unceal insane. :In due course'he was removed to the infirmary. About.eaine a.m. on Monday a detective armstecl a man known as "Leather Apron:" His real 4-iciane is 'John .Tiser, but his frienerk deny that he had ever been known under the Vickname f)i "Leather Apron" '-When the detective called at the house, the niaor wag opened by the prisoner himself. "Just , the man I want," said the detective, who chsrged him, on suspi- cion, of being connected with the murder of the woman Chapinae. The detective searched the house, and took away some .nishing took, which the prisoner was in the ,habit of using in his work. By, trade he is a boot finisher, and for .some time has been living at Mulberry-street with his stepmother,: (Mrs. Tiser) and a married brother, who works at cabinet-making. When he was arrested tisbrother was at work, and the only inmates of the house were the prisoner's; stepmother, his sister-in-law, and a Mr. Nathan, far whom be has worked. His stepmother and his sisterAmlaw declared positively to a reporter that* Piser arrived home at half-past ten on Thursday night, and had not left the house since. They further stated that the prisoner was unable to do much work, on account of ill-health, and that he is by no means strong. Some time since lie was seriously injured in a vital part. Abcut GiX weeks ago he left a convales- cent home on account of a carbuncle in 'the stomach. He is about 35 years of age, and since he was three years old, has been brought up by Mrs. risen He lost his fattier some seventeen years ago. At the Leman-street Police Station, whither -the prisoner was taken, a large force of police was kept in readiness, with drawn staves. Only a few people amongst the crowd outside seemed aware that an arrest had .been made; and so quietly did the police act in Mulberry-street that few, even in the neighbourhood, connected the arrest with the murder. It is stated that a large number, of long-bladed knives and several hats were found in the prisoner's possession. The arrest was made by Detective-sergeant Tiiicke. The excitement upon the arrest ef "I,,eather apron" was intense, large crowds surround- ing the police station discussing the aaair. ' THE INQUEST. The inquest was opeped on Monday morning, by Mr. Wynne bitter, district coroner, at the Working Lade' Institute, Whitechapel-road. inspector Nelson (1 Divi- si9ll) xeiVeAPAied the police.. The .;917,rt R-Vd Mune-

diate vicinity were crowded. Mr. CcAlier, deputy coroner, accompanied Mr.. ta,xt,er. The jury, having been sworn, went to view Ih;e body at the mortuary. On their return,":,)_ John Davies depock.d-.. I live at 29, Hanbury-street Spits}fields. lam a catman, and occupy a front room with my wife and '1.1.1w son. On Friday night I went to bed at e:ght n'c'.inck, and my sons came in at different 'times. 'the last arrived home at about a quartcr to eleven. I was awake between four and five o'clock, but fell asleep for about half an hour, and got:up nt a quarter to six. I went about the yard on the/ground floor. There is a front door leading, into a paar',-1.. which passes through the basement. There is a .Inor in this passage. Sometimes the doors are open 'during the night. I have never known either of them to be locked. Anyone could open the treat door by the latch, and enter the yard `by the passage. 1 cannot say whether the back door was latched when I got down ; but the front street door was thrown Vide open, which was not an unusual 'circum- stance.

Witress being told to describe the general appearance of. the'yard. was not very clear in his stateme.ats. The Coroner said the police in country places generally prepared a plan of the locality, winch was the subject of an investigation. Certainly this was a case of sufficient importance for such a plan. Inspector Chandler promised that a Plan should be prepared. "The Coroner remarked that delay might prove fatal. The witness, resuming, said: When I opened the back door of the yard. I found a woman lying on her back. I called two men in the employ of Mr. Bayley, packing case maker, Hanirery-street, 'three doers from No. 29. They came and looked at the body. I do not know them personally. In reply to the Coroner, Inspecter Chandler said the men referred to were not known to the police. The Coroner expressed surprise at this. file said the men must be foterd,if they flad not already been seen and identified.

Davis, continuing, salt: 'I informed the inspector at Commercial-street what I had seen in the yard. TI heard no noise on Saturday mornirm • Amelia Palmer, 'living at '3O, Dorset-street, a 'lodging- house, was stext examined. Shcsaid her husband was an army Trensiontrm. FIN 'knew the deceased for five years, and idientifiedthe'beidy a that,of Annie Chapman, a widow. Mer litishadci died at Windsor, eighteen months ago. Priorto that 011 e-received los, a week from him. The deceased was called Mrs. "Sievey," because she lived 'with a man who was a sievemaker. She had been staving at 35, Dorset-street Witness had seen her several 'times the worse fordvink, and she was frequently :iut in tie -streets late At night. On Friday afternoon witness saw 'her-in Dorset-street about five o'clock. She said she had no nv)riey, and had been in the casual ward, as she ocotild•not pay' for RAO ngs. She was somewhat the wutse•forliquor,.srid when she left in the morning witness saitl'"Youtan'find money for beer, but not for your 'bill:" Be did neit see her .with any man that night. Sornetimes.ahe Jame to the hnuse with a man, said to be pengioneroind.sometimes'With other men, and witness had atfusedloqillo* heri 'bed. _

Timcithy 'Donovan. 36, Dorset-street, deputy of the cretninorflodeing-house, identified the body at the mor- tuary as' that of a woman who had lorhred at his house occasionally. She was not at No. 35 last week until Friday afternoon, ,about three o'clock. She went into theiritclven; and he'did'not see her again till Saturday morning-rail '45. .... Inspector Chat-idler, in answer to the Coroner, said ,othingwas known of the man called the pensioner. Donovan,-resuming, said on August 28th the deceased bad wrow with another woman in the kitchen, and sus- tained a'bruise over her eye. 'John -Evans, night watchman, 35, Dorset-street, said he saw the deceased gu out on Saturday morninA She never returned she waS the worse for drink. Witness knew She was outitr thestreet at nights, but only knew .of oneman with whcnn she associated. He used to come to her on Saturdays. He called about half-past two on .Satufday last, and when he was told of the murder. went away without saying anything. He did not know this man's name or address. The inquest was adjourned.

-The inquest- was regal/A. on Wednesday, and a good, 'lealfavdenCe was taken, but no light was thrown on. 'the motive for the crime. or the identity of the assassin. Uohii`Piser, who waSdately arrested and set at 'liberty agaimand who ii known as "Leather Apron," gave a 'satidattory explanation of his movements, and the coro- ner added that his statement was completely corrobora- ted. The inquest was resumed and again ad- journed. Mr. Phillips,' the divisional police surgeon, sta- ted atan inquiry thatile• arrived on the scene of the mukclertst half-past six' o'clock in the morning, andohis. •opihionwas that at that' time the woman must have, 'beerideAd'at least twOrbotirs.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.
The Rev. Francis John Payne, vicar of Leeds, has accepted the bishopric of Chester. _ .
The Queen has conferred the honour of knighthood upon Mr. Edlin, the assistant judge of the Middlesex Sessions.
A DRISNKEN WOMAN CHOKED.—At Glasgow, on Sunday, a woman named Sarah Gallocher, 48, while intoxicated, attempted to eat some raw liver and choked herself.
The 58th anniversary of the Earl and Countess Fitz- william's marriage took place at Wentworth, on Monday. Several addresses and presents were given to them. - •
Bodfary Rectory, near Denbigh, was partially burnt down on Saturday, the fire, it is suspected, being due to incendiarism. Some feeling prevails against the rector in connection with tithe disputes.

At l3arnsley, on Monday, Hy. Hey, of the Blacksmith's Arms. Hillhouse, was committed for trial for the wilful murder of his servant, Margaret Hill. The medical evi- dence was to the effect that the prisoner was suffering from delirium tremens. ,

At the Sunderland Police Court, on Monday, Margaret Johnson, Rose Ann Augusta, and Michael Mullaney, were remanded, charged with causing the death of Captain George Harris, of the barque Lily, of Harwich, at present at Seaham. An inquest will be held on Harris, whose body was found on Sunday morning in West Avenue. .

AN EXTRAORDINARY WAGER.—A peer's son is just now fulfilling the terms of an extraordinary wager. He is going about the East End of London visiting the various public-houses and performing conjuring tricks in the bars and taprooms. The lordling is an adept prestidi- gitateur, and is said to be getting by his performance quite a substantial pecuniary return. The wager is said to be for £lOO.

The body of a girl, named Clara Underwood. whose parents live at Gloucester, has been 'taken from the river Derwent, near Derby. The deceased appears to have committed suicide through disappointed love. Before jumping into' the stream she wrote a note and pinned it to her jacket In this she expressed the hope that the young man would never be deceived as he had deceived her. •

BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WITS.—At Bolton, on Monday, a bricklayer, named Richard Cruise, was sent to prison for three months with hard labour. and a judicial separa- tion was granted to his wife, for his having brutally assaulted her. une of the magistrates said he saw the woman immediately ' after the assault, and she was nearly butchered. The prisoner had a long record against him. A RAT CATCHER WANTED AT A POLICE STATION.—On Monday, at Bury, 'Jimmie"4 Mulligan made his 78th appearance in court, when he was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and fined 10s. and costs. witb•the alternative of 14 days--Superintendent Henderson said prisoner was very violent.—Prisoner: You would be. too; there is a hundred rats in these cells. They eat the prisoner's handkerchief and meat. If he wants quietness in the cells he should get a rat catcher.

The authorities at Manchester have received a letter from his Royal Highness 'Prince Albert Victor of Wales, intimating that he has fixed Saturday, 20th October, for the date of his vfeit to that city. During his stay, he will be the guest of 'the Corporation, and occupy the State apartments at the Town Hall. The object of his Royal Highness's visit is to lay the foundatiomstone of a 710 W wing in thP A uconts Hospital and open a lads' club.

Mrs;RoOth, vrife,of a Leicester shorthand clerk, was riding on the Great Northern Railway, on Saturday. night, near Red Mile, with her children, when her little boy, aged three, playing with the door, suddenly fell out. Mrs. 'Booth jumped out after him, and sustained injuries to the brain, causing death. She fell between the metals, and a train passed over her without touching her. The boy was afterwards fottnd on the line, running after the train, having been only slightly bruised.

MYSTERIOUS DEATH AT TiOLTONt PPOSED POISONING. —An inquest was opened, on Monday, by the Bolton Borough Coroner, relative to the, death of a girl named 'Jane Ann Blinkhorn, who died at the Infirmary on Fri- day morning. She was under treatment for a diseased knee,,and was going on well until Thursday night, when she became sick and vomited, death ensuing. The house surgeon attributed death to some irritant poison. The inquest was adjourned for the purpose of analysing the ,contents of the stomach. MURDER AT FICTDDERAFIELD.—At Huddersfield, .on Tuesday, an inquest was held on the body of Elizabeth .Bulsver, factory operative, who was murdered on Mon- day night by her husband, Charles Bulwer. The evi- dence showed that the couple had lived unhappily to- gether, and at the time of the murder the }unbend was .under security to keep the peace, ha7ing recently illused the deceased. The jury returned a verdict of wilful •murder against him, and he was committed to the York- shire Assizes on the coronet's warrant. ' Ex-Towtt Ctstut or SALFORD.—The Official

'Receiver in bankruptcy, on Monday, applied to 'Registrar Smith, in the Salford 'County Court, for an order of adjudication in bankruptcy against John Graves, who had been dismissed from his office of Town Clerk of Salford, and against whom a receiving order WAS made last week. The Official Receiver said the act of bankruptcy was the absconding of the debtor. 'Diligent inquiries had failed to discover any clue to his whereabouts. The order was issued.

In -acknowledging a present of an ivory porcelain 'bovtl, in commemoration of his golden wedding, Mr. Gladstone has written as follows to the Reading Radical Club Dear Sit—The Radial! Club's present was _ . . . .

duly received, and' I am deeply touched by Mr. Critch- ley's.account of the manner in which it was procured, ancPbeg to assure you the kind feelings expressed in address and letter were,rnost gratifying. The proposal to tvisit Redding I am Obliged to decline, as I must hus- band ;any strength for the work I have to do.—Your faithfuLservant,' W. E. GLADSTONII." TRUSTNE SAVINGS BAN/CS CLOSED.—Since the issue of the Hon :1460i Stanley's report on the Cardiff Bank, andthe institution of legal proceedings against the trus- tees; the following Trustee Savings Banks have closed, thenbtilk et the deposits being transferred to the Post Office and certificates of indemnity granted to the trus- tees,-41awkhurst, Hereford, Camden Town, Castle Hedingham, St. Jame A's (Piccadilly), Sevenoaks, Eccles- hall, Newry, Stafford, ,Loughborough, Newport (Mon.), Sweihatn, Great Marlow, West Mailing, Shipston-on- Stour, and Bristol. STIAANOZ SCRNII•AT A TOWN COUNCIL MEETINO.—At a meeting of*, Grimsby Town Council on Monday, Mr. Maddoektnade certain charges against members of the Council,who rose in a body. Alderman Keetley told Mr. Maddock that he wanted kicking out, and , the strongest epithets vvere freely applied to the offending member, accompanied by loud threats as to what would be done to him. Amid the general disorCer,' the Mayor adjourned the meeting, and Mr. Madd,Nck left the room surrounded by an angry crowd, one of the members saying he "would adjournitint on the nose" when be got outside. EXCIIKLUBS: RETTYRKs.—The total receipts into the Exchequer•between the Ist of April last and the Bth of :4eptemberwas £34,190,568, against £33,944,535 during the corresponding period of last year ; Customs, £8,394,600, -aged nst 48,23000; Excise, £9,944,00, against £9,8924001 Stamps, £5,904,000, against £5,682,000; Property and IncorrieTax, £3,141,000, awl in st V,739;000; Post office,. £1790000, against £3.650,000; Telegraph Service, £935.000, against £905,000 ; Miscellaneous, £1,303.311, against £1,061,522; Balance in the Bank of Ungland on Saturday last, £1,707,847; Bank of Ireland, £509,591.

DISTRESS:NG Burcmit orSovEns.—On Sunday, the body of a young man named Harry Evans was found in a mill dam at Queensbury, 'Bradford, and the body of a young woman named Annie Pickles was also found in a tank on her father's farm, near Queensbury. The two had been keeping company, but a rumour is said to have reached the girl's ear chat he had been unfaithful to her. They met on Saturday evening, and from the contents of a letter found in the girl's pocket, appear to have quar- relled. Evans had told her he would keep her company ,no longer, and it had driven her mad. The affair has ',caused a painful sensation. TECHNICAL EDOCATION."—MUNIFIC,ENT GIFTS TO STOCK- V)ll.T.—The foundation atone of the new Technical School for Stockport was laid by the Lord Mayor of , London, on Saturday afternoon, with full Masonic rites. An address from the Corporation was first presented to him, and subsequently he and a number of other gentle- men were entertained at lunch by the Mayor of Stock- port, Mr. J. Leigh. The latter read a letter from Lady Whitworth, in which she conveyed to the promoters of the ,new school the gratifying intelligence that the legatees of her husband had resolved to give £5,000 to- wards the building fund and a second .E 5,000 towards the scholarship fund. The Mayor of Stockport and "A Fried' have each given £3,500 towards the cost of the school, and, including the gift of the Whitworth legatees, the funds promised and in hand nto amount .o over E2IROQ.

&MOEN DEATH OF A MINOSTER.—A sad incident oc- curred rduring the meeting of the Manchester Presby- tery, on Menday. One of the ministers present was the Rev. R. T. Cunningham, of Bowdon, who was ordained six years Ago. During the proceeduigs he complained of the closeness of the air, and then was suddenly seized with illness, and falling unconscious, was carried out of the room. It was then seen that the seizure was serious, and whilst medical aid was sent for prayer for his re- covery was offered by the assembly. In a few minutes two medical men arrived, but they were too late, as Mr. Cunningham had died almost immediately on being carried out, and without recovering consciousness. The Presbytery expressed profound sympathy with Mr. Cunningham's aged mother and his bereaved congrega- tion. Mr. Cunningham was not married. In the morning he seemed to be in perfect health, and had never shown signs of heart disease, to which his death hi Attributed. Mr. Charles Sugden, the actor, was on Wednesday com- mitted to prison for three monthsby Mr. Justice Denman for contempt of court in performing at the Olympic Theatre in defiance of an injunction. Mrs Charles Turner, a Liverpool lady, has placed at the disposal of the Archbishop of York the sum of £lO,OOO towards the creation of a fund for assisting with pensions the clergy of the diocese who may become unfit for the discharge of their duties through infir- mity.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present :—The Rey. G. E. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Harrison, Isherwood, Bonnell, T. Jones, Jol- ley, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Clarke, Wright, Eckersley, Humphreys, Kilsball, Owen. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. 11. Ward (workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superinten- dent of Padgate Schools.
THE PADGATE SCHOOLS. The DOCTOR reported that• the health of the children at these schools was satisfactory.
SCHOOL FEES cmdltiVrEE.
This committee reported that fees had been allowed in 65 cases, 2 of which were new and 63 old.—The minutes were confirmed.
REPAYMENTS.

The Local Government Board wrote that they had paid to the treasurer of the Union the sum of £494 Os 10d being the amount repayable to the Board in respect of the salaries of medical officers, school teachers, &c.
TILE LOCAL GOVERNMENT QUESTION.

A letter was read from Mr. Hulton-, Clerk of the Peace, I for Lancashire, dealing with the county government question and mentioning that under the recently passed Act the question, Council for Lancashire would consist of 105 members, 85 of which would be elected by the county exclusiveof the boroughs.—The CLERK said he wrote to Mr. Hulton, asking as to the propOrtion of population toeach county councillor, and the reply was that the population per councillor would be about 20.000. The rural district of the Union had a population of about 12,000, and Newton and Haydock townships combined probably some 15,000. Newton made an attempt to get a separate councillor for itself, but it was found to be impracticable, but one was agreed upon for Newton and Haydock combined, and another for the rural district of the Union in Lancashire. They had fixed " Winwick " for the name of the rural district. They could not fix Warrington as Warrington would have councillors of its own, and Winwick being central and an ancient village, the name was thought appropriate. • With regard to Newton, there were two other Newtons in Lancashire, and he (the Clerk) had suggested that Earlestown would be a very appropriate name. The Clerk of the Peace concurred, but the proposal was very strongly opposed by Mr. Brown on the part of Newton. Proin its increas- ing manufactures and very respectable population, both in point of numbers and position, he thought Earlestown would be a very proper place to give its name to the dis- trict. (Hear, hear.) They had got a very good propor- tion in getting these two representatives.—The matter then dropped. •,
TRE BOUNDARIES QUESTION .-A DISCLAIMER FROM MR. I. _ C. PARR.

The Chairman said he had received the following let- ter from Mr. J. C. Parr :—Grappenhall Heyes Warrington, September 3rd, 1888.—To the Chairman of ' the Board of Guardians, Warrington Union.—Dear Sir. I was much surprised to read in the report of your Board meeting on Wednesday last in the local papers, a state- ment from one of your members that he believed, indeed that it was almost a certainty, that secret influence had been brought to bear, upon the Boundary Commissioners, to guide their decision, and that a deputation had actually waited upon ther'n in a clandestine manner with the same object. Having had the honour to represent, with other gentlemen, the ratepayers and inhabitants of the town- ships interested—Grappenhall and Thelwall—l feel quite certain that nothing of the kind could have occurred without my cognisance and as far as I know and belier no action of any kind has been taken to approach the Boundary Commissioners either secretly or onenly,private- ly or publicly since April last, when the matter was fully and fairly fought out, be- fore the Commissioner, in the Town Hall of- Warrington. Apart from • the stigma thrown upon the Boundary Commissioner by suggesting that their decision was affected by side influences, it is unworthy of a public body occupying the responsible position of a Beard of Guardians to be the medium for making charges of con- duct characterised as "atrocious" and "monstrous" with- out first ascertaining that such charges have even the smallest foundation. May I hope you will find out from whom these charges emanate and let the public learn to whom they are indebted for such sensational misrep- resentations, and when you find that there is not a sha- dow of evidence to support these serious allegations. I am sure you will be the first to regret that they should have been made, and such epithets used reflecting upon those who, though they may differ in opinion from the Union Authorities, have every wish to treat them with courtesy and consideration, and to meet them Openly and in a straightforward manner. Yours faithfully, J. CHARLTON PARR.—III reply to that letter he (the Chairman) wrote the following :—Beech- field, ,qtlasebrook, September 4th, 1888.—Dear Sir. Your letter addressed' to me has just reached its destination through Mr. Sutton this morning, and I am very pleased to hear that no such deputation or influence, as provi- sionally alleged, has been brought to bear upon the Boun- dary Commissioners; indeed, on consideration, I thought it impossible that such should be the case. In reply to your observation that" it is unworthy of a public body occupying the responsible position of a Board of Guar- dians to be the medium for making charges of conduct characterised as atrocious and monstrous, &c.," I would point out to you how difficult it is for a Board to con- trol the utterances of individual members made in the presence of reporters at a quasi-public meeting. I have not a local paper by me, nor do I know from which your information is gathered, but what actually transpiral, in my opinion is rather a question between the indivi- dual who made the statement complained of, and the gentlemen concerned, whoever they may be. I cannot see that the Board is in any way implicated by state- ments for which it has in no sense made itself respon- sible. As a matter of fact, observations were made practically to the effect you quote by a member as to whose personality there is no question, and the clerk at once said, "Do you mean to say so and so and so and so, Mr. —? Then, if so, it amounts to a very grievous offence, &c." Then it was that an offence of the kind was characterised as "atrocious," &c., by different members. The Board, you see, made no statement at all on the merits of the question, nor did it make any charge whatever of conduct characterised as atrocious against any one. I very much personally regret the in- cident, and can assure you that so far as! am concerned, and I think I may say the same Of the Board, as a whole, the only wish felt is to attend to the interest committed to our charge, honestly, showing always the greatest possible consideration and courtesy to those whose views on any question that may come between us may differ from ours. With much respect, believe me, dear sir, tally yours*, GEORGE FARRAR ROBERTS.—P.S. I wish to lay your letter, with this reply to it, before the Board at its next meet- ing unless you wish me not to.—G. F. R.— In reply to the Chairman's letter, Mr. ,Parr wrote : " Grappenhall Heves, Warrington' September sth, 1888. Dear sir,—l thank you for your letter of the 4th inst. As the statement in question was made publicly I think the correction should also be published, so I quite ap- prove of your laying my lettex lefore the Board as sug- gested. YOU'S faithfully, J. CHARLTON PARR. The Rev. G. F. Roberts."—The CLERK said that what was observed at a previous Board meeting was as the Chairman had explained, a remark that something had been done of which they had not heard but of which they thought they ought to have heard, but he was now in a position, on the authority of a right hon. gentleman who was one of the Boundary Commissioners, to say that no deputa- tion had been received. He afterwards called at the Town Clerk's office, and it seemed to have arisen in this way so far as the naming of it there was concerned. If the Secretary of the Boundary Commissioners had done what the member of the Boundary Commission had done, that is answered the question put to him, Mr. Harrison would not have been under the misapprehension he was. He (the Clerk) had seen the correspondence with the secretary of the Boundary Commissioners in which the Town Clerk asked if a deputation had been received by the commissioners. The Secretary in reply to that merely referred to it at the end of his letter in words to this effect.: "Adverting to the latter portion of your letter I have to say that the proceedings of the Boundary Commissioners are now at an end." Well, when they received an answer of that kind to a direct question it naturally suggested that there was sonic truth in the matter inquired about. The difficulty would have been removed if the Secretary had answered the question, and Mr. Harrison did not make his statement till after that correspondence. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. HARRISON was glad the Clerk had made these remarks because they showed that he did not make his statement without some authority. He would have been the last to make any remarks at that Board reflecting upon any deputation, or supposed deputation, unless he thought he had sufficient reason for it. It was from the Town Clerk at a meeting 734 the General Purposes Committee that he got the infor- mation. Speaking of the apparent change of front of the Boundary Commissioners, the Town Clerk said he had good reason for believing that a de- putation had been received by the Commissioners, and that such representations had been made to them as had induced the altered position of affairs. He (Mr. Harrison) need hardly tell them that the members of the General ,Purposes Committee were quite as emphatic in their condemnation of such proceedings as they bad been at that Board. They were quite right in doing so for the Awn Clerk said it was almost a certainty that such a deputation had waited upon the Bounden) Commis- sioners. He also said that he had written asking to be favoured with a copy of such representations as were made, and also to ask if they would be so good as to favour him with a list of the gentlemen who had waited upon them. He (Alderman Harrison) thought that seemed very clear, and he thought he might be excused for having made those observations, seeing they were forced from him by observations made' previously. In conclusion -Mr. Harrison said he could assure Mr. Parr that he was one of the last gentleman he should have supposed capable of lending himself to any movement that ' was not characterised by strict straightforwardness,' and that would not stand open -discussion of the freest and most public kind. He had had no intention to give Mr. Parr or any other gentle- man the slightest offence. Whatever epithets had been used at that Board meeting fell to the ground as inap- plicable and absurd inasmuch as there had been no de- putation waiting upon the Commissioners, and it must

div.p: HFBIGNATION OF THE NURSE.
A letter was read from Nurse Watkins resigning her position at the Workhouse on the ground that she had been appointed matron at the Warrington Infirmary. -
THE ESTIMATE.

The CLERK read a statement with regard to the esti- mate' of expenditure, which contained the following The probable expenditure for the half-year ending at March, 1859, is estimated at £lBB for separate charges, £8,240 for common charges (61d in the £), £2,307 for county rates, and £1,373 to meet expenditure before another call can be made, inski.pg a total of £12,108, compared with £12,168 for the corresponding period of last year. Deducting £677 from the £12,108 leaves the amount of contributions required £11,431. Although often hitherto named, it may be useful to repeat that the purpose of estitnates is to provide a sufficient sum to enable the treasurer to comply with your Board's orders upon him in the ensuing half-year. They have no effect upon the expenditure, save that when considerable balances result at the close of the half-year the surplus enables reduced calls for the following half-year,whereas the actual expenditure may vary but slightly from the average of corresponding half-years."
