THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. SEPTEMBER 15. 1588.

There has been some talk of the possibility of 'between England and the United States as outcome of the rejection of the Fisheries ,j by the United States Government. There 4've Jingoes on both sides of the water, but they TZ:ft small section only, and there will be no war. CI bill of retaliation upon Canada, which has 1 rushed through both Houses in the States, i 7 in the first instance an ominous look; but it ziew seen that it was, in its main feature, an 'aetioneering move in view of the struggle for the 23ency. The Democrats, as the party in pos- on, felt that they could not afford to give the :tiler side a chance in the matter of patriotism- -6_7 what passes for patriotism: hence the Retalia- -671 Bill, which the Republicans were bound to ort lest it should be said of them that they indifferent to the interests of the country. is legitimate to suggest that a feeling of this $ stimulated by both the great parties in the "tea, might lead to further hostile acts; but the Itq seems to be that the Fisheries card is regarded Played and done with. In the letter issued by -4 CLEVELAND, on his acceptance of the _nomination for re-election, the Fisher- clUestion is not even mentioned; while General who is nominated in the Republican , refers to it as a side issue of little or no "Our fisheries," he says, "should be . and protected. The hardships and risks C't are necessary incidents to the business should }:4511 be increased by an inhospitable exclusion from e hear lying ports. The resources of a firm, and consistent diplomacy are un- iy equal to the prompt and peaceful of the difficulties which now exist." ith these closing sentences we may all agree- -Irl as well as Americans. The battle of ' Presidency will be fought not on the Fisheries On the Tariff question. President CLEVELAND thNirs a reform—that is to say, a reduction of t: tariff, with the object of enabling Americans obtain their raw materials cheaper. and thus them in a position to compete, with a greater 1-tmtlee of success, in the open markets of the ktkicl• He is not a Free Trader, though ho is ng in the direction of Free Trade. The Re- b()(Ticaris urge that his policy is a Free Trade tot tY ; and they seek to make headway in the arki4trY by posing as patrons of high tariffs, and 14Of, high wages to working-men. General aaasox says :—" We believe it to be one of the th:tbY objects of tariff legislation to preserve 4rnerican markets for American producers, ki to maintain the American scale of wages by tvate?ilate discriminating duties upon foreign corn- ti„ 4g products." There is no denying the fact 47t labour in the United States is remunerated at t0,r.44, higher than rules in this country ; but as CotZt that it is important to remember that lifti rent, clothing, and other necessaries of are so much more costly than they are at 1.171, that it is a nice question whether the trilage workman is better off in America than in ha, and. But it may be asked—" How does it if Free Trade is a-good thing, that the tl;47rjeans, who are Protectionists, can hold their kal With Englishmen " The answer is, that eent " is a vast country, with vast natural krnlerees, and that these resources have proved Iltotelitepensation for what has been lost by c": 1. Let England, as to her wages, be

compared with any of the old countries on the Continent—with Fran, Austria, -Italy, or Germany. It will instantly be seen that Protection has not served thorn; and that relatively speaking, their workmen are very badly paid. However, in the United States wages are high, and it is not unnatural that the workers should seek to keep them high. Whilst we are convinced that Free Trade would benefit America enormously in the long run, we feel bound to say that the immediate effect of the abolition of the tariff would be injurious. It would disturb trade by disturbing prices, and there woluld, in all likelihood, be a downward tendency until the' level of English rates was reached, when a keen competition would set 'in which would result in our having to share the neutral markets of the world,instead of monopolising them as we do at present. But there is no prospect of Free Trade, out and out, being adopted, in the United States during the present electoral contest. Presi- dent CLEVELAND goes part of the way, but a part 'only; _while General HARRISON will not budge an inch. The struggle is one which we in this country may watch with complacency; it does not seriously involve the Fisheries question, and therefore does not, except in a minor degree, affect either England or Canada.

THB krimrose League appears to be a fair- weather institution, for there is little heard of it except in connection with fetes, and junketings, and out-door sports. There are worse things in the world of course than out-door jollification; but it is somewhat puzzling to know what that has to do with "loyalty, patriotism, and religion." There was a Primrose League Demonstration at Newton, on Saturday, which commenced with sports, was enlivened with fireworks, and ended in dancing. In the course of an address, Mr. ALFRED MORRIS, a district agent of the League, observed that "he wished to remind them that it was the knights and dames who subscribe to the Central Authority. It could not too openly be said that the associates were not called upon for one farthing of expendi- ture for the maintenance of tile Central Authority." We have all along been at a loss to understand how and why "Knights and Dames" were distinguished from ordinary members. But the murder is out; they are a privileged class, and their privilege is to pay whilst the ordinary members enjoy them- selves. One cannot, of course, expect to. be a "knight" or a " dame " for nothing; but it is just a little hard on these exalted personages that they should have to stump up for everything and every- body. CoUldn't the " associates " be advised to pay a trifle—say, 'a half-penny each towards the Central Authority, when sports, fireworks, and dancing are provided? It is net to be suggested that there would be nothing left of the Primrose League but the officials if there were anything to pay. Of course, if the object is to swell the num- bers, irrespective of cost to the "knights and dames," it might be worth considering whether it would not be advisable to add a pint of Wilderspool ale to the sports, fireworks, and dancing. There are people who will join any sort of League for a pint of ale, and especially if they know the pint is to be paid. for by" knights and dames" againd whom, at "in. tervals," they will be allowed to rub shoulders, Sir GILEERT GRBENALL, as a knight of the League might see to it that the ale was supplied at cost price by MOWS. GREENALL, WHITLEY,/ and Co., especially as the League is, after all, one for the maintenance of " loyalty, patriotism, and religion." There is to be sure one little difficulty in the Fay, and that is that some disagreeable Radical, who has not been invited to the sports, fireworks, and dancing, and who has not even had a taste of the ale, might, at an inconvenient time, say something to somebody about bribery and corruption. But, as the proverb has it—" As well be hung for a sheer; as a lamb," and the "lambs" are certainly being looked to. The "primrose path of dalli- ance is invariably delightful--that is until it be- comes "the primrose way to the everlasting bon- fire." What a pity it is that Shakespeare ' uses both phrases; it is like lmighing (in anticipation) at the Leaguers. But the "Knights and dames" never go too far; for they are "Knights and dames"; and besides, whatever the League may do in the way of encouraging sports, fireworks, dancing, and the drinking of Wilderspool ale, it, must never be forgotten that it is based upon "loyalty, patriotism, and religion."

STILL amongst the primroses and" his favourite flower." The other week we took upon ourselves to correct Mr. ROBERT DAVIES as to his coun- tenancing the error that the primrose was Lord BEACONSFIELD'S favourite flower. He has replied —after a fashion—to our brief comment. The local organ of the Primrose League reports Mr. Davies as follows: _ _ _

lie hapnened to say in speaking of the Primrose League—the objects of which had been so eloquently described by Mr. Wright—that, the primrose was Lord Beaconsfield's favourite flower, lie was told that the editor of the paper—who only recognised the green ray in the Irish prison and surveyed man- kind from China to Peru through Gladstone glasses —had written a kind of correction of what he (the speaker) said. He could not make much of that cor- rection from what he had heard, but the substance of what he had been told was that Lord Beaconsfield hated primroses bat liked peacocks, because they ate primroses, The ditor of the -"Examiner" went on further to say that her Gra- cious Majesty the Queen, who was not infallible they did not suppose she was quite the Pope of Rome—made a blunder in her grammar when she spoke of " his favourite flower," meaning the Prince Consort's favourite flower and not Lord Beacons- field's, lie knew—but he was not:much of a logi- cian, although he did know something of the ele- ments of that science —of a thing called non sequitur, where a person drew an inference -from certain remarks not warranted by them. But he would not go further into the matter that night, but would deal with it further at the next meeting. We must wait, we suppose, till the "next meet- ing". for the "kind of correction" which Mr. DAVIES has in preparation. Meantime, we would suggest that it would perhaps be as well if ho would take the trouhle to read what was said, and not depend upon "what he had been , told ;" because, as it happens, what he has been told is very much different from what was written. For instance, we did not say a single word about Her Majesty having "made a blunder in her grammar." Nor was it stated that Lord BBACONSFIELD "hated primrodes." What was affirmed was that his lordship had stated that "he preferred peacocks to primroses." Gran- ted that Mr. DAVIES jS not—as he modestly puts it —"much of a logician," he is still, we are quite sure, so familiar with " the elements of that science" as to be aware that a re- ply is not a reply which is an answer— not to what an opponent has said, but to some- thing which somebody else has imagined. We hope we shall be forgiven for failing to understand what Mr. DAVIES means by his reference to the "green ray in the Irish prison." A green ray in a prism would have been intelligible. Can it be that our townman's rhetoric as well as his logic is, for once, at fault? Or shall we conclude that this is another case in which someone has blun- dered?

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

St. Helens is in a very satisfactory condition as to health. For the past five weeks, the death rate has been 18.37 only. This is a great improvement upon the corresponding period for last year, when the rate of mortality was 22.1.9.

Whilst Mr, Stringer was preaching at the Vic- toria-road Wesleyan Chapel, Widnes, on Sunday night, the gas went out. It was a little awkward, of course, but Mr. Stringer could console himself with reflecting that he was not the first expounder of a text who had found himself "in the dark."

The "Pall Mall Gazette" describes what took ' place the other day at a seance, when the spirit of Thomas Carlyle was called upon by the medium. The messages received were about as much like Carlylese as chalk is like cheese. His spirit wis al- together spiritless—not even the ghost of him- self. ,

The RuneOm Rural Sanitary Authority are taking steps to close certain premises at Weston Point, which are deemed unfit for human habita- tion. The process is one that might be usefully applied in other places. If disease is to be kept under, to say nothing of stamping it out, there must be an abolition of its hotbeds.

"Truth" says:--"I learn that the Prince of Wales intends to join the Oddfellows, and he will probably be initiated into one of the Norwich lodges before the end of the year." It is rather a come down for His Royal Highness, is it not, to be- come a "hod-fellow," after ,having been for so many years a "master mason " ?

Bicyclists will take to the footpath, when the footpath is nice and the roadway is ugly. Henry Bednall was brought before the Newton Bench, on Saturday, for offending in this particular way. Ile pleaded that he had a "blazing lamp" on his machine; but the magistrates seemed to think it was a "burning shame" notwithstanding, and fined the trespasser one shilling and costs.

It is stated that hop-pickers are scarce in Kent. This is both a good sign and'a bad one. It means that the hop-growers will probably suffer a loss for lack of labour, but on the other hand it Means that the East-enders of London who usually do the picking are in better feather than usual. They would not neglect the hops if they had not a bet- ter job in hand.

From a return which is given in another column, it will be seen that Warrington has dis- tinguished itself; it is the most heavily rated borough in Lancashire. Wigan is placei first ,with a ratage of bs 8d in the pound; but, as the intes of Warrington have averaged bs ,10d for a period of thirty years, Wigan must give way. And what a feather it is in the cap of Warring- ton I

It is not generally known that women will be eligible for election as members of the new CountY Councils; but the Association for Women's Rights are aware of the fact, and they have under eon- sideration.the advisability of submitting four lady candidates fdr the London County Council. What can be done in the metropolis, can of,, course be done in the country. So" Walk up, ladies, walk up; the show 'a just a-going to begin."

The latest murder of wornen in the East-end of London, is absolutely fiendish in its atrocity. Murder most foul, as in the best it is, But this most foul, strange, and unnatural. It is no use blaming. the police.; they are human, and we may be sure they will do their best in such a case to discover the murderer. Still, there is a tendency to flag in the pursuit afteratime, and the offer of a reward of £lOO, by Mr. S. Montague, M.P., is to be welcomed as a powerful stimulant.

At Spalding, five clergymen, the Dean and Chap- ter of Lincoln, have keen struck off the voters' list because they were members of a corporate body. In another court several militiamen had to be struck off, .nuch as the Revisina Barrister dis- approved of having to take such a course. There is something very annoyino• and very absurd in citizens losing their votes through these legal dis- tinctions. We need manhood suffrage to do away with nonsense of this kind.

The weather has been bad, but not wholly bad. It has been full of variableness and shadows of turning. It was wet for the cricketers at the Oval, on Monday; and asdar north as Holbeek, near Leeds the Anglo-2nstralian match had to be abandoned. On the other hand, the weather on Monday was brilliantly tine at Ilfracombe. There it was one of those perfect days when "tee, and bird, and butterfly, were on their lightest wing." So there is weather and weather in England—small as it is.

It will be anything but creditable to the town of Warrington, if the band performances in the Park are abandoned for lack of funds. The music has been good, and the attendance has been large, but the collections have been ridiculously small. Why, and we repeat the question, should not the Town Council take the matter in hand? If they can see their way to voting money for bringing plaster coats from Italy, it would be no great strain upon them to vote a sum for the band performances.

It is in some degree reassuring to 'Aril on the authority of Sir Charles Wilson, and Sir Francis de Winton; both of whom have had considerable experience of Africa, that there is not as yet any cause for alarm respecting Stanley. When a fellow goes on the tramp, and gets to a place where the locomotive, post office, and telegraph are unknown, it is not unusual to lose sight of him for a time. There is still therefore hope of the daring explorer being in the land of the living: he takes his motto from " Marmion "—" On Stanley, On !"

Tight-lacing was under discuaiion at a moot- ing, the the other day, of tho British Association; and there was a good deal said for the nine hun- dred and ninety-ninth time as to its highly in- jurious effects. "Our Girls" will hear an echo of the speeches, but they will go on cultivatinc, wasp- like waists. They have somehow got it into their pretty heads that it improves their appearance; but if they could hear the occasional comments of "Our Boys" on the subject, they would have their doubts as to whether a very small waist was an ad- ornment to the human form divine.' That is a point worth thinking about, for they do want to please "Our Boys" after all. , ,

The Venus de Medici is a figure of about average size; it is ri.garded as perfection in the way of . proportion, and the waist is one of twenty-three inches. What would be thought of a sculptor who gave his statue a wasp-like waist? ITh handi- work would not be admired; and if an unnatur- ally small waist is objectionble in stone, it is not less objectionable in the flesh. "Our Girls" are making a mistake.. When the poet wrote—" Just an armful of heaven to enfold "—he had in his mind a waist, not of seventeen, but of twenty-three inches.

The Rev. John Robertson, of Stonehaven, has been preaching a rousing sermon. It would seem that there is little hope for those without the pale, for this Scotch clergyman says that even the " born communicant" is too often "the robber of God's heritage, the filcher of Judah's message, the doomed and deluded garroter of Christ's holy cove- nant, the unconverted, unsaved believer, the kirk- going child of the devil." Mr. Robertson appears to have had in his mind those—to quote Tenny- son— Who never naming God except for gain. So never took that u.eftil name in vain.

Mr. Michael Davitt is getting impatient, under the brutalities of the Coercion Act, but we do not see what he is to gain by resorting, as he threatens to do, to violent methods. Speaking at a Nation- alist denaonstration on Sunday, he said the alliance of the Nationalists with the English Liberals had proved a handcuff instead of a shield. But that is not the general opinion of Irishmen; and there can ben() question that, with constitutional agitation, the Coercion Act would disappear on Mr. Glad- stone's return to power. Unconstitutional agita- tion, if accompanied by outrage, would make the abolition of the act impossible; and as to the hand-
cuff Mr. Davitt might find that it Again encircled his wrist.

div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

THE WIDNES FOOTBALL CLUB RBFEREE.—Mr. Arthur Hufton has resigned the post of referee to the first team of the Widnes Football Club. SCALDED TO DEATH AT RIINCORN.—A child named James Taylor, son of a flatman, was on Wednesday playing on the foot-board of a boat when he fell into the cabin. In his fall he upset a kettle of boiling water 1 and was very seriously scalded. He died from his in- juries on Thursday morning. SINGTJLAR ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—Dr. Hutchinson, of Widnes, had a rather singular case under his treatment on Saturday. On that day a woman brought her little girl to his surgery, and on examination he found that the child had pushed a glass bead up one of her nostrils. Chloro- form had to be administered beforethe intruder could be removed. Tint NEW WIDNES WESLEYAN MINISTER.—On Sunday the Rev. T. Law, formerly of Ripon, who has been recently appointed to the Widnes Wesleyan Circuit, preached his first sermon at Hartland Chapel, Oakland-st., Widnes. The reverend gentleman, who occupied the pulpit at both the morning and the evening services, was very attentively listened to. SIAM:MAR DROWNING CASE AT 1117NCORN.-011 Satur- day Mr. J. E. Worsley, Coroner, held an inquest at Run-' corn on view of the body of a child named John Mahar, five years of age, son of a foreman at the lead works at the Sprinch, who on Thursday evening week fell into a tank of water at the works and was drowned. The jury found that the death was accidental. THE ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN COMMISSIONER.—It Will be remembered that last week M. J W. Lightburn, a member of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, was out driving, when his vehicle was upset and he was violently thrown to the ground. He sustained some- what serious injuries, but it is a pleasure to report that he is progressing favourably towards recovery. SCHOOL CENSUS AT RDNCORN.—SchooI Attendance Officers Bowery and Howard have during the week been busily engaged in taking a census of the number of children in Runcorn under thirteen years of age. It is nearly eight years ago since a census was taken, and at present there is no reliable information before the Board to afford guidance as to how many children the Board has control over. _ .

- MASONIC MEETING AT RUNCORN.—On Wednesday, the annual meeting of the Bridgewater Chapter, (No 758) was held at the Masonic Hall, Runcorn. The following officers were appointed.—Companions G. Bell, M.E.Z.: James White, P.Z.J.- J. Ashton, H; W, Mellor, P 2., P.P.G., P. 5.0. J., S.E., and treasurer; T. Kirkham, S. N.; T. H. Annett, P.S.O.J. The installation ceremony was performed by Companion Stevenson, P.Z. RUNCORN PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH. On Sunday, in celebration of the anniversary of the Sunday Schools connected with this church, sermons were preached morning and evening by the Rev. E. Parry, M.A., of Newtown. There were good congregations, and the sermons were listened to with interest. In the afternoon a service of song entitled "There's help at hand," was rendered by the choir and scholars. A collection was made at the close of each service in aid bf the Sunday schools. THE ESTATE OF MR. W. A. :RHODRS, OF RIINCOIIN.— An arrangement has been made in this matter by whiph the estate of Mr. Rhodes, carrier, of High-st., Runcorn. has been assigned for the benefit of creditors. It is shown that the liabilities are £1.128 4s Bd., £203 of , which are secured, and the remainder £9lB 4s Bd.is due to unsecured creditors; whilst the assets are put down at £497 3s sd. The trustee appointed is Mr. G. J. Knight, chartered accountant, and the ;following have been ap-. pointed a Committee of Inspection :—Messrs. .7. Meadow.' croft (Runcorn), B. Kniveton (Runcorn). lt. Lewis (Wad.. nes), J. J. W. Potter (Runcorn), and J. Howard: DROWNED IN A WASH-TUB AT WIDNES.--The death of Francis Wallace, a boy of a little over three years of age, formed the subject of an inquiry held on Saturday by the coroner of South-West Lancashire, Mr. S. Brighouse, at Widnes. The lad, who was the son of Francis James Wallace. labourer, of 28, Davies-st., West Bank, Widnes, left his father's house on Thursday evening with his brother, aged five years, to play in the street. About seven o'clock-the mother went out to look for them, for the purpose of putting them to bed, but ohe was miss- ing. The neighbourhood was searched, but the child could not befound. Mrs. Wallace sent for her husband from his work, and he also made search for the boy, and at length found him in the backyard, head foremost in a washing-tub. He took the deceased out of the tub, but found life was extinct. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." RUNCORN Smoot Ron.—Aß adjourned meeting Of the Board was held at the Greenway-road schools on last evening week Present Mr. J. Pritchard (chairman), Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs F. A. Lake, E. Imison, S. C. Beckett, and Mr. George Moss (clerk.) The Board inspected the school playgrounds, which are cavered with cinders, and are in a. rough state, causing much dirt to be carried into the schools. After consider- ing various systems of paving, it waa decided to adopt the granitic stonefaced pavement of Mr. Alfred Walker, London and Leeds, costing 2s 9d per square yard. -This pavement is largely used all over the country, and has recently been adopted by the Liverpool School Board, be- ing guaranteed good at the end ot 20 years.—lt was also decided to apply to the Education Department for the sanctionto borrow the sum of £l5O from the Public Works Loan Commissioners to pay for the pavement This was the whole of the business. ' WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of this committee was held at the public offices, Widnes, last evening. The chair vial occupied by Mr. H. Wade Deacon, and there were, also present—Dr. O'Keefe, Messrs. R. H. Davis, E. Carey, J. Morrison, W. Sadler, T. H. Parkhurst. J. Midwood, S. Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk) and Miss Proctor (librarian.)—The com- mittee passed accounts amounting to the sum of £9O 6s. —The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board, which was worded as follows :—" I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the re- ceipt of your letter of the 11th inst., and to state that they have considered the application for their sanction to the expenditure by the WidnesLocal Board of the sum of £2O, for the provision of the proposed free lectures of a scientific and educational character. The Board do not consider that the Local Authorities' Expenses Act of 1877 was intended to enable them prospectively to sanction expenditure of a recurring nature." It was dei- cided to again communicate with the Local Government Board, with the object of inducing them to allow the ex- penditure—Miss Proctor, the librarian, reported that during August 4,439 books were borrowed from the library, that number being an increase of 166 on the corresponding month of last year. The total daily atten- dance had been 12,09, an increase ef 578 on the corres- ponding month of last year. The average daily atten- dance had been 481.—This was all the business. RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS —A meeting of this body was held on Thursday, at the Town Hall, when there were present—Messrs. W. Fisher (chairman), Dobson, H.. 7. Grice, E. Timmins,W. Hankinson, E. Imi- son W. Mellor' P. Smith, W. R: Was.s, J. Pritchard, S. Tay‘or, F. A. Lake, F. Wis wall, W. Whittaker, W. H. Linaker klaw clerk), E. Marshall .(secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor).—The Chairman said that the ex- penses of the returning officer in connection with the recent election amounted to £l3 24 31—Mr. Lake pro- posed that a cheque be drawn on the treasurer for the amount, and on the motion being seconded by Mr. Tay- lor, it was carried.—The committees were appointed for the ensuing 'year as follows: Canal Boats and General Purposes: Messrs. Dobson, Grice, Smith, Whittaker, Hankinson, Taylor, White, and W. R. Wass.—Highways I and Building Committee : This committee consists of the ' whole of the members of the Board.—Finance: Messrs. J. Meadowcroft, J. W. Lightburn, J. Pritchard, P. Speak- man, E. linison, W. Mellor, S. Taylor, and J. Dobson.— Parliamentary and Legal : Messrs. I'. Speakman, Pritch- ard. Meadowcroft, Taylor, Lightburn, Once, and Lake. —Health Committee: Messrs. J. W. Liglitburn, H. J. Grice, W. Mellor, W. R. Wass, J. Dobson, .1. Meadow- croft, F. Wiswall, and P. Smitlx.—Waterloo Bridge : Messrs. Pritchard, Taylor, Lake, Timmins, Speakmaa, White, and Wiswall.—Library Committee The old coin- mittee was re-appointed, with the substitution of Mr. Pritchard's name for that of Mr. Frith. STunas• Funarrerts CREAM.—For giving a brilliant gloss to all kinds of mahogany and French polished furniture with half ths usual labour, use Stubbs' Furniture Cream. Sold in bottles, Li., 21., ant 34.--Isaao Stubbs, Lowlands-road, Run erza.—.flebet.

GRRICNWAY-ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS, RUNCORN.—The an- nuli treat of the scholars attending this school was held yesterday, in a field off Norman-road, lent by Mr. Ackerley. Fes, RAL SEISSION AT WIDNES.—The Rev. Hugh Owens on Sunday evening preached a sermon in memory of " the late Mr. Edward Roberts, of Frederick-st., Widnes, at the Lacey-st. Welsh Wesleyan Chapel. MARRIAGE AT WEASERHAM.—The marriage of Miss Edith Mary Fligson, daughter of Mr. J. Higson of Oak= mere Hall, to the lion. J. W. Mansfield, was solemnized at Weaverham Church on Tuesday. ALLEGED THEFT' BY A WIDNES SERVANT.— At the Widnes Police Court on Tuesday, a woman named Ma- tilda liarnish, who belongs to Chesterfield, was remanded ! until Monday next on a charge of having stolen several articles from her employer, Robert Yearsley. MISSION SERVICES AT WIDNES.—On Sunday evening Wesleyan Mission services were commenced at Maas Hall, Simm's Cross, Widnes, the service being conduc- ted by Mr. J. Matey and other friends of the moryement. There was a good attendance. Last year the mission services were very sneessful. A CONNUBIAL SQUABBLE AT WIDNES.—A marriedcouple who live in Peel-st Widnes, had a disagreement on Sun- day morning. The result was that the husband struck his wifc.- with a stick, cutting her left cheek. A Widnes policeman, who is a member of the St. John's Ambulance Association, staunched the wound, and the injured woman was afterwards attended to by Dr. Hutchinson. ACCIDENT TO A WIDNES LABOURER.—A labourer named Corrigan, who lives in Nelson-st., was at work at one of the chemical works in Widnes, on Wednesday, when a pick that he was wielding rebounded and struck him on the neck. The pick penetrated to the extent of about half an inch, and just missed one of the main arteries. TIA injured man, who was attended by Dr. Hutchinson, is now progressing favourably. A NEGLECTFUL FATHER AT RUNCORN.—Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, a farm labourer named Joseph Lightfoot was charged with having neglected his two children, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Union. It was stated that the ratepayers had been put to an expense of £9 odd in maintaining the defendant's children.—Defendant offered to repay that amount at the rate of 45 per week, and the offer was accepted. • A WIDNES Row.—During the early hours of Sun- day morning a man named Kerwin. who lives in Peel- st., Widnes, had a quarrel with his wife, during which he inflicted a wound on her cheek by striking her with a stick. It happened that Constable Holbrook, who is a member of the St. John's Ambulance Assoc4t- ion, was near at hand at the time, and he staunched the blood flowing from the wound, which was an inch long and half an inch deep. Dr. Hutchinson afterwards attended the injured woman. SALVATION ARMY FUNERAL AT RUNCORN. The TO. , mains of Mrs Elizabeth Swindells, of 3, Cross-st., a mem- ber of the Salvation Army, were interred at the Runcorn General Cemetery, on Wednesday. The deceased was 84 years of age at the time of her death, and was much respected. In the funeral procession were a number of the members of the Salvation Army, all wearing either white bandages or scarves, and the service at the grave was conducted by Captain Seymour, of the Wi4ms contingent, who was assisted ',II. Runcorn offiens of the army. A WIDNES MINISTER AND CONGREGATION IN THE DARK. -Kr_ Stringer, who preached at Victoria-road Wesleyan Chapel, Widnes, on Sunday evening, was, together with his contregation, somewhat suddenly disconcerted by the gas suddenly ceasing to give its wonted light. This mishap, it is stated, was consequent on the defective state of the meter. At the time of the occurrence the Preacher had got about half way through his remarks, and it became necessary for him to cut his sermon very short. The last hymn was sung in darkness, the preacher reading the verses by the flickering light of matches which he happened to have in his posses- sion. KICKING A POLICEMAN AT RUNCORN. On MoniAay,

at-th-e-lin-ncOrti Petty S-elsi.C;ile, a man named Martin Casey was charged with haying been drunk and disor- derly, and with having assaulted Constable Ratcliffe, on the Bth mat, whilst that officer was in the execution of his duty. The affair happened in Church-St. The policeman was near the Fleetwood Arms when he saw the prisoner, who was drunk, behaving in a disorderly manner. He advised prisoner to go home but that per- son declined to do so. The officer then placed prisoner under arrest, and in consequence was struck in the face and kicked on the legs by Casey, who was with difficulty removed to the lock-up. For the two offences Casey was ordered, to pay afine of 20s and costs, or in default, to .go to prison for a month. ALLEGED ASSAULT AT WIDNES.—At the Petty Sessions at Whines, on Thursday, a woman named Eliza Glee.: heen was summoned for having used threats to Ellen Roberts, who keeps a shop in Caroline-st. It was alleged that the defendant told Mrs. Roberts that she would cut her hehd off, and used other unpleasant language. She was ordered to find surety for her good behaviour for the next three months, or suffer imprisonment in default. Mrs. Roberts also charged a youth named George Brady, who lodges with the previous defendant, with -having assaulted her. It was alleged that he struck'her a violent blow on the side of the head. Mr. Knowles, appeared for the prosecution. After a number of witeessee had given testimony on both sides, the defendant was fined ss, and 12s 6cl costs. KICKING A PARAMOUR AT WIDNES.—On Thursday, at Whines Petty Sessions, a rough looking man named Aaron Clayton, was brought up in custody on a charge of having, on the day before, assaulted Margaret Molyneaux. Complainant told the magistrates that she had been hying with the prisoner ae his wife. On the 'day in question he quarrelled with her, and seizing her by the hair, put her in a corner and "abused her shame- fully." She had many a time` requested prisoner to keep away from her. After knocking her down he thrashed her terribly about the heal and hdv. She was black and blue all over. See had no brought witnesies, as she thought her face would be sufficient evidence. The Bench fined prisoner 40s and kosts. or. in default of pay- ment, a months imprisonment with hard labour. THE RENOWNED RUICORE RELISH 13 prepared from the choicest herbs, roota, and spices, which retialer it of most valuable assistance in the digestion of food.--Preparerl and .sold wholesale by Isaac Stubbs. Lowlands-revel. Ituuciern.— Airs. • MIPLACED SYMPATHY AT WIDNES.-Wiltialll McNamara, of Marsh-st, Widnes, was brought up at the Police Court in that town, on Monday, on a charge of having deserted his three children, who on the 29th of May last became chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot. Union. All the children are under sixteen years of age. Pri- soner secured an order for admission to the Workhouse, and, on condition that he would come back next day, he was allowed to go in search of work. He did not return, and since his departure the sum of £8 14s 4d had been expended on the maintenance of his children. The Guardians, it was stated, had out of pure sympathy let him leave the Workhouse. It was a privilege that had been accorded him. The Magistrates sentenced McNa- mara to undergo imprisonment for two months, with hard labour. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN PLATMAN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, John Mason, a flatman, was charged on remand with having assaulted Harriet Osborne, a young girl under the age of 16 years, on the 3rd inst. He was further charged with abducting Emily Fishwick, who is under 18 years of age, against her will on the same date. Osborne and Fishwick, ac- cording to the evidence given, were together on the day named, when they saw the prisoner, wh I asked them to go for a row an the river in a small boat They got into the boat, and were rowed to the fiat True Briton, of which the prisoner is the captain. Prisoner took the girls to Spoke, and promised each of them a new dress on their return to Widnes. On the way he assaulted the girls, and afterwards brought them back to Weston Point, where he left them. Mr. C. T 'Peters, solicitor, of Widnes, defended, and the case, which lasted several hours, was adjourned till yesterday, when Masoe was committed for trial. AN UNSATISFACTORY LODOER AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, a married woman named Catherine Smith was summoned for stealing some sheets from a dwelling-house where she lodged, with her hus- band.—Catherine Burns. a widow, 21, Major Cross-st., said on Saturday, the 28th July, the prisoner and her husband took lodgings with her. Witness supplied them with the two sheets produced, together with other bed- clothes. Prisoner left her house without giving notice. and witness found the two sheets missing. They were worth about as. Prisoner denied having stolen them, saying that the prosecutor lent them to her to pawn. as she was short of money.—The manager to Mr. Neild. pawnbroker, said that on the 13th August prisoner went to his shop and pledged one of the sheets and a jacket for Is 3d, saying they belonged to her. On the 3rd Septem- ber prisoner. went again and pledged the other sheet for 60.--,Prisnner said she was guilty of pawning the sheets, but not of stealing them, assuring the Bench that they were lent to her.—P.C. Massey received the woman into,, custody from the Walton police on Saturday, and when' he charged her with the offence she saieu," I didn't steel them ; she lent me the sheets to pawn. --The magis- trates considered the offence proved, and fined the pri- soner 20s, or 14 days. ' A SEERHOUSE QUARREL.—On Wednesday, at Runcorn Police Court, Alfred Holmes, an engine driver, was charged with haying been disorderly at the Village Inn, Halton, on the 21,st of July, and with refusing -to quit when requested. Mr. Whitfield. the landlord, gave evi- dence showine that the prisoner with others went to the Village Inn. Halton, on the day named. As they ap- peered to be, in drink, he refused to supply them wittil beer. They then created a great disturbance in the house, and, although witness repeatedly requested them to leave. they declined to do so. Witness afterwards went into the pantry, and the men fastened him in, and on Woe liberated he discovered that a hoard had been taken away. Witness sent for the police, and on Con- stable Fryer arriving, he went to the Elephant and Castle beerhouse, which is a short distance away, where the men were found. They were taken into custody, but were afterwards released, summonses being issued against them. Two of the men, • named Lambert and Jones. answered the summonses, and were each fined; but Holmes went away, after having told the prosecutor that if he summoned .him he would "pay him by the mile," meaning that he would .walk out of the neigh- bourhood. Prisoner was fined 10s and 17s 4d costs, or 14 days' imprisonment in default:
Itrk

- Fox TERRIER CODRSING AT WIDNES.—The following is I the result of the coursing contests concluded on Satur- day at Millfield ground :—First round : Canagher's Cash beat Jones's Nell, Harrison's Prince beat Edwardson's Pop, Smith's Lill beat Middleton's Soda Water' Edward- son's Pop beat Smith's Tea Rose, Middleton's Daisy beat Canagher's Push Along, Smith's Tea Rose beat Edward- son's Pop, Morris's Yacht beat Twist's Lady, Canagher's Cash beat Edwardson's Trix, Bin's Trap a bye. Second ' round : Cash beat Trap, Prince beat Yacht, Cash beat Tea Rose, Daisy beat Pop, Lill a bye. Third round: Print beat Daisy, Cash beat Lill. Deciding round: Cash beet Prince and won the first prize, £3 lOs ; Prince and Cash divided 30s, second and third prize. TEEM AT RONCORN.—At the Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, a navvy named Thomas Brown was charged with having stolen a coat,' value lOs 6d, the pro- perty of Harriet Dodd, clothier, of Church-st., on the 10th inst. Complainant saw the prisoner on Monday afternoon, about four o'clock, in an entry opposite her shop, tryinc, to put the coat on, and she went to him and took it from him. The coat was hanging on a nail in front of the shop five minutes previously. She charged the prisoner with having stolen it, and he said that he was in drink, otherwise he would not have taken it. Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was fined 20s, or 14 days' imprisonment in default of payment.—At the same court, on Thursday, Patrick Duffy was charged, on re- mand, on suspicion of having stolen a pair of boots, the property of someone unknown. Inspector O'Donnell explained that the prisoner offered the boots in pledge al a pawnshop in the town, and the assistant, having his suspicions aroused, called in the police, with the result ' that the prisoner was taken into custody. As no infor- mation could be obtained as to the ownership of the ' boots prisoner was discharged. WIDNES INTER-WORKS FOOTBALL COMPETITION.-011 Thursday afternoon a match was played between the , teams of the Alkali No. 1 and Messrs. Pilkington's. The kicleoff. WaS at a quarter to six. Notwithstanding the splendid play of Clark, which has gained him such a wide., reputation, the team he was assisting got the worst of it, they not gaining a point. Clark made some good runs, often taking the leather more than half the length " of the field Farrell for the Alkali's obtained a try, but ' failed at goal. Near the close Gordon grounded the ball , and secured another try, which Farrell amended by land- . ing a geol. Finally the game stood at one goal, one try, and four miners for Alkali tonil. The teams were :—Alkali: Back, D Burton; three-quarters, Gordon, Donoghue J. Hurtles; half, Farrell (captain) and Beesley; forwards, Hughes, Gandy, 4. Currie, W. Wright, T Whaling, .1. Dolan, R. Roberts, J. Morecroft, and T. Gregory Pil- kington's : Back, Hewitt; half backs, Wilkinson and Bryan; three-quarters, Clarke, Bell, and Glansey ; for- wards, Holt, Smith, Pa.isey, Burke, Lea, Johnson, Dutton, Sauce, and Brennan W. Kiddie and J. Parkinson were the umpires, and H. Wilcock was the referee

- BOWLING AT HOST'S Cuoss.—A shilling handicap sweep- stake (with one guinea added by Mr. Hilditch, pro- prietor), was played on the groud of the Hunt's Cross , Hotel, on Thursday afternoon. The game was 15 up, limit 7. There were forty-four entries, and Mr. J. Stone, of Widnes, officiated as handicapper. The result was sthat the first prize. 21s, second. lOs 6d, and third, 7s 6d. were divided by Messrs. W J Moreland, It Wright, and W Ince. In the evening a meeting was held at the hotel, under the presidency of Mr a Rideal, solicitor for the purpose f, forming a bowling club. This was done, and the following officers were elected :—President, Mr W. J Moreland; honorary presidents, Dr McDonnell, Dr McCambridge, Messrs G Rideal, W Gerrard, R Wright, J Milner, and W Dainteth ; vice-presidents, Mr H A Richards and Mr J Stone; treasurer. Mr H flilditch•, secretary. Mr J Stone„. committee, Messrs P Price, W H Turner, NV Melvin, W Wright, T Dean, W. Hunter, and .1 Lecomber ; handicappers, Messrs P Price, W J More- land, and J Stone. A code of rules were submitted and Passed, and prizes to the value of £2O was arranged to be competed for xext season. .

, FLAT AOIIBEIURS ar WIDNES. - On Tuesday, at the Widnes Police Court, a flatman, named, Joseph Gillot, of no fixed residence, was charged with having broken into a flat called the "Four Brothers," lying the Wid- nes canal, and having stolen several articles, the pro- perty of Walter Abel, flatman, and Arthur Prentice, flatman, both of Runcorn. The evidence given by these two men was to the effect that on the night of the 31st ult, about eight o'clock, they made their flat secure, fastening the hatchway and cabin with chains ; but next morning, on returning to the boat between time and ten o'clock, they found that the cabin and hatchway had been broken into, and the articles named stolen.—rPolice- constable Holbrook prOve:l that he apprehended the prisoner. Ile took hint to the police station, and in re- ply to the charge he said, "I took thestrousers, knitted jacket, and a tin of salmon. 1 took no flute." He was wearing the trousers, waistcoat, and knitted jacket pro- duced. Witness had since found the flute in a Liverpool pawnshop. Prisoner was committed to • the Quarter Sessions for trial.—Prisoner was further charged with haying, on the 22nd Oeltober, 1888, stolen 2s, the property of Thomas Perry, flatman, 28, Mersey-road, Widnes.—Prosecutor stated that on the 22nd October, 1888, his flat, Mite, was lying in the Widnes Canal. The prisoner came and asked him for a job, and he took him on board out of charity, because he had nowhere to go. Witness had 22s in his trousers, which were hung in the cabin and while his back was turned the prisoner, who had cabin, cleaning the cabin, ran away: Witness at once examined the trousers, and found that the money was gone.—Police-constahle Holbrook said that when he charged the prisoner with the theft he replied, " Old Perry owed mu money, and for that reason I took the moneY."—He was sent to the Quarter Sessions for trial on this charge also.

DEATH OF MR. JOHN WHITE, OF WIDNES.—MT. John White, foreman of the caustic department at Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s chemical works, Widnei, died on Tuesday evening, at his reeidence in Hutchinsou-st., Widnes, at the age of 62 years. The debeased had for thirty years occupied the posi- tion of foreman at the works in question, and he had only been confined to his bed for two days pre- vious to his death, which was due to inflammation of the lungs. The late Mr. White, who was highly respected, leaves nine children to regret his loss. His mortal remains were yesterday interred at Farnworth. • TECHNICAL Enucs.rrosr.The list of successful candidates in the examinations in connection with the" City and Guilds of London Institute, for the advancement of Technical education," includes the name of Mr. Henry Budge, of St. Helens, who has passed in the gas manufacture department. GOOD Wawa FOR TRE DOGS. —Some satisfaction has been given to the owners of dogs in the county of Chester by the announcement tit the withdrawal of the Rabies Order, under which dogs have had to bemuzzled all summer. Power is reserved to the police to seizenny dog which they may suspect to be suffering from rabies. "NEW INFALLIBLE TURF SYSTEM."—This is the title of a little work issued by "An Eminent New- market Correspondent," and is an explanation of what appears to bb a safe and reliable system for individuals interested in horse-racing. Its concise- ness is a recommendation; and the publication is one calculated to secure a large sale among the sporting classes. LANCASHIRE SESSIONS.—The annual general ses- sions for the county of Lancaster were held on Thursday, at Preston. when the Earl of Derby was elected chairman and Mr. J. T. Ilibbert vice-chair- man for the ensuing year. Considerable reference was made to the Local Government Act, and Sir U. J. Kay-Sh uttleworth, M.P., made a statement on the subject. THE COUNTY SHOW AT LANCASTER.—The receipts from the three days' show last week at Lancaster have been much better than. was anticipated. The total amount taken was ..£1,406. This is about .£196 less than was received from the same sources at Manchester last year, when fonr days were devoted to the show. Had the weather been fine at Lancaster on the first day there is no doubt that the receipts would have been considerably in- creased. THE COST OF HOLDING INQUEBTS.-IProm the just issued accounts of the County Treasurer, it appears that during the year ended 31st May last Mr. S. Brighouse, West Derby coroner, held 562 inquests and travelled 6,563 miles, at a cost of £1,242 as 44, including ' his salary of .£900; Mr. F. Smith, manor of Prescot, 7, at a cost of .£'2s 19s 6d ; and Mr. Buckton, the coroner for the manor of Hale, held not a single inquest, but got his salary of XI. BOWLING Mkretr.—The Hunt's Cross bowling match, in which 64 competitors competed for prizes of the value of ..£l2 16s, has now been completed. William Gleave, of Warrington, won the first prize, £5; William Ice, of Widtieli, carried off the second prize, £2 ; the third and fourth prize, 15s each, fell to W. Baines, Old Swan, and J. Shaw, of Warring- ton. At the conclusion of the match a game for three teas was played between Messrs. A. Parkes and J. Stone, both of Widnes, when the latter won by one point, 21 to 20. JOURNALISTS' MEETING AT CHESTER. The quarterly meeting of the Liverpool district of the National Association of Journalists was held at Chester, on Saturday, when there was a large and representat ve gathering ot pressmen from the towns forming the district Warrington was represented by Messrs. G. W. Murdoch, W. Bowen, James Law- ton, 11. Isherwood, and Harrison. At the busi- ness meeting in the evehing the Secretary reported that the district had now 601110 78 members, which would be made into 104 by the election of 26 candi- dates he had to propose for election that night. They would then be, he.laelieved, premier district in the country after London. He reported the exten- sion of the district so as to include Warrington and St. Helens. It was decided to call the new sub- district "The Warrington and St. Helens." Other business having been disposed of., the proceedings terminated

3 VACANT CHURCH LiviNGs.—There are at present - four livings vacant in the diocese of Liverpool, 1 namely :—St. Luke's, Bold-st, Altcar, Hale .vood, and 5 St. Peter's. Warrington. This is a rare event. DANCASHIRR SITHMARY JURISDICTION' Counts.— The amount of fees and fines, and salaries of inagis- , trates' clerks, in the various petty, sessional divi- sions of the county, for the year ended 31st May. have just been published in the County Treasurer's accounts. The local statistics are as follows : Prescot Division —Prescot and Widnes: Fees and 'tines, £BBl 28 6d, salary of Mr. C. Spenceley, £B5O. St. Helens: Fees and fines, £99 10s 3d, and salary of Messrs. Spencely and Brewis (15 months), £125. Warrington Division—Legh : Fees and fines, £795 125, and salary of Messrs. Marsh and Son, £650. Warrington and Newton-le-Willows : Fees and fines, £383 19s, and salary of Messrs. Buckton and Nicholson, £350. MiNnits' Watuss.—lt is stated that the miners of South-West Lancashire, and probably the other coal producing counties pf England. are demanding an increase of ten per cent, upon their wages. At a meeting of the Federation in Manchester recently, it was decided to call a national conference for the purpose of getting all the counties to co-operate with Lancashire in their endeavour to obtain an in- crease. With a view to ascertaining the feeling of the miners in this district, Mr. Thomas Glover, the St. Helens miners' agent, has called several meetings of the men, who generally appeared to be in favour of notices, asking for the increase, being sent in as early as possible. Whether the other districts go in for the increase 'or not, there appears to be no doubt, that the South-West Lancashire miners will make the demand for the increase, to which they consider they are entitled. FURIOUS DRIVING AT Nsw2olv.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Colonel George ,McCorquodale, Messrs. R. Houghton, T. ,J. Gillespie, A. C. 3fcCorquedale, and IV. F. Gooch, William Dixon, of Newton, was summoned for furiously dri- ving a horse and cart at Newton, on the 24th ult.— Defendant pleaded not guilty.—P.C. Spencer stated that about four o'clock on the afternoon of the date named he was in High-st., near the Post Office, when he saw the defendant coming along the road furiously driving a horse and. cart. There were three children in the road and if he had not pulled them out of the way the defendant would have run over them. He was going at the rate of 10 or 12 miles an hour, and he did not seem to care for any- thing. Witness shouted to him, but he took no no- tice.—The defendant said the horse was an aged one and could not go more than six miles an hour. The Bench imposed a fine of 2s 6d and costs.

WILL OF TUB LA.TB DOWAGBR BARONESS GERARD. Probate of the will, with a codicil made the 20th June last, of the Right Hon. Harriet Dowager Baroness Gerard, of Twryford Abbey, Ealing, who died on July 20th, and was the eldest daughter of the late Mr. Edward Clifton, of Lytham, has been granted to • the executors—her nephew, Mr. Frederick Gerard, of Kinwarton House, Warwick, and Sir John Law- son, Bart., of Brough Hall, Caterick, Yorkshire—to each of whom the testatrix bequeathed £lOO, to Lord Gerard £l,OOO, to her sister (Miss Charlotte Clifton) .£lOO, and to her daughters (the Hon. Monica Mary Oliphant and the Hon. Katherine Frances Gosselin) her jewellery, furnitdre, and household effects. All the residue of her property the testatrix devised and bequeathed in equal shares to her son, the Hon. Robert Joseph Gerard, and her said two daughters, but as to the share of Mrs. Oli- phant in trust, subject to her appointment, or in de- fault of appointment, to her for life, and on her decease for division amongst her children. The value of Lady Gerard's personal estate has been declared for probate at £29,321 is 2d.

MEDICAL OFFICERS OF HEALTH AT CARRINGTON Moss.—A number of members and associates of the North-western Branch of the Society of Medical Officers of Health and one or two friends paid a visit on Thursday to the Carrington Moss Estate of the Manchester Corporation, to inspect the sys- tem of dealing with that portion of the sewage of Manchester which is collected at the Water- at. yard. The party consisted of Dr. Tatham, Salford; Dr. Niven, Oldham; Dr. Hughes, Ash- ton-under-Lyne; Dr. Gornall, Warrington; Dr. Barr, Bury; Dr. Graham, Middleton; Rhodes. Glossop; Dr. Smith, Woodley ; Dr. Bower, Macclesfield; Dr. Adams, Runcorn; Dr. Jordan, Heaton Chapel; Dr. Fox, Mid-Cheshire; Mr. S. L. Helm, of the Manchester and Salford Sanitary Association; Dr. F. M Pierce, Mr. J. Corbett, and Mr. H. M. Hobdey. The visitors were accompanied by Mr. Alderman Schofield, chairman of the Health Committee, and were subsequently joined by Mr. Alderman Windsor. chairman of the Carrington Estate Sub-committee.. Mr. M'Connell, manager of the estate, was in attendance, and gave much in- teresting information about the treatment of the soil, the crops grown, &c The party returned for tea to the Wind-mill Inn, Carrington, where a vote of thanks was passed. to Alderman Schofield, on the motion of Dr. Hughes, seconded by Dr. Barr. MYsTratiouS DEATH IN RAINHILL ASYLUM.—At Rainhill Asylum. on Wednesday, Mr. Brighouse held an inquest on the body cf a female patient named Frances IPKee, aged eighty-three years,who formerly resided in Court 3, Ltanrwst-street, Liver- pool, but who was admitted to the institution on December 13, 184.—Annie Roby. the nurse in charge of No. 2 Ward, stated that about two o'clock in the afternoon of the 4th inst. she saw the de- ceased in the gallery, but an hour later she was ly- ing on the floor of the lavatory a few yards away. She complained of pain in the stomach, and was at once put to bed. It was the day but one following when the medical attendant found she had broken her thigh bone. It was within the regulations of this ward for apatient to go into the lavatory with- out an attendant.—Annie Oliver said she. took the deceased into the lavatory, and went for another patient. On returning, the woman was on the floor with nurse Elliott standing by her.—Mr. George P. Symes, resident medical officer, stated that he visi- ted the woman when he made his rounds the same night. He examined her, and asked her if any- thing beyond the pain complained of was the mat- ter. She said no. Two days later his attention was called to a bruise on the thigh, and he found it broken. The woman practically had been dying for months, but he had no doubt the shock from this fracture was the finishing touch. Another patient named Meadows might have pushed her, but she would not do it maliciously. There were blankets on the floor. Death took place on Tnesday.—The Coroner said there was no evidence t o show how the injury was received, but it undoubtedly hastened death. The jury returned an open verdict in accor- dance with the coroner's remarks.

An open verdict has been returned at the incruest rela- tive to the death of George Harrod, captain of the sail- ing vessel Lily, who was found lifeless in' West Avenue. Sunderland, a few days ago. Our advice is consult him. throw away your life-torturing trusses, be cured and happy. Don't procrastinate till he leaves England and ever after lament it. Be prompt, send 65 for his books of American and English cures and endore menta. and inform yourselves.—Adrt. BRITISH ASSOCIATION.—This Association closed its meetings on Wednesday. Three sections met which had not disposed of the papers before them on Tuesday. In one—the Economic Science Section—the whole question of over-population was raised, some of the speakers ex- pressing great anxiety for the future of the country from this point of view, and urging the working classes to re- , f rain from early and improvident marriages and from drink. The Mechanical Science Section discussed some proposals for an improved description of underground railway worked by electric motors. At the general com- mittee meeting various grants were voted for the promo- tion of science. The attendance at Bath was reported as 1,984. At a subsequent general meeting of members votes of thanks were passed to the Mayor awl Corpora- tion and to the local secretaries and treasurers, d:c.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. Margaret Didham and Thomas Farrell, residents of Hill-st. were charged by P.C. Monaghan with having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st. on the previous evening and were each fined 5s and costs. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alder- man Harrison, and Councillor John Pierpoint. DRUNKE,VNEIS.—The following cases were disposed of for this offence :—Thomas Cmhan, in the Market-place, on Saturday, fined as, including costs; John Ryan, in Bridge-st., on Saturday night, fined ss, including costs; Mary Swift, in Buttermarket-at., on the previous even- ing, finens and costs; Jane Bentley, in Rylands-st., ' on Sunday evening, fined ss, including costs; Julia. Shields, in Green's court, on the 4th September. fined 53 and costs; Mary Jae Clifton, in Naylor-st., on the Ist Sept., fined ss, including costs. STRIKING A WOMAN.—Henry Wilson, Chrimes's Yard, was charged with having disturbed the peace by assault- ing Mary Swift in Scotland-road on Saturday evening. The case having been proved, defendant was bound over in two sureties of •£lO to keep the peace for six months. SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A SHOPKEEPER.—Edward Burke, Haydock-st., was charged with having been drunk and , disorderly in Winwick-et., on Saturday evening and also with assaulting John Underwood. Complainant said that defendant came into his shop—a fried fish shop— and asked for some chip potatoes. As he was being served without the slightest provocation he struck com- plainant in the face, causing blcod to flow.—The Bench considering that the assault was most savage and un- provoked committed the defendant tp gaol for two months, with hard labour, without the option of a fine. AN UNLUCKY COLOUR.—A lad named Patrick Kenny, was charged with having played cards for money, on Friar's Green, on Sunday afternoon. P.C.'s Critchley and Monoghan gave evidence in support of the charge, mentioning that defendant was easily identified by his red hair.—The Bench imposed a fine of 2s ed including costs. A Row.—Catherine Farrell, Hill-st. ; Bridget Farrell, Hill-st.; and Bridget Farrell. Angel-yard, were all sum- moned for having been fighting in on the 6th Sept. The charge being considered proved defendants were each ordered to keep the peace for six months in sums of £5. DISMISSED.—Arthur Appleton, a respectably dressed lad, living at 7, Baxter-st., was charged with having thrown stones, to the danger of passengers, in Mill-lane, on the 2nd September. Evidence for the defendant was, however, called, and the case was dismissed. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor R. W. Francomb. BEGGING.—James Bryan, a tramp, was charged with having asked alms in Church-st., on Monday. • It was his first appearance, and he was dismissed with a cau- tion 4 WEDNESDAY.—IIefore Mr. R. Garnett. STREET DlSORDER.—Margaret McLoughlin and Eliza- beth Harrison, residents in Dial-st., were convicted of disorderly conduct in the street on the previous night, and were each committed to prison for a month •\ with hard labour. FISIDAY.—Before Mr. John White, Alderman Harrison, and Dr. Gornall. 'Pitt tinclorno NITISANCE.—EmanueI Mulligan, tramp, Was committed to prison for seven days for having beg- ged in Buttermarket-st., on the previous evening.— Thomas Mochan, for a similar offence, when drunk at the same time and place, was fined 109 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. AN ABSENTEE.—Peter Henrette, described as a musi- cian, was charged with having been absent from thelBBB training of the Royal Scots Militia, at Glencorse, and was remanded until Monday for inquiries. SANEST BRIDGES SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—The following cases were brought forward by Mr. Basil Shearer on be- hale of the Sankey Bridges School Attendance Commit- tee :—Patrick Bentley, for his three children, and was fined 5s and costs in each case. Mr. Shearer stated that _ the children were frequently begging about the town, / and were not properly cared for by the parents.—Wm. ••• Naylor, for one of his children, was fined 2s Bd, includ- ing costs. BRUSH-TAIL versus BASEST.—Jane Foster was eharged with having assaulted Ann Foley on the 10th September. Witnesses were called on both sides, and it appeared that complainant quarrelled with the defendant, the latter using the stick of a brush and the latter a basket.—Tho magistrates decided to dismiss the case. ILLICIT REMOVAL OF FURNITURE.—Bridget Mahoney was charged with having illegally removed some of her furniture to avoid distress for rQnt. Mrs. J. Naylor, the owner of the property, stated that defendant owed her about £2 for rent, and she had secretly removed furni- ture worth about that amount.—The Bench inflicted a fine of 20s and costs.

James Ford Parker. 182, Mushroom-lane, Sheffield, was charged with being a wandering lunatic. P.C. Dean found him on Saturday moraine near St. Paul's Church, about three o'clock. He was then shouting. A telegram was sent to his parents for them to take him away, and he was detained until they arrived. Parker was very respectably dressed, but by his conversation it was quite evident that he was not in possession of all his faculties.

Ruscons TRINITY CHURCH V. MOORE.—Played at Moore on Saturday. Score :—Moore, 28; Runcorn Trinity, 56. WARRINGTON V. BOLTON (SECOND ELEVENS.) This match was played at Bolton on Saturday, and resul- ted in a win for the home team by 28 runs. NORTON PRIORY V. RUNCORN DISTRICT OF MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.—Played on Norton Priory ground on Satur- day, and resulted in a win for the home team by 24 runs. Score :—Norton, 43; Ship Canal 19. FRODSHAH v. Kninsmcv.—Played at Frodsham, on Sat- urday, and ended in an easy victory for the home team, for whom Maddock and Carpenter played splendid cricket for their respective scores, while Crosfield bowled admirably, taking seven wickets for 13 runs. Score :-/- Frodsham, 167; Kingsley, 31. WINWICIC V. VIADUCT INSTITUTE.—Thig match (the last of the season for both clubs) was played at Earlestovrn, on Saturday, and resulted in a draw slightly in favour of Winvrick. For the visitors, R Carson, (29), J. Wads- worth, (22), and G. Hill, (15; not out), batted well; whilst Scott (19, not out) showed the best form for the Viaduct. Score :—Winwick, 107; Viaduct, total for five wickets, 47. PADGATE V. PEEL (Isle of Man.)—The Padgate team, through the kindness of two of the hon. members of the club, viz.. Messrs. G. H. Wood and W. H. J. Jenkins, who between them defrayed the costs of the travelling expenses, journeyed to the Isle of Man yesterday week in order to play the above club. The team left Liver- pool by the 11 a.m, boat on Friday, and arrived in Douglas about 3-30 p.m.; and after visiting several places of interest there they went by waggonette on Saturday morning to Peel in order to fulfil their engage- ment. The match commenced at 3 p m., there being a great number of spectators on the ground. The home team batted first and scored 53. Mr. Smythe, a master at King's College Douglas, played splendidly for 22, as also did Mr. T. Fives for 17. The bowling of Mr. James Monks for Padgate was very good, he taking 7 wickets for 16 runs. The visitors then went in and were dis- missed for 41, Mr. W. Barton scoring 15 of this number by very good cricket. The team thoroughly enjoyed their out. WARRINGTON V. BOLTON.—Tho last match of the Sta- son was brought to a close on the ground at Arpley on Saturday, when a fair muster of persons witnessed the encounter. The recent heavy rain rendered the wicket against quick scoring, consequently the bowlers claimed an advantage, which the.small scoring indicates. Both teams were strongly represented; and Warrington hav- ing won the toss decided to place their opponents in on a fast drying wicket. Berry (pro.) and Walker opened to Crosfield and Fleetwood (pro.) With the 'score at three, a straight ball from the amateur dismissed Walker, and Stanley came to the professional's aid. Both played patiently and took no liberties with the bowling, but at 20 Berry had a life at the wicket. Jolley relieved Cros- field, but the separation came from the opposite end, Jolley taking Berry smartly in the slips off Fleetwood, after contributing 20. Wadsworth (pro.) came next, and soon knocked up seven. The splendid fielding of Clarke and Jolley, however' sent him back to the pavi- lion, and Williams soon put together eight, a smart catch at mid-off dismissing him. Staten followed, but re- turned a tame one to the bowler after he had added four to the score. Wincup came next, and after surviving a doubtful decision he succumbed next ball, being bowled middle stump. Jolley, who had bowled exceedingly well, but was unfortunate in not obtaining a wicket, was here relieved by C. G. Lawton, who bowled Ben- bridge when he had added four. Bankes now came to Stanley's assistance, and Lawton was also successful in getting Stanley "lbw." The last-nanaed had batted carefully, and although he gave a couple of chances in his score of 20, the victory gained by his side was in a great measure attributable to him. The brothers Whit- worth brought up the rear, and eventually the innings closed for 77. Warrington commenced the task with J. J. Crosfield and Tinsley (pro.), to the deliveries of Wads- worth and Benbridge. The amateur was disrgissed with- out scoring, and Tinsley had only gcored three when Walker secured him. Warburton rattled eleven up in a merry style, but the bowling was good, and but for the good stands made by Clarke and Fairclough the score of the local team would have been poor in the extreme. However, Wallington was dismissed first ball, and Bolton were round victorious by 15 runs. Score : WARRINGTON. BOLTON. WARRINGTON IST TEA3I-..P:iiiliT 18.—A match under the above heading was arranged to be played on Satur- day, on the ground at Wilderspool, but only a small muster of those who were to officiate with the first team put in an appearance, consequently a sides game was in- dulged in, 13 players, chiefly of the senior team, oppos- ing 16 juniors. The game, which was very evenly contested, resulted in a win for the 13 by 2 tries 4 minors to 1 try and 3 minors. Frank Turner and Evans scored for the seniors, whilst Unsworth did similar service for the 16.

WIDNES INTER-WORKS FOOTBALL COMBETITION.—A match was played on Saturday afternoon, between the teams of Messrs. Deacon and the Alkali Works No. 2. Deacons' proved the best, and the rtsult was that they gained 31 points to nil—one goal, three tries, eleven minors. On Monday afternoon the result of the draw from Thursday last of the match between Messrs. Pil- kington's and Sullivan's teams, was decided. Pilking- ton's won the toss, and played with the wind for the first half. Sullivan's kicked off. Pilkington's proved the stronger of the tw?, and the game resulted in their favour—three minoili to nil. The teams were :—Pillting- ton's : Full back, Hewitt; half backs Wilkinson and Bryan; three-quarters, Clarke, Bell, and Glansey ; for- wards, Holt, Smith, Passey, Burke, Lea, Johnson, Dut- ton, Sauce, and Brennan. Sullivan's: Full back, Abrams; three-quarters, Barker, Boyle, and CoStello ; half backs, Bradshaw and Clare; forwards, Bowles, Flynn, Boyles, Boyle, Hewitt, Minton, Crosby, Cook, and Rooney. The umpires were J. Evans and T. Liw ; J. Smith was the referee. RUNCORN V STOCKPORT.—On Saturday afternoon the Runcorn Football Club opened the season in a highly creditable manner, meeting the Stockport club on the ground in Irwell-lane, in the presence of over two thou- sand spectators. There is every prospect of the wearers of the "myrtle green" having a successful season be- fore them, and the list of fixtures will compare most favourably with any previously arranged. Under the captaincy of H. Hughes, the team will no doubt be led to their utmost to retain the laurels they have gained, and, if possible, to add still more to their credit. The first match this season, as stated above, was with Stockport, and the list comprises engagements with Salford, Brad- ford, Site, Kendal Hornets, Burton-on-Trent, Broughton Rangers, New Brighton, Birkenhead Park, Man ter Rangers, Oldham, Rochdale Hornets, Owen's College, Free Wanderers, Liverpool Old Boys, Stockport, Mr. T. R. Sutton's team, and Leeds St. John's. In addition to these there will be the county matches with Westmore- land, Lancashire, Durham, and Yorkshire, in wbich players from the team will be selected. The game, which was hotly contested, and which was witnessed with much interest by the spectators, resulted as follows —Runcorn, three goals, two tries, and seven minors to nil. The Runcorn team was as follows :—T Woods, back T H Davies, J Brazendale, and Riley, three-quarter backs; H Hughes (captain) and J Hollinevorth, half- backs; W H Broady, W Hughes, G T Wainwright, W Faulkner, F Hancock, W: Stubbs, J Gayter, R. Dolan, and P Riley, forwards.

At Oakengates, Shropshire, +3n Saturday, Allen, of Warrington, competed in the three miles bicycle handi- cap. He was unfortunate enough to have a spill when two laps from home, and his fall brought down four other riders. A team of English cricketers will visit the Cape some time during November. The following players are men- tioped as being likely to undertake the trip :—C. A. Smith, M. P. Bowden, Hon. C. Coventry, C. M`Master, B. A. F. Grieve, with Briggs. Lohmann, M. Read, Abel, Fothergill, and one or two others. The Colonials will make them Welcome. There were thirteen "ducks" in the Australian match

at Scarborough, three men getting a pair. The trio' were C. I. Thornton, S. P. Jones, and J. D. Edwards. The Warrington club played the last match on their caM for the season on Saturday,when they were honour- ably defeated by Bolton. A benefit match for the "pros." will be played to-day (Saturday.) In a cricket match at Leeds on Wednesday between the Australians and Shaw and Shrewsbury's English Eleven, the Colonials were beaten by five wickets. The results of the Association League matches played on Saturday may thus be briefly summarised :—Everton 2 goals, Accrington 1 goal ; Derby County 6 goals, Bolton Wanderers 3 goals ; Aston Villa 1 goal, Wolverhampton Wanders 1 goal; Stoke nil, West Bromwich Albion 2 goals ; Preston North End 5 goals, Burriler2 goals. The following team has been selected to play to-day in the opening match of the Warrington football season against Tyldesley back, Buxton; three-quarters, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey ; half-backs, Speakman and Antrobus ; forwards, W. Dillon (captain), H. Ashton, Fair. Turner. Frank Turner E: Dillon, R. Littlevrood, Povey, Randles,,and Isherwood. Reserves: Full back, Sanson ; three-quarters, Evans and Daniels; forwards, Cragan, Hayes, and Unsworth. It will be seen that the team differs little from that of last season. Many people will be glad to see that Bux- tnn again figures at full back. For the last season or two this has been the weak 'point of the Warrington team, and, taking things all round, there is a pretty general feeling that Buxton, is the best qualified player to fill the place. In spite of all the rumouri to the con- trary, Barnes is down for his old place of centre three- quarter, and it may be expected that this smart player will for another season do yeoman's service for the club ' in connection with which he, has gathered all his laurels.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT INCE. On Monday afternoon, Dr. Churton, Chestor, held an inquest at Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, on the body of a boy 13 years of age, who was killed on Saturday, on the Ince Section of the Manchester Shia Canal.—Frederick Hall, engine driver, said deceased was employed turning points on the railway at the works. After witness had passed the points he missed the deceased, and afterwards found him on the line, unconscious and bleeding, but still breathing,.—The Coroner: Have you been in the habit of seeing boys of 13 at work of this kind ?—Wit- ness: Yes, they suit the work very well.—The Coroner (to Mr. Broom, agent for Mr. Walker, contractor) : Do vOu ever engage boys younger than 13 ?—Mr. Broom: The men who engage them have instructions not to em- ploy boys under 14. Deceased told me he was 14, and it is only since his death that we learned he was only 13. He was earning quite 13s a week. Evidence was given that the boy died from his injuries, and the coroner re- 'marked that the most singular part of the affair was, that no one saw the boy struck. It seemed a very tender age at which to engage a boy.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

FINANCIAL ASPECT OF THE SCHEME. (moat TIIE "FINANCIAL NEWS.) The finahcing of the Manchester Ship Canal was a task which at first sight seemed no less stupendous than the engineering difficulties which had to be faced. As it turned out, there was no great trouble in raising the ne- cessary money, for of the £8,000,000 of share capital (reinforced by £2,000,0000 in debentures) only £BlO,OOO in £lO shares remains unsubscribed, and of these the company has the right to allot 50,000 fully paid to the contractor, in lieu of cash. Over £1,000,000 has been paid up in advance of calls; but to enable the company to pay their way until next spring, it is proposed to is- sue debentures to a like amount. The total cost of the undertaking, as estimated in the prospectus, is £9,032, 972. The shares are not held in large proportion by Manchester merchants, but by "all sorts and conditions of men," the number of shareholders being 40,000. It is essentially a popular undertaking, and while some of the wealthier commercial class in Manchester hold aloof, sanguine expectations of the increased affluence which Cottonopolis is to attain as a port, and of the flourishing business to spring up throughout the route of the canal, are very prevalent. In the prospectus it was estimated that a traffic of 3,000,000 tons of goods on the canal would pay a dividend of eight per cent, on-the share capital, but that a greater traffic was probable; that at the end of seven years more than 9,500,000 tons per an- num the company might expect to carry, and this would be sufficient to pay 18 per cent. dividend. The revenue, on the latter basis, is estaiated at £1,783,905, including £BO,OOO, the actual net earnings of the Bridge- water Canal undertaking, which forms part of the pro- perty. The working expenses are put at £104,200, and the interest on borrowed capital at £72,000. The amount of traffic the canal is really likely to obtain is the subject of great difference of opinion, even in Manchester itself, and it is obvious that the action of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, and also of the railway companies, must be an important factor in the calculation. As it is intended to make the canal tolls only half the existing railway rates between Liverpool and Manchester, and the wharfage but half the present dock and town dues at Liverpool, it is urged that sufficient saving will be obtained by the use of the canal to ensure for it exten- sive patronage, apart from the great advantage in the avoidance of transhipping or breaking bulk. It is con- tended that this latter item alone will effect a saving greater than any possible reduction in the Liverpookdock dues or in railway charges, and that competition from ths Liverpool authorities is really out of the question, as the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, if it made mate- rial reductions in its charges, could not possibly find in- terest on its £18,800,000 of bonds. The canal will have another important advantage in the sill of its entrance being Bft. deeper than that of any dock at Liverpool, and its possession of entrance locks, by which large ves-. eels will be able to enter at almost any state of the tide, and small vessels at any' time, whereas at Liver- çl only 40 minutes of each tide are available for large I ships. With all the advantages thus contemplated, the shares of the company are at a discount, the price being about £8 15s. With so many holders as 40,000, and a large proportion of them persons of humble position, shares are naturally thrown on the market from time to time, notwithstanding the reiterated injunction of directors to 'stick to "Ahem; but it is asserted that so large a num- ber as 1,000 is never obtainable except at the office of the company. However near the mark may be the estimates formed on either side of the account, we can only say, from a close supervision of the works, that there is no present prospect of the expected outlay being exceeded, and that the canal, from its geographical posi- tion and surrounding conditions, may reasonable be ex- pected to prove a very busy waterway. Great emphasis is laid by its promoters on the probability of new indus- tries springing up along its banks, and as the company has been compelled to acquire a good deal of surplus land, such a result would probably furnish an important item of income.

I FIRE AT A. CATHOLIC CHURCH : A PRIEST'S CORPSE BURNED.—A piteous scene was witnessed on Wednesday, at St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, Chorley. The mortal remains of the Rev. Father Hawksworth, the priest of the mission, who died on Saturday, had been placed on a catafalque in the chancel to enable friends to do honour to his memory. On Tuesday night many people who gratefully remembered his ministry visited the church, and then the doors were locked. On Wed- nesday morning the housekeeper at the presbytery dis- covered that the church was on fire, an alarm was given, and the brigade was quickly in attendance. Knowing that the priest's corpse was lying near the altar, the fire- men hesitated a little before they played on the burning building; but the fire grew in strength, and at last the brigade were compelled to cope with it vigorously. In half an hour the flames had been put out, and creeping through the dense smoke towards the bier, the specta- tors were saddened to rind that the 'Coffin and the dra- peries had been destroyed and the priest's corpse reduced almost to ashes. The ashes of the priest were reverently placed in another coffin, and the interment, which took place in the afternoon, was attended by thousands of people.
