div.head: WEDDING OF MISS RYLANDS AT THEL WALL.
div.p: WEDDING OF MISS RYLANDS AT THEL WALL.

On Saturday afternoon the marriage of Miss Caroline Louisa Tate Rylands, of Massey Hall, Thelwall, second daughter of the late Mr. P. Ry- lands, M.P., to Herr Louis Wolff, of The Hague, Holland, was celebrated at Thelwall Church in the presence of a large assembly. The church was very neatly decorated for the occasion. A little after 12 o'clock the bride entered the sacred edifice, leaning on the arm of her brother, Mr. Louis Gordon Ry- lands. She was attired in a bodice and train of white moire antique, over a petticoat of white corded silk, trimmed with silver, and she also wore' a tulle veil, with orange blossoms in hair and on corsage, and' a sapphire and diamond ring, the present of the bridegroom. • The bridesmaids—Miss Georgiana Rylands (sister of the bride), Miss Dora Rylands (cousin of the bride), and the Misses Evaline and Sally Wolff (sisters of the bride- groom)—wore, the two elder salmon-pink dresses of Pongee silk, with waistcoats and' sashes of green silk; and coarse straw hats turned up with green velvet and trimmed with white ribbon and pink flowers, and the two younger bridesmaids cream dresses and hats to match. The bridesmaids also wore brooches and earrings, the gift of the bride- groom. The best man was Mr. William Peter Ry- lands, third son of Mr. and Mrs. Peter Rylands. The bride's bouquet was comprised of choice white flowers. The two elder bridesmaids carried posies of Gloire de Dijon roses, and the younger baskets of white Marguerites. Th 3 ceremony was per- formed by the uncles of the bride, the Rev. C. L. Reynolds, vicar of Wray. Lancashire, and the Rev. G. F. Reynold, curate of Buxton. Before the ser- vice voluntaries were played on the organ, and at the conclusion Mr. F. W. Reynolds, of Liverpool, gave a rendering of Mendelssohn's " Wedding March." During the eervice the hymn, "The voice that breathed o'er Eden," and the 67th psalm were sung. After the ceremony the bridal party drove to Massey Hall. The following is a list of the guests :—Mr. Van den Berg (Chancellor of the Dutch Legation in London), Mr. and Mrs B. L. DEATH OP Ma. RICHARD PRocron.—Mr. Richard Anthony Proctor. the well-known English astronomer and scientist, died in new York on Wednesday night from an attack of yellow fever. He arrived in that city on Monday from Florida, and intended to sail for Europe on Saturday. Mr. Proctur was in his fifty-second year.

div.head: WARRINGTON REVISIONVOITRT.
div.p: WARRINGTON REVISIONVOITRT.

On Monday evening Mr. J. T. Foard, revising bar- rister, sitting at the Lion Hotel, Bridge-st., com- menced the revision of the voting lists for the borough. The Liberal party was represented by Mr. Browne, solicitor, and Mr. John Clayton, the agent, and Mr. Hampson, Conservativ,e agent, appeared for his party. The sitting was held for the hearing of claims and objections to voters and burgesses from all polling districts. The number of voters at pre- sent on the list, it may be mentioned, is 7,472. The Liberal claims numbered 168, and the objections 237, while the Conservative claims numbered 254, and the objections 232. There were no objections to lodgers at present on the list by either side. ,

A BROKEN LEG AND A LOST VOTE. . An objection was made on the partbf the Liberals to John Frederick Williamson's name being retained on the list. It transpired that in January last Williams, who is a furnaceman, had the misfortune to break his leg whilst at work. He was taken to the Infirmary, and in that institution he remained for some time. Whilst he was there his wife made application for and obtained relief. The Revising Barrister said that that unfortunately dis- qualified Williams, who could not retain his vote.
A.MISLAID RENT BOOK.

Thomas Bridge, 4, Edelsten's-yard,—ntade a claim to be put on the list. He said that he had mislaid his rent- botlk, but he maintained that he went into the house of which he is now occupant a week after the Jubilee cele- bration.—The Revising Barrister ruled that in the ab- sence of any evidence to the contrary, the man's word must be accepted, and allowed the vote.

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE,
div.p: A NARROW ESCAPE,

Frank Pickard, who was represented by a friend, al- most failed to sustain his claim for a vote in consequence of the rent-book having his name written on it as "Pickers."—The Revising Barrister was inclined to amend the name to " Pickers," but the Liberal agent objected on the ground that the Barrister had no power to so amend.—The Revising Barrister said that he thought he had some power in the matter, notwithstanding that this was a claim.—Ultimately it turned out ,that the claimant's real name was Pickard. and the vote was allowed.

div.head: LIVING WITH HIS MOTHER-IN-LAW.
div.p: LIVING WITH HIS MOTHER-IN-LAW.

Martin Connor, of 65, Pierpoint-st., but formerly of Furness-st., claimed a vote in respect of his occupation of the former hove. In answer to questions he said that when he lived in Furness-st., he "supported the house."—The Revising Barrister: Why should you sup- port the house of Bridget Flynn P—Claimant': Because I married her daughter ;(laughter.)—Mr. Hampson : Bridget Flynn is on the list for the house in Furness-st.— The Revising Barrister: This man is not a tenant, from his owa showing. He gave her money, but she earns money of her own —Mr. Brown: Since leaving Furness- st. hA has lived in Pierpoint-et. eight months.—The Re- vising Barrister: He would be entitled if he had had a twelve months' occupation in Pierpoint-st.—Mr. Brawn° said that the fact of Mrs.'Flynn being on the list did not prove that she was the tenant.—The Revising Barrister: But she is now ; no doubt she has always been the ten- ant, although he found her help to go on with. I have no doubt that she would have asserted herself as mis- tress oisthe house if need be.—The claim was refused.

A PARTNMRSHIP CLAIM. Patrick Magian, on behalf of himself and brother Fe- lix, claimed two votes in respect of premises in Arpley- st. Ho said that there were three partners in the firm of Maginn Bros., but the eldest brother had other qualifica- tions. The rent was formerly £4O a year, but now it was £6O, as the accommodation had been increased.-- The claim was allowed.

MISCELLANEOUS. 4112' A lodger claim, made by Philip Edward Lake, was disallowed. Applicant lodged at his father's house, which let at 7s weekly, that sum including rates and taxes.l The Revising Barrister held that there was not suflicient value.—Ann Monks, a Liberal, was put upon the list, her husband having been dead two years, and she having been tenant of the house claimed fo4 during that'period.—Richard Barrow, 1, Heath-lane, had his vote disallowed by reason of a break in the occupa- tion caused by his attendance at the Militia training. • TUESDAY. The revision was resumed by Mr. J. T. Foard.

div.head: ME PATT'EN ARMS.
div.p: ME PATT'EN ARMS.

In the first case of public interest, Henry Kiernan, landlord of the Patten Arms Hotel, claimed a vote in respect of tenancy at the hotel. It appeared from ques- tions put by Mr. Hampson that the claimant's wife was the recognised tenant, and carried on the business.—Mr. Browne : But it is practically your business, and is sit- ply in your wife's name.—Claimant: That is so.—The Claimant further said that he had a. business in Man- chester, and had a railway contract.—Mr. Browne said that the clainiant's wife was practically the agent of the husband, and to all intent and purpose he was the occu- pier.—The Revising Barrister decided that Mrs. Kiernan was trading on her own account, and under the Mar- ried Women's Property Act she was entitled to a position independently of her husband.—Mr. Browne said that as a married woman she had no vote, and the Revising Barrister said that her name would have to come off the list. The vote of the husband would be allowed. mils( BY A CURATE.

The Rev. W. E. Glynn claimed a vote as a lodger at 18, Parker-St. The claimant, in answer to Mr. Browne, said that there were two other lodgers in the house, and two rooms downstairs, and three bedrooms upstairs.— Mr. Hampson submitted that the case was before his Honour at a previous revipion, when it was decided in the case of Mr. Glynn's predecessor, that he had the best rooms in the house, and was therefore entitled to a vote. —The claim was allowed. THE CLAIMS OF COUNTY ELECTORS. James Monks, 3, Brown's-yard, Winwick-st., claimed a county elector's vote in succession from Doctor's Nook, Leigh, Lancashire, Mr. Hampson, in support of the claim, contended that the Act appeared to hdve been made for the purpose of assimilating the county quali- fication with that already existing in boroughs by the extension of an existing Act, in order that persons oc- cupying in boroughs and persons occupying outside boroughs in the same county, each being, entitled to a county elector's vote, should have it for occupation of equal value, so that whatever Occupation in a borough would give a burgess a vote should outside a borough give a county elector's vote. The qualifying property need not be throughout the 12 months constituting the period of qualification the same property or in the same 'parish. This seemed to Show that in the same manner that a borough was one notwithstanding its being divi- ded into electorial divisions called wards, and an occupier had StlCCeSsiOn from one ward to another. So a person who occupied in more than one electoral division in a county, whether in a borough, not being a county in it- self, or any other portion of the county outside a borough, was entitled to succession to any other portion of the county whether in a borough or not. Mr. Hamp- son stated that if this were not intended to be the mean- ing of the Act, in section 2 sub. s. 2, the wbrd " apply" would be used, as it was three times used in section 4, and not the word extend," which was used. The interchangeability of the burgess's and county elector's qualification was further shown in sec. 4 sub. (1) (6) : "Provided that a person whose name appears in any list of county electors or burgesses in a county may object to the name of any other person on a list of county elec- tors or Wurgesses for a parish in that county, and may oppose the claim of a person to have his name inscribed in any such list." Thus, a burgess of Warrington, ac. cording to this section, could object to a county elector on the list for the township of flu- line, and a county elector on the Billinge 'list can object to a burgess on the list for the township of Warrington. There could not be any mistake about the word "burgess "meaning a person on the list for a quali- fication in a municipal borough, for the Act went on to say—"ln the construction of the Registration of Electors Acts, for the purpose of their application to a parish not situate in a municipal borough, there shall be made the variation following, county electors' shall be substi- tuted for 'burgesses.'" He submitted that this Act had so extended the burgess qualification that in com- mon justice aonafi coming to Warrington from any por- -tion of the county of Lanealkter (not being a county borough) ought either to be placed on the burgess list of the trough or on a separate list as a county elector only In sueh a case where one county electoral division was partly municipal and partly county, would it not be anomalous to allow succession outside the borough, or successionyinside the borough, and not succession from one portion to another of the same electoral district? Would it not be an injustice, even if done as in Warring- ton, namely, succession given when a person goes from the borough portion of the division to the portion out- side th# borough (which is doubtless correct), but no succesAon and neither county nor borough vote for the person who leaves the county portion of the electoral division and goes to occupy a house in the borough portion of the same electoral division ? The Revising Barrister: I think you must have the &rel. ling house qualification, the actual residence from the 15th July to 15th July.—Mr. Hampson remarked that in certain cases great injustice would be done if succession was not allowed from any part of the county.—The Revising Barrister said it ap- peared to hini that on the face of it there might be a possible injustice, but it would be limited to a few
. _ persons mdeed.—The vote was not allowed, Mr. Hamp- son announcing that he should not trolble his Honour with any more claims on the same ground. WEDNESDAY. ' '
- - • The sitting of the Court was resumed at ten o'clock.
A TEST CASE.

The Liberals objected to the :;;;;.e of Henry Hewitt, of 319, Winwick-road, being upon the list.—Mr. Ramp- son said that this was a test case, and a number of other and similar cases would be decided by it. The number affected on each side were about equal. He wanted to know if Hewitt was entitled to a vote under what was called tk " Medical Relief Disqualification Act, of 1885," which was an Act passed to prevent medical relief, hav- ing been obtained, disqualifying a person from voting. The Act said that "where a person, had, in any part of the United ,Kingdom, received for himself, or for any member of his family, any medical or surgical assistance, or any medicine at the expense of any poor rate, such person should not ,by reason thereof be deprived of any right to be registered or to vote." The term "medi- cal or surgical assistance" in the At included "all medi-

cal and surgical attendance, and all matters and things supplied by or on the recommendation of the medical officer having authority to give such attendance and re- commendation at the expense of any poor rate." Mr. Hampson said that in the present case, Hewitt's wife was in a lunatic asylum, but he submitted that in Apite of that fact there was no poverty or loss of independence on the part of the voter. The Revising Barrister: It will be desirable to have the facts upon which lam to decide this question, because I do not know under what circumstances the wife was removed.—Mr. Browne: By order of the magistrates.— In answer to Mr. Hampson, claimant said that previous to July, 1887, he asked the doctor to allow his wife to return home. He had made that request twice. He considered it a grievance that the doctor did not allow his wife to return to hinn. He thought it hard that she should be at the asylum. The justices of the peace, on the recommendation of the doctor, ordered her to be taken to an asylum.—Mr Hampson said that it appeared to him that the present case was one of compulsory removal; there was no poverty. She was ordered by the magistrates to be taken to the asylum. The whole arrangement was a medical one, and he submitted that it came under the Act that he had cited. It had further been held that a person should not be disentitled to be enrolled as a burgess by reason only did he had received medical or surgical assistance from the trustees of muni- cipal charities, or had been removed, by order of a justice, to a hospital or place for the reception of the sick. He contended that this was a similar case.—Mr. Browne: That refers to a contagious fever hospital.— 'Mr. Hampson urged that this was a case of medical relief within the meaning of the Act.—Mr. Browne: I shall submit that the Medical Relief Act simply says "upon the recommendationof a doctor," and that that applies only to naaPs where persons go into the Workhouse on the recommendation of a doctor—where they cannot be attended to in their own homes. In this case the woman has been codipulsorily removed by tte order of a magistrate. She cannot return without the visiting justices of the Asylum permit her, and without the doctors order. Mr. Browne contended that in thiS case a person was taken away commilsorily by thereliev- ing officer and brought before a magistrate, who, after hearing the evidence, made an order whicla could not be rescinded except by an appeal to the Lunacy Commis- sioners. Mr. Browne said, that Mr. Hampson had said that the clothes in the Lunatic Asylum were fitted to the treatment of the case; but that seemed to be absurd. The clothes were supplied by the parish, apart altogether from the treatment, medical or surgical.—The Revising k Barrister: You mean to say that goes in relief of the husband P—Mr. Browne: Yes.—The Revising Barrister: Then, on the other hand, you take away the wife's as- sistance from her husband—you deprive him compul- sorily of that. He would probably have to find a substi- tute in the house, which might impoverish him. If a man for any reasons—either infectious disease or any- thing else---has his rights interfered with or disturbed for the good of the community, it appears to me that it is only right and fair that it should be no disqualification, because he had no power to control it.—Mr. Browne: Do you not think that the Act only applies to pemle taken to the Workhouse ? If it were meant to extend to such a wide area as to include these persons it would certainly have mentioned lunatic asylums.—The Revis- ing Barrister: Section four says "medical and surgical attendance, and all matters and things supplied by or on the recommendation of the medical officer." When an order is made by the magistrate it is clearly made on the recommendation of the medical' officer.— Mr. Browne: The wife is sent away compulsorily. lint he is not bound to send her to a pauper lunatic asylan. —The Revising Barrister: That is true; but probably he might be perfectly able to sustain himself, but not be able to sustain the extra burden imposed upon him of maintaining his wife in an asylum.—Mr. Browns; He has the option of sending to another asylum if he says he is willing to pay.—The Revising Barrister': Nc doubt. That would be one of the most pressing reasons on your behalf. But the entailing of extra expense is one that the Legislature never contemplated, and this does not affect his liability to.maintain himself. It is supposed that a voter who is entitled to the franchise should be perfectly independent, and he should not be under the domination of any other person. He should be able to maintain himself. A man might be perfectly able to maintain himself, but not to maintain his wife in an asylum.—Mr. Browne: My point is that she is supplied also with food and clothes, and ,not alone with medical assistance. The Revising Barrister said that he supposed she would take her clothes with her. It was merely as a sanitary or medical arrangement that she would be required to change them. —ln answer to Mr. Browne claimant said that hl wife had been in the asylum for two years. She did not go without clothes.—The Revising Barrister said he should allow, the vote.—Before leaving, Hewitt expressed a wish to address the Court. iDid they (indicating the Liberal representatives), he asked, suppose for one moment that he wished to "put on "England's kg,tand and noble in- stitutions ? (Laughter.)—The Revising Barrister :We cannot have a public speech here. You must do that at the hustings.—llewitt : But they have a prejudice against me. They know what I am. I have had a few words with the best of them they have in the town, and I am capable of facing the very highest man you can bring before me. You are a lot of Socialists. (Laughter.)
A FOOTBALL ACCIDENT.

A claim entered -13-y-JO-IiTI-liiii)i,--lia.ttersby-lane, was contested by the Conservatives on the ground of a break „in the occupation. It was shown that the claimant was a football player, and had the misfortune to receive in- juries whilst playing.—Mr. Browne said he went to Cam. forth for the benefit of his health, and his expenses were paid by the 'Football Club.—The Revising Barrister: Your family lived at Ilattersby-lane during', that time ? Claimant : reply to Mr. Hampson, Rigby said the house was during his absence put in the name fif his wife's father, John Poison.—The vote was al- towed.

div.head: MILITARY QUESTION AGAIN.
div.p: THE MILITARY QUESTION AGAIN.

Major James Ritchie, who was represented by Sergeant Murrall, claimed a vote in respect of field-officer's quar- ters at Orford Barracks. In reply to Mr. Browne, Ser- geant Murrall said that claimant was away on leave and had been since the 16th of August; he had not gone to India, and was, so far as witness knew, not going. Major Ritchie was adjutant of the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment. He was away with the battalion at Altcar, but was at liberty to, and did, come back to the barracks as often as he wished during the training. —Mr. Hampsoft observed that the claim was allowed last year.—Mr. Browne said that was by arrangement.— The Revising Barrister said his impression was that it was not by arrangement. At any rate, he decided the year before that the votes of the officers were to be al- lowed. He allowed them on the ground of the state- ment, made on oath at the time, that the officers had in point of fact perfect freedom of action, and could return from Altcar on any day they pleased, and without ask- ing permission of anybody; therefore that they were not compulsorily away for any period, not necessarily for even twelve hours. He allowed the claim.—Mr. Browne gave notice of appeal.—ln the case of Quarter-master Frank Hawes, a similar objection was raised.—The Re- vising Barrister: If you intend to revive this question, and Mr. llawes is compelled to appear in support of his claim, I shall give the heaviest costs that the law allows 40.—The objection was not pressed, and the claim was accordingly allowed. THURSDAY.

The revision was resumed at ten a.m. by Mr. Foard, the Revising Barrister. The Liberals were again repre- sented by Mr. Browne, solicitor, and Mr. John Clayton, Liberal agent the Conservative claims being advocated by Mr. Hampson, Conservative agent. BOATHOUSE OR RESIDENCE? The Liberals objected to. Mr. Robert Capner, boat owner, Wilderspool Causeway, On the grounds that the premises were a boat-house and not a residence, and also that they were of insufficient value. Examined by Mr. Browne, the claimant said that he lived at Chester, and sometimes at Warrington. His house was at Ches- ter, where his wife also lived; all his furniture was, however, not there, as there were chairs, tables, and a bed at the boat-house at Wilderspool. The bed was put there at the beginning of the season, and taken away at the end. It was taken away last week. He had slept , there for a month in February and March last, and though his son usually took charge of the business, he came over occasionally.—Mr. Hampson : Is it a fact that you somotiMes stay longer at one of your places than another? Yes, sir.—The Barrister : Really and substantially his residence is in Chester.—Mr. Browne: And lie has a vote for Chester.--Mr. Hampson contended one was as much a residence as the other.—The Bar- rister; No! He ispnly here six weeks out of the twelve months. I shall, however, allow the vote, but without expenses.

MISSING RENT BOOKS AND NOTICES. Wm. James Edde,s, 23, Powy's-st., was objected .to lv the Liberals. Claimant, in answer to,Mr. Browne, said that he had not brought his rent book. The vote was allowed.--L-Mr.Brovrne, I see from the printed notices issued from the Conservative Club that the words "If you have rent books bring or send them" have been crogied out in ink.—Mr. Eanapson : That was done be- cause I did not think it necessary to produce the rent book. It was said last year that they were not neces- sary.—The Revising Barrister But an inference can be drawn from the circumstance that a man does not pro- duce kis rent book.—Later on, Mr. Browne, on being in- formed by a claimant that he had not brought his rent book, asked if a notice to bring it had been received.— Claimant: No.—Mr. Browne: It is a very curious fact that about 120 notices have miscarried.—The Revising Barrister: The notices may have been delivered at the houses, but the persons objected to might not have re- ceived them; there is no evidence to show that the per- son objected to has received the notice.—Mr. Browne: I will call a person to prove that he posted them.—Mr. Hampson said that the Liberals had no right to tell any one to bring their rent books.—A man was then called by Mr. Browne who swore to having posted the notices.— The Revising Barrister. said he did not know who was re- sponsible. The man might have dropped one out of the bundle by accident. He once heard of a man who had been sent out with 300 or 400 notices to post, and he put them down a sewer. He had known such a thing done th save the trouble of disposing of them in any other way. He could not say that these notices had ever been posted. He must have the strictest proof possible that the notices were actually posted, and Mr. Browne must call upon the post-office authorities for an explanation if

A policeman found him asleep in a closet in Wilderspool-1 Prisoner pleaded to be allowed to go, but he reminded that he had not kept promises preiri° made, either to remain in the Workhouse, or hisway to Kenilworth, where his wife and fa reside.—Major Litton said that if prisoner wei his wife and daughter he would be nothing trouble to them. div.p: TRE public may remember a brief statement published some time ago from Mr. Charles Moore, District Manager of the Provident Association of London (39, Lombard Street), touching a fearful experience of his earlier life, and his remarkable and unexpected deliverance from danger and suffering. His story attracted such wide attention that he thought it best to furnish a more full and detailed account, which he hopes will (in part at least) ba accepted by the people as a sufficient reply to the multitude of letters of in- tliry that are written to him on the subject. At the same time he would have it understood that he will cheerfully answer any fur- ther inquiries should any person feel that what is herein set down does not wholly meet his own case or satisfy his judgment. Mr. 40ore's address is No. 129, Chatham-street, Old Kent-road, S.E., London, where he has resided for the past ten years. He says: "I have great pleasure in making a plain and simple statement of my own experience, taking for a standpoint a time now about ten rears ago. For a long period previously I had undergone terrible agony and torment from what was said to be a kind .of rheumatism. have dropped down with it, all in a moment, like a bird shot with a gun- . My dear mother and father were both sadly afflicted with tile same thing, the former being a cripple for years up to the time when death mercifully released her. "As for myself, I was at times so maddened with pain that I would kick and tear the bedclothes to pieces without a thought of the I.lBehief I was doing. For years I was more or less in the hands of medical men, yet none of them seemed to be able to cope with the !isease, or to understand it. Afterwards I was paralysed for a while, hand and f00t,.,50 that I could not feel myself or stand alone. ,llen ray mind became affected, and as no local or home treatment availed anything, I went to Guy's Hospital as an out-patient. Here •( as examined by eminent physicians, who said I was suffering from a loss of power and vitality in the muscles, and that I ought to ttY the effect of the galvanic battery. This I did, very many times, with only momentary benefit." [Alas, how many poor creatures have had their hopes dashed to the ground in the same way, and been led to see what a vain thing ila the boasted skill of many who are Called men of learning! It makes me think of what the Bible says about God having denied knowledge to the wise and prudent and revealed it unto babes.] "One day, when I was feeling a trifle better than common, I called to see a friend of mine who was a herbalist, and hi g remarks set IllY thoughts off on a new line. • ' Friend Moore,' he said, 'you are indeed suffering from rheumatism and sciatica, but you will never Ret well so long as you regard and treat them as separate and distinct complaints. The. truth is, they ,are merely symptoms of your l'eal disease, which is nervous dyspepsia and indigestion. Your stomach, liver, and probably the kidneys, are all out of order. Instead ef being digested, and so imparting health and vigour to the whole body, your food lies torpid in your stomach, and gets sour and cor- .kipt. The poison thus developed is absorbed by the blood and carried to all the other organs and parts of the system. A deadly acid frofli the fermented food goes to the joints and muscles, and causes the terrific pain from which you have suffered so long. The nerves •te starved because the poor, thin blood can give them no nourishment, and this causes the deadness and coldness in your limbs, and tile paralysis. The blood cannot circulate unless it is set in motion by nerve power, and there can be no nerve power while the stomach full of poison, and digestion is practically stopped. Cure the dyspepsia and you banish all its results.' "My friend then described a number of symptoms as follows, and asked me if I had not had them: Irregularity of the bowels, constipation, coated tongue, yellow skin, hig'a coloured urine, dull and sleepy sensations, giddiness, loss of appetite, bad taste in the lnonth, pains in the back and sides, difficulty of breathing, &c., and I replied that I had these before the rheumatic trouble appeared, lkt it had not come into my mind that rheumatism was only an advanced sign of dyspepsia. "But what should I do? The disease was now plain, but where was the remedy? I had heard of a popular medicine called Mother Beigers Curative Syrup, and the cures it had effected, but I treated such stories with contempt as mere advertising fables. Said I, 'lf the doctors don't know what to do who does ? ' Soon after I met with another friend who had been recently ailing, and aiked him: What makes you look so strong and well?' and he answered: 'l've come around all right through the virtues of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup.' 'Then,' said I, 'l'll try it.' I began by taking two of Mother Seigel's Pills at night and ten or twelve drops of the BYrup in sweetened water, night and morning, and soon found myself improving, though slowly. The worst symptoms abated as my digestion grew stronger, and the body felt the new, rich blood.

"But how foolish we all are in some way or another. With the road to health straight before me I had a fearful set-back by taking bad advice. I was urged to discontinue the Syrup and try a certain physician. I did so, and grew rapidly worse. The good the Syrup had done was overthrown and I became so weak, my hands and limbs trembled and shook, and I could not hold a cup of water without spilling it. Once, feeling chilly, I asked my wife to wrap a blanket around me, and as she did so I fainted and fell to the floor. I Gould not get warm in the height of summer, even when I sat before a large fire. "This would not do. Alarmed at the effects of my folly, I gave up the doctor's medicine and returned to Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. It was a struggle, but in less than a month I was able to go out for a walk. Made hopeful by this, I continued with the Syrup, and I thank God that He made it the means of my complete recovery. Hezekiah's sun dial was set back ten degrees, but I think mine is turned back twenty, for I feel twenty years younger than I did in 1878. Look at it! lam sixty years old; was crippled and worn out with disease, and yet I now walk many miles daily, and am often taken for a man of forty-five. All this I owe, under God, to Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. One day, about twelve months after I first began taking the Syrup, who should I meet on London Bridge but one of the physicians who had prescribed for me when I was ill. When he saw and recognised me he was struck with surprise, and said: "Mr. MoOre, is this indeed yourself? I can scarcely credit my own senses. I never expected to see you in health again. What under the sun have you been doing to Tire that old trouble?. Tell me all about it." 44 So, stepping aside, to be out of the way of the passers-by, I told him the whole story of my experience since he gave up my case as incurable. I related how I came at last to use Seigel's Syrup; how I prayed the Lord to bless it as a means of healing me of all my ailments, and how He had done so. 'And now, Doctor,' I said, 'I stand before you to-day strong and well, and you, as an honest man, must admit that Seigel's Syrup has done what neither you nor any other medical man was able to do." "He then tried to laugh me out of that idea, but I added: Doctor, facts are facts, and there is no disputing a plain truth. You know very well that when you gave me up I could not put my feet close together and close my eyes without falling to the floor, unless I laid hold of something. Now I can stand as firmly and walk as vigorously as any man. If Seigel's Syrup did not work this great change, what did? I used no other medicine 1' "To this the Doctor merely replied; Be that as it may, you certainly look wonderfully well.' 'Yes,' I responded, 'and I give thanks where they are due.' "When the people ask me how the Syrup cures so many different complaints, I tell them it cures no complaints except those that are caused by indigestion and dyspepsia, and they include almost every trouble that now prevails. I spoke of having dropped suddenly as though I had been shot. This was vertigo, a sympthn of advanced chronic dyspepsia and nervous prostration. "I have said enough, though I could write a book on what this safe, simple, and wonderful medicine has done for me. Knowing how common the fearful diSease from which I suffered is among the people of Vngland; and how sure Seigel's Syrup is to cure it, I write these lines in hope they may catch the attention of many poor victims, and show them the way to health and happiness. [Signed] CHARLES A100RE.77

" P.S.—My own dear brother was badly afflicted with asthma and bronchitis. As he was a member of a club he did not like to use an advertised medicine lest he should forfeit the benefits of the club. But after his doctor had said he could do no more for him I urged him to try Seigel's Syrup, and bought two bottles of the Syrup and a box of Seigel's Pills. In a week he was smoking his pipe and. able to walk about. In a few weeks more he went to the doctor to get WAR to sign the paper so he could draw his dues from the club, 4vhen the doctor looked astonished and exclaimed, 'What! man, are ojiive and really getting well? What a change!' I also knew a lady who was nearly crazy with the pain of neuralgia of the face, clad Seigel's Syrup cured her. .A nd a tradesman, with diseased. liver, who had been discharged as incurable from three hospitals, and been given up to die. He was cured by a few bottles of the Syrup, and is a marvel to all who know him. C. M." PATENTS IN SOUTH AFRICA.

Sir,—The New South African Republic, presided over by S. J. P. Kruger, is now so far advanced in civilisation and settled government that a patent law has been passed by the Volksraad, and signed by the President, for the purpose, as expressed therein, of "encouraging new and lawful inventions by granting to inventors for a certain time the exclusive right of deriving the full benefit of their inventions." The law, like most of those of our own colonies, largely corresponds with the Eng- lish Patent Laws, and patents are granted for 14 years to citizens of the Republic and to foreigners for any in- ventions not known therein. The initial cost of obtain- ing a patent will not be great, as the stamps and fees have been fixed about equal to what we are 'accustomed to in England, and less than either of the British posses- sions of Cape Colony: or Natal. A law granting copy- right for 50 years in published writings, engravings, charts, music, theatrical pieces, lectures, and in perform- ances of operas and dramatic pieces has aLo recently been passed. These laws extend over a wide territory, gradually increasing in importance, and British manu- facturers and traders doing business with South Africa will do well to take advantage of the protection thus afforded.—Toilis truly. WM. P. THOMPSON 8z CO

THINK OF THIS!

Sir,—The "Methodist Times," of to-day, says : " We are informed that the meagre reports of the Chief Constable of Warrington, upon which we, as well as the Liverpool newspapers, commented last week, result from the instructions of influential persons in authority, and must not be regarded as the expression of his own conviction and wishes. One who has known the Chief Constable for many years thinks that our Notes convey a mistaken impression of his attitude in relation to the Licensing Session, and bears a high testimony to his sympathy with all that is calculated to promote temper- ance and purity." This is all very fine; but what about the line I have italicised? So fond is our Chief Constable of having "his little say." that I had concluded it was impossible to muzzle him, and it would be intensely interesting to know who has accomplished the trick. It would also be interesting to learn why it has been done. Has it been done to whitewash the character of the town a little, so that a slight pretext might be found to grant an extra license or two, and thus afford facilities to dye the ; town's disreputable name still blacker in the years to come? Why was it? Let us know by all means, and let us know at once. If our reports are to be " dooked" after the style hinted above, they had better be aban- doned altogether. It would be much better than pub- ' lishing statements that are simply written "to order."— Yours, 14c., _ _

div.head: FREE SPEECH.
div.p: FREE SPEECH.
NEWTON BUILDING SOCIETY.

Slr,—After several years of indifferent management of the funds of the society, the members aroused them- selves, and by requisition called a meeting. A duly qualified accountant, after re-valuation of the properties in the hands of the society, gave in his report that it , was quite in a solvent position. The members passed a unanimous resolution that business should be resumed, and that a barrister of known reputation and eiperience should be called in to suggest an alteration in some of the rules to meet the requirements of the present times. This was done; the scheme was fully discussed at the annual meeting ' • and it was decided that the wishes of the members should be carried out. After several months of delay, we now find that the solicitors are the scotch in the wheel of progress. The solicitors say that ' the days of building societies are over; but building ' societies will never be things of the past so long as there are men who want a house and have neither money to build-nor buy. The argument has been musty for fifty years, and requires fumigating before trotting out. It is all very well for firms of solicitors who have lots of money from their clients to invest, to say that the Build- ing Society bubble has burst. But intending builders had better consider before getting advances from such sources. Their clients have a knack of calling in the money every two or three years and requiring fresh mortgage deeds. This action increases the " bonuses r considerably. What the Building Society wants is a rising solicitor, who can grasp the position and draft a scheme to meet the time. To do so, the rules must be drafted to enable the managers to regulate the rate of interest, and so compete vith wealthy solicitors, who have clients' monies galore.—Yours, A MEMBER.

div.p: SUNDAY OPENING AT THE WOOL PACK INN.

Sir,—ln your issue of September Ist "A Resident" (evidently a commendable, wide-awake, moral-minded person) obeyed the voice of his conscience, and did his duty in his able letter under the above heading, Will you kindly allow me also in a similar manner to obey the internal monitor, and do my duty in reference to the baneful practice of Sabbath drinking? Now, sir, Sunday drinking is either good or bad, sin- ful or holy, right or wrong, a blessing or a curse to humanity, wherever practised in town or country, and somebody must be responsible, and, if so, who? Your correspondent, "A Resident," ,eave vent to the painful feelings of many who are grieved at the sight of the wool Pack Inn again casting "its alluring lights in the path- ay of the young" on Sundays. Such persons know the evils of the sale of such pernicious stuff on the Lord's Day, as the prince of English genius and writers stigmatised, saying of it— " Let me call thee—devil," while Charles Johnson has fittingly branded its deadly effects, &c,, when he says- -0 when we swallow down
Intoxicating wine, we drink damnation; Naked we stand the sport of mocking fiends Who grin to see our noble nature vanquish'd, Subdued to beasts. Yes, sir, I r we know but too well the unutter- .. _

_ repeat .. able, dire results of Sabbath desecration by the sale of what the book of books, that heralding and guardian angel of the Sabbath, denounces as like unto the "poison of dragons," "the venom of asps ; " hence cries, "Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth alight. At the last lt lieth like a rpent, and stingeth like an adder." Nor is it other than a sin against God, and a curse to humanity, whether sold on that day by the landlord at the Woelpack Inn, Sankey-et., amid its rush of busi- ness, roll of wheels, clatter of feet, gloom and smoke of the town; or by such men as keep the Bottle and Birch in the lovely village of Stretton, with its thinly-scattered cottages, meetly trimmed and fertile gardens. Too often those who are in the bloom of youth, others in the flower of minhood, and some in the decline of years, find themselves travellers to both town and country publicans, in order to obtain on Lord's Day during pro- hibited hours some of their liquid frenzy water which, though pleasing their sense of taste, steals "away their brains.' Many such pitiable creatures have been scholars in our Sunday schools, and church or chapel-going peo- ple ; but now feel themselves almost as helpless to resist the pernicious influence of the publichouse and strong drink as a single attom of matter is to re- pel the gravitation of the globe we inhabit. It is high time the Wesleyan Methodists of the town had their eyes opened, their hearts touched, and, praying for the lost mantle which has fallen from their shoulders, again grasp with unyielding force the banner which they have trailed in the mire, lift it high, and henceforth sustain it there, in the name of the Author of the Sabbath, the interest of their scholars, &c., as well as the morality of all concerned.—Yours, &c., Warrington, September, liBB.
ON GUARD.

div.head: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this body was held on Wednesday, at the office at the Cemetery, the fol- lowing members being present Messrs. R. Morris (in the chair), Rogerson. Littler, Coleburn, Whittaker, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary).—lt was announced that the interments for the past five months. ending August 25, had been 134, corresponding period last year 126, showing an increase of eight. The fees received during the same period amounted to .£l3B 3s 6d, as compared with .£l4l Os 2d in corresponding period last year, or a decrease of .E 3 5s Bd.—Mr. Rogerson brought forward the question of the fees charged to persons living outside the parish for inter- ments. He considered that it was a great injustice to those people to charge them double fees, and that there should be a reduction made in the charges for the clergy, ministers, sexton, and for digging the graves. He could, however, quite understand why the non-residents should be charged double cemetery fees for graves and re-open- ing,s —ln reply to one of the members, the Secretary said that the fees for the clergy were not fixed by the Board, tut were claimed by the late Vicar of Runcorn, who would not inter unless the claim was paid. Therefore the Burial Board sanctionad the claim —Mr. Cole- burn said that the double fees were not paid from time immemorial. .They had been paid ever since the cemetery was purchased, and he supposed that the question of allowing double foes to be charged was agreed upon by the Board of that day.— After further discussion Mr. Rogerson said that, to bring matters to a conclusion, he should propose that the charges be the same to people living outside the town as to those living in the town, with the exception of the purchase of graves and re-openings. As the outsiders de- rived the same benefit from the cemetery to which the people of Runcorn had to pay, and which they contribu- ted nothing to, he thought there would be no injustice done by charging them double for the purchase of graves and for re-openings.—A prolonged discussion followed this proposal, after which Mr. Rogerson said that he would move "That the charges and fees of the Burial Board, with:the exception of those relating to the pur- chase and re-opening of graves, be the same for the in- habitants of Weston and Halton as they are for the in- habitants of Runcorn." Mr. Little seconded this proposition, which was carried.—This was the principal business.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this 'Board was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There wear present Colonel Ashton (chairman), Bev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Speakman, Taylor, P. Hall. Bran- dreth, Jones, Parr, Wallington, T. Hewitt,. W. Hew- itt, Ifeywood ; H. Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Lin- aker (deputy clerk). . _

THE' IVY Oir MEETING.—On the motion of the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner it was unanimously resolved to change the day of the Board's meeting from Tuesday to Thursday, the change to come in force at the end of the quarter. The change of day, Mr. Tanner said, made little differ- ence to any of .the Guardians, but it would be a great advantage to the relieving officers, as it would give them More time to make out their accounts. RESIGNATION OF THE NURSE—A letter resigning her situation was read from the nurse at the Workhouse (Miss Harrison), the reason for resigning being that she had secured a better situation.—The resignation was accepted. THE CATHOLIC 'too-rms.—Mr. Speakman gave notice that he would move at the next meeting that Dr. Gas- taldi, of Runcorn, be aepointed Roman Catholic priest for the workhouse at a salary of £lO per annum. THE TENDERS.—Mr. Jones, in accordance with notice previously given, asked the Workhouse Master several questions with respect to the mode of accepting goods on tender. He explained that he did not intend to make any charge against anyone, his object being simply to get a better method of carrying out the contracts.—The Work- house Master said his attention had been directed to a cutting from a newspaper, in which it was said that a charge had been made against the contractor and master. The contractor was present and would answer any question put to him as to what he supplied. He thought the contractor ought to be invited into the room—The Chairman said Mr. Jones • did not make any specific charge against any tine, as the matters he referred might date back for years past.—The Deputy Clerk: Then you make no charge against anyone ?—Mr. Jones :• No charge whatever.—The Workhouse Master said he took it that Mr. Jones withdrew what was repor- ted, and what he (the Master) had heard.—The Work- house Master then,answered several questions put to him by Mr. Jones.—Mr. Jones said certain things were ready not according to samples in quality.—The Chairman re- marked that Mr. Cunnah had answered certain questions and if Mr. Jones was not satisfied with the answers he might move that a committee be appointed to consider the matter.—Mr. Speakman ,moved that the answers' given to Mr. Jones's question by the Master were satis- factory to the Board.—Mr. Aaron seconded this propo- sition.—Mr. Parr: I think there /is great credit due to Mr. Jones if he sees anything wrong in bringing the matter forward —The proposition was carried.—Later on Mr. Jones handed in a notice of motion to the effect that he intended at the next meeting to move that the Board re-consider the present system of tendering. UNPAID CALLS.—It was decided to take proceedings agsinst the overseers of certain toWnships if the calls I I were not met. . .

„ TREATS TO Tnic INMATES.—Mr. Cunnah having repor- ted that the Rev. W. Fielding ;1,1.0 Mrs. Hayes had given treats to the children at the Workhouse, and the Rev. E. and Mrs. Marsden to the adults, on the proposition of Mr. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Taylor, 'votes of thanks were accorded them for their kindness.
This was the whole of the business of public in- terest

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Colonel Ashton (chairman), Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Aaron, W. Hewitt, Bran- dreth, Hall. T. Hewitt, Parr; IT. Linaker (clerk). W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), Farrington (nuisance inspector). THE WELLS AT KEILEWICII.-MT. Farrington said, with regard to the public, wells and cottages at Kekewich mentioned at a previous meeting, he saw that Mr. Evans had got the work in hand and no doubt the thing would be attended to. He therefore asked for a further adjourn- ment of 14 days, which was granted. THE INSANITARY COTTAGE AT WESTON AND LOWER WAD. TON.—Mr. Farrington said he had visited the cottage at Weston which had been reported as being in an unwhole- some state. A very poor attempt had been made to cleanse the place, the whitewash being placed over the , old paper.—Mr. Aaron said he had been at the place and found it in a most wretched state. It was only fit for hens and pigs but certainly not for human beings to live In.—lt was agreed that the medical officer should be asked to examine the place to see if it was fit for human habitation.—Mr. Farrington also reported having visited the unwholesome cottage at Lower Walton. He found that the bed-room and pantry had been lime-washed and the woman promised to continue the cleansing process. This matter was accordingly left in the hands of the inspector. BUILDINGS AT ACTON GRANGE.—Permission to occupy four cottages erected in connection with the Ship Canal works at Acton Grange was granted, and also houses erected for the engineer and missioner in course of erection at the same place. TECI3 SHIP CANAL AND THE AUTHORITY'S SEWERS.-Mr. Aaron wished to know how the Authority stood with re- gard to encroachments on the sewers in connection with the Ship Canal works.-The Chairman said the Authority was protected, but he thought the best plan would be to ask the law clerk to look into the matter.—Mr. Aaron stated that if they did not mind they would put the next generation in a rather serious position with regard to those sewers. He moved that the law clerk be asked to consider the matter and report to the next meeting.— This proposal as agreed to. THE COUNTY GOVERNMENT QUESTION.--Tho Chairman moved that a committee be appointed to meet the magis- trates of the petty sessional divisions of Runcorn, Eddis- bury, and Daresbury, and also to meet a committee of the Runcorn Commissioners, to take into consideration a scheme for dividing the county into electoral divisions. The population of the county at the last census was 644,037, but from this had to be deducted a total of 165,803, the population of boroughs to be made countie' of themselves. That left 478,241, but from this numl- - must deduct the population of those municii boroughs not made counties but the number of whose representatives had been fixed by the Local Government Board. This left 348,558 as the population from which electoral divisions had to be formed, and as there were to be 43 electoral divisions, if they divided 348,558 by 43 they would get a population of 8,106 for each electoral division. The population of the Authority's district was 18,897, and that of the urban district of Runcorn 15,826 —total, 34,023. This was about the tenth of the 348,558 and they were therefore fairly entitled to four represen- tatives, but hardly to five. If they had these four, the question would arise how they were to be distributed. Runcorn with its population of 15,826 would be entitled to two, and in that case the rest of the district would have to be divided into two parts, each of which would have a population of from 9,000 to 10,000. Already he had gone into the matter to a certain extent with Mr. Linaker, and Mr. Greenall, clerk to the Daresbury magis- trates, and they came to the conclusion that they could not very fairly ask for more than four representatives when they came to meet the magistrates. Supposing they had four, Runcorn should have two of the four, and the rest of the Union would have to be divided for the other two. The Frodsham side of the Weaver, including Weston, Sutton, Aston, Aston Grange, and Clifton, might form one district with a population of 9,879, leav- ing the rest of the Union—including the townships of Grappenhall and Thelwall which were to be added to the Union—to form the other district with a population of 10,525. He moved that the chairmAn, Messrs. Mclntyre and Stokes, with the clerk, form the committee he pro- posed should be appointed. He should mention that all they could do was to suggest ti the magistrates; the scheme would be formed by the quarter sessions.—Mr. Aaron seconded the chairman's proposal, which was ag,reed to.

MARRIAGE OF MISS NESSIE MUSPRATT. At Sefton,. on Wednesday, a marriage was solem- nised between Mr. Egerton Stewart Brown, eldest son of Mr. Stewart H. Brown, of Quarry Bank, ana Miss Nessie Muspratt, second daughter of Mr. Ed- mund K. Muspratt„of Seaforth Hall. A large gather- I ing, composed chiefly of young ladies, assembled at the church to witness the bridal procession, which arrived at half-past twelve o'clock. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a dress of white satin brocaded in silver, with long court train car- ried by a page, and tulle veil, with orange blossoms. She wore diamond ornaments, presented by the bridegroom, and carried a magnificent white bou- quet, also his gift. She was attended by nine bridesmaids viz., Misses Hildegarde and Steil° Muspratt (sisters of the bride), Misses Emily, Hen- rietta, and Marian Stewart Brown (sisters of the bridegroom), Misses Ethel and Ida Forward, Miss Bains (cousin of the bride), and Miss Timmis. Four of the bridesmaids were dressed in sea green pongee silk, trimmed with Valenciennes lace, while the five others wore costumes of pink pongee silk, also trimmed with Valenciennes lace. Their hats were all alike, and wore a sapphire and pearl broach and carried a posy of pink roses, the gifts of the bridegroom. The bride's page was Master Clifford Muspratt, her brother, who appeared in a costume of green velvet. with white lace collar and cuffs. The best man was Mr. Henry Stewart Brown, brother of the bridegroom. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. E. Honey, MA., rector of Sefton, and the Rev. Fitzgerald Smithwick, vicar of Seaforth. Besides the wedding party, nearly a hundred friends and spectators assembled in the chan- cel, which is divided from the nave by a handsomely carved screen. Among the invited guests were Mr. and Mrs Stewart Brown, Sir William and Lady Brown, Sir Mark and Lady Collett, Colonel and Mrs. A. H. Brown, Mr. A. B. Forwood, eI.P.. and Mrs. Forwood, Mrs. Mus- pratt, Mr. and Mrs. J Clifton Brown, Mr and Mrs R. D. Holt,.Mr. E R. Russell, Mrs. Richard Muspratt, Miss Muspratt, Mr. and Mrs. S. K. Muspratt, Mr, Talbot Baines, Mr. and Mrs. F. C Baines, the Rev. and Mrs. Abbott Brown, Mr., Mrs., and Miss De Ruyter, the Rev. G. Blenkin, Mr. and Mrs. Schwind, Mr. and Mrs. Hamilton. Miss Purnell, Mr and Mrs Birkett, Mr. Canoe, Mr. H. G. Kellock, Mr Bateson, Mr. and Mrs Hammond, Mr. and Mrs G. H. Horsfall, Mr. and Mrs James Birkett, Miss Birkett, Mr. John E. fir- kett, Mrs Sarah B. Brown, the Hon. Assheton Curzon, and Mr. H. B. Steel. The "Bridal march" from " Lo- hengrin" was played by the organist when the party entered the church, and Mendelssohn's "Wedding March " was performed as they left. After the ceremony, the wedding party drove to Seaforth Hall, where luncheon was served to over sixty guests. At three o'clock the newly married pair left for London, en route for the Continent. Between three o'clock and half-past five a reception took place at the Hall, which was attended by about three hundred friends, at which the bride's pres- ents, which number over 200. and which are very beautiful, were exhibited.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this body was held on Tuesday. at the Public Offices. Widnes. The chair was occupied by Messrs. T. H. Gossage, and there were also present Dr. O'Beeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, H. Handley, D. Wright, W. W. Gossage, J. Midwool, S. Sadler, J. Houghton, 11. Gaskell, junr., J. Taylor, F. Heyes, J. T. Allen (clerk), T. Higginson (surveyor), J. Dickenson (inspector), and J. C. Carr (en- gineer). A DANGEROUS ROAD.—The Clerk read a letter that had been received from John Fitzpatrick. 10, Birchfield-road, Appleton, who stated that a part of Birchfield-road that was at present under repair was in a very dangerous state. It was dangerous to traffic, the ground being un- level and soft. A horse had on one occasion fallen down there, throwing the occupants out of a trap, and on another occasion a furniture van stuck fast in the mud, and could not be removed until some of the goods had been discharged and fresh horses had been obtained. On another occasion a conveyance from Ditton came to grief, the horse falling and tile occupants being thrown out of the trap. Mr. Fitzpatrick added that as a rate- payer he had no desire to pay towards compensation items, to which the Board might be liable in consequence of the state of the road. After further correspondence had been read on the same subject, the consideration of the letters was referred to the Highway Com- mittee. A letter from Messrs. W. Pilkington and Sons, chemical manufacturers, complaining of the state of the road from Appleton station to their works, was also re- ferred to the same committee.
THE AUDIT.—On the 17th August the auditor wrote that he had completed the audit of the accounts of the Board, and stated that he had only had occasion to dis- allow one small account.

GAS AND WATER COMMITIES.—TO this committee the Engineer, among various other matters, reported that up to the present he had been unable to obtain a satis- factory teli, pf the working of the fuel economiser at f the unavoidable stoppage Stock' s Well in cOriSequen,7.: 9 of the engine during the time the tests were :2 ProZress• Early on Monday, the 20th ult., a fire broke out at Messrs J. White and Company's oil works. The brigade attended and succeeded in extinguishing the fire, which had taken hold at the hack of the property facing Vic- toria-road ; the works themslves were completely de- stroyed. The arrangemement for calling out the brigade at the time of fire required some consideration. At pre- Sent the police were solely depended on for giving the alarm to the men, but on the occasion of the last three fires this had, through some want of understanding, been badly done, one or two of the men only having been called. Consequently before the brigade could be got together much damage had been done that might have been prevented had the alarm been given with prompti- tude to the whole of the firemen. The mean rainfall for the month had been 3-12 inches, and the water in stock August 29th, 1888, was 5,669,030 gallons. The illumina- ting power of the gas during the month had averaged, 17.33 candles. The wages required during the next foul weeks were £BO per week for gas and water works, and for piecework during the month £250. The month's accounts amounted to £733 16s 2d for gas works, and £ll3 13s 5d for water works. The committee recom- mended the acceptance of various tenders.--=The minutes were confirmed on the motion if Mr. 11. Gaskell, jun., seconded by Mr. Wright. HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.—This committee recommended that accounts amounting to £1,016 18s 3d, including £832 13s for main sewer and private improvements, be passed for payment. The estimate of wages for the next four weeks was £37 per week. Tne• Surveyor repor- ted that the contractor was still proceeding with the Birchfield-road contract, and application had been made by the Warrington Building Society to have their cellars connected with the new drain when completed. Plans, sections, and estimates had been prepared for West Bank and Milton streets. Notice.i had been posted in the following streets as to their becoming public highways: —Witt-road. Marsh-st., Fisher-st., Ellison-st., Lea-st., Farrant-st., New-st., Victoria-st., Margaret-st., James-st, Irwell-st! West-st., Parsonage-road, and Viaduct-st., from Church-st. to Parsonage-road. The steam roller had during the past month been engaged in rolling public roads 6A. days, private roads 18i days, and had been in the yard 5± days. Various other matters of an unim- portant character were mentioned in the report of the committee, which was adopted, on the proposition of Mr. Sadler, seconded by Mr. Taylor. HEALTH Commrraa.—The minutes of this Committee were adopted on the motion of Mr. E. Carey, seconded by Mr. Wright. They stated that accounts to the amount of £7516s 4d, including£6oo for Fever Hospital, had been passed for payment, and contained the report for August of the Medical Officer. The report stated that there had been 108 births and 60 deaths. Mr. Con= vide had been appointed, subject to a month's trial, in a probationer at the Fever Hospital. The Inspector re- ported that in August there were four deaths from typhoid fever, two of which occurred at the Fever Hospital. Scarlet fever was very prevalent in the district, but their had been no fatal cases. There were eight deaths from diarrheea, and one from measles. Disinfec- tion had been attended to. Instructions were given to serve notices to abate several ffuisances. It was also recommended that application be made to the Local Government Board to sanction the re-appointment of Mr. Cooper, Medical Officer of Health, for the ensuing twelve months, at a salary of £6O per annum. MISCELLANEOUS. —The minutes of this Committee which contained the usual financial statement, were adopted on the proposition of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Midwood. The report of the, General Purposes Com- mittee, which contained matters of routine, was also adopted. This was all the busine,sss before the meeting.

FIRES AT WIDNES. The Widnes police were on Thursday, shortly af- ter half-past twelve in the afternoon, informed that a fire had broken out at the premises of Mr. Rich- ard Balshaw, joiner and builder, Widnes-road, Wid- nes. It appears that Mr. Balshavv and his son left the shop to go to dinner at noon. Mr. Balshaw, on returning soon afterwards. was surprised to hear a crackling noise, as though of burning wood. On going into the workshop he found that a fire had broken out, and sent information to the Fire Brigade Station. The fire, however, had got a firm hold of a quantity of buildings, and it quickly spread to the buildings, which were soon a mass of flames. The first hose to arrive was that belonging to the Simm's Cross Board School, which was brought by Mr. Showan (head master) and Mr. Birkenhead (caretaker). They quickly fixed the pipe and commenced playing on the Nouse adjoining the yard, which is occupied by Mr. Tracy. Soon afterwards Mr. Duxbury, assistant superintendent of the Fire Brigade, arrived from the gas works with the reel cart; and about one o'clock the rest of the Brigade, with the manual engine, were on the spot, and in a very short time four or five pipes were pouring water on the flames. It was thought that the two houses adjoiaingthe yard, occupied

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 15, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 15, 1888.

by Mr. Tracey. and Dr. McCambridge, would be des- troyed, as the wind blew the flames against them, but the firemen turned a strong force of water in that direc- tion and succeeded in preventing serious damage. Mr. Tracey, however, is a loser by the panic, for the people 'wiled into his house and pulled his furniture out, with the object, of course, of saving it from the flames. Much of it was broken or otherwise damaged, and it will cost itt least £2O or £3O to replace it in its former condition." A strong force of police were present, under Superintendent Johnston, Sergeant Mc- Gregor, and Sergeant Clarkson. At half-past one the fire was practically out, the workslop and saw-shed be- ing gutted, and most of the timber reduced to ash. The damage is estimated by Mr. Balshaw at about £5OO, and it is only partially covered by insurance ih the Lon- don and Lancashire 'Office. The origin of the fire is un- known.

On Wednesday evening an arch at the Lancashire Al- kali and Sulphur Co.'s Works fell into a portion of the caustic plant. The flames flared up for a moment, and set fire to a beam overhead An alarm was spread that the works were on fire. Whistles were blown at several adjoining works, and the fire brigade were called out; but really there was no occasion for commotion, the flames being extinguished by the workmen, who had a plentiful supply of water and buckets The fire brigade got their manual engine out, but turned back before they reached Ditton-road Very little damage was done.

div.head: SERIOUS EXPLOSION AT WIDNES.
div.p: SERIOUS EXPLOSION AT WIDNES.

On Wednesday night, between eight and nine o'clock, a rather serious explosion occurred at the works of the Lancashire Alkali and Sulphur Com- pany, Widnes. It appears from what can be gathered of the matter that one of the large revolvers used in the manufacture of chemicals burst with considerable violence, and set fire to the roof of the building. An alarm was given by th e workpeople,who promptly set to work to extinguish the blames. By the aid of a copious supply of water, which they carried in buckets, they succeeded in putting out the fire before the arrival of the brigade. Very little damage was occasioned by the accident.

div.head: ALLEGED ATTEMPTED INCENDIARISM AT WIDNES. •
div.p: ALLEGED ATTEMPTED INCENDIARISM AT WIDNES. •

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, two men named John Kiernan, 11, New-st., and Richard Scott, 23, New-st., were brought up on remand on a charge of having attempted to set lire to a haystack at Farnworth; on Sunday night. Mr. Knowles, solici- • tor, appeared for the defence.—P.C. Heaton deposed that at about 11-30 on the night in question he was on duty in Derby-road, Farnworth. He was pass- ing the stack-yard of Richard Alcock, when he heard some one strike a match. On looking round he saw prisoner Kiernan with a lighted match in his right hand. His left hand was in the haystack. Ile could see Kiernan's face by the light from the match. Witness called out to him to stop, thinking that he was going to set fire to the stank. He then turned his lantern, and saw the prisoner Scott come out of a small gate leading to the farm-yard. Kiernan was running away, and witness followed him. Being closely approached, Kiernan turned round, and at- tempted to knock the constable down. He, how- ever, knocked him down, and put the " snaps " on him. Asked what he was doing there, Kiernan said, "We have missed our 'way, and lam going to light my pipe." There was no pipe in his hand or mouth at the time.. Prisoner Scott was also taken into custody. Next morning witness examined the hay stack, and found a hole in the stack about ten inches deep, near where he had seen prisoner Kiernan with the lighted match. He also picked up four burnt matches and an empty match box off the ground at the side of the stack. On being searched at the police station at Widnes Keernan was found to be in possession of a wooden pipe, but no tobacco. Scott had a piece of tobacco, but no pipe. Witness charged both prisoners to- gether with the offence alleged against them. Kiernan replied "I did nothing of the sort; it was the last thing in my head." Scott replied , "We did not do anything to the hay- stack." Both the prisoners had had drink. but they knew what they were about.— Richard Alcock. farmer, Derby-road farm, said that he had some haystacks close to the side of the road. There was a hole in one of them which appeared as if some ono had had his hand in it.—Evidence was also given by Inspector Keighley, and William Leeche, a barman.—Mr. Knowles submitted on be- half of the prisoners that there had been no evid- ence whatever adduced against them to warrant the Bench sending them for trial. It was not at all unreasonable that Kiernan should go tothe shel- ter of the stack to light his pipe. He submitted' that there was nothing but mere suspicion in regard to the case, and that it was one which, if sent for trial, would be dismissed.—The magistrates decided to send the case for trial at the Liverpool Assizes, bail being allowed.

The intervening waggon was completely smashed, and a bolt from it struck a young man named Hollingwortlt, from Heatley, on the forehead, and knocked him off the engine insensible. Of course, the waggons hi which the men were being conveyed tipped again (being specially made for the purpose), and the occupants tumbled about. Those who had been in the previous collision declined to "try again," and walked on to their work. STANLOW POINT.

At Stanley. Point something like/ 30 huts are erected for the accommodation of the men, as well as a general stores. On Saturday a train leaves the Point to convey' the shoppers to the more advantageous place of Elles- mere Port, and returns some two hours afterwards. On Sunday the new mission hall was bpened. Three ser- vices were held, the preachers being Mr. Pickles, mission ary at Ince, in the morninz ; the Rev. Dr. Statham,vicar of Ellesmere Port, in the afternoon ; and Mr. Cleverley, the missionary stationed at the Point, in the evening. All the services were very well attended. At the east end a communion table, reading desk, and prayer desk are erected, and at the west end is a gallery for the choir. At present the musical instrument used is a harmonium, but this will shortly be replaced by an organ. The whole accommodation of the hall is 260. The interior is fitted with pitchpine, and.the seats are made so as to be re- versed to face each other for classes. The building also contains two large classrooms, the whole being heated with hot water. The missionary has charge of the old mission room, which is now used as a recreation room and the reading room at nights and during wet weather. Here the men can peruse the ordinary dailies and local weeklies, and 'amuse themselves with draughts, 'dominoes, &c. In connection with this room a lending library has been established, the books being supplied by I the Navvy Mission Society. Not only are religious ibooks supplied, but some really good scientific and dra- matic literature may be obtained. Mr. Cleverley has I also established a Sunday school, which has a roll-call spine.3o strong.
TERRIBLE CILLISION OFF THE CANARY ISLANDS. '

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

Recently the pottery and bid Quay flour mill were submitted for sale, the site being required for the pur- poses of the canal. So far as the pottery is concerned, the buildings have been razed to the ground, and soon there will be little sign of such works having been in ex- istence The machinery has been removed from the old mill, and the building will shortly cease to exist. The first of a series of cargoes of dressed granite copings has been deposited near to the Ship Canal engineering offices at the Old Quay. At the wharves there is at present at work a ten-ton locomotive crane, which has the merit of working as a railway engine, and also can be used in shunting During the week it has been used with suc- cessful effect in unloading the fiats of timber brought up the river, and depositing the material in the railway trucks which are at present engaged on the rails which. have been laid from Norton to Messrs. Brundrit and Co 's ship-building yard in Mersey-st. The course of the river is being tested, in close proximity to the ferry, to ascer- tain at what depth rock may be encountered. The result is awaited with m-uch Interest. The work in the cutting between Norton and the Old Quay is still progressing satisfactorily, and the difficulty which seemed at one time to exist in giving the works of Mem.rs. Wigg Brothers and Steel a Supply of water to enable them to continue in operation has been sur- mounted by the laying down of two pumping engines, which are kept at work supplying water from the river.

WESTON. Operations are being pushed forward with much suc- cess, and the course of the canal so far as Frodsham Marsh i 3 concerned is being delved out, and over a quar- ter of a mile of the land has been excavated. About 3,000 tons of soil, &c., are removed by the German navvy per day. It is anticipated that at no distant date there will be quite a village of dwellings on the Marsh. Pro- vision is being made for a locomotive shed and the neces- sary workshops, and also for the supply to the inhabi- tants of the dwellings on the Marsh of good water, the well, which has reached a depth of almost 120,geet, pro- mising excellent results. MOORE, &c. The German navvy continues to make headway at Moore. Another block of huts is being erected at Acton Grange, to face those which are already tenanted. A mission chapel is also being built, and a residence for the missionary is in course of erection. From Morley Com- mon the main cutting of the canal has been extended right through Lower Walton village as far as Townfield. The new road, which will connect the Chester and Northwich roads, is near completion. A powerful steam navvy is at work at George's bank, which is the name given to the piece of land lying on the north side of the Old Quay canal between Tom Paine's and Twenty-step bridges. With but few exceptions the whole of the houses in the canal route at Stockton Heath marked out for demolition are unoccupied, and one terrace between Twenty-step bridge and St. Thomas's church has this week been razed to the ground. THELWALL AND STATHAM.

Two steam navvies are now actively at work between Morris Brook and Cedar Lawn, and every day the al- ready large and deep cutting here is lengthened and en- larged. This part of the works is regularly visited by large numbers of sight-seers as it is near the road and easily accessible. The making of the new road, which will commence at a point near Morris Brook farmhouse and terminate in Grappenhall-lane near Latchford Sta- tion, is being pushed forward rapidly, and already a 'large quantity of macadam has been deposited ready for use. Owing to the inconvenience caused by many of the workmen on the canal not being able to obtain lodg- lOgS near the scene of their labours the contractor has arranged that a locomotive and A number of waggons should run from Latchford along the ballast line, and leave the men down at their several places of work each morning. The majority of the men travel by this means to and from Warrington. On Monday the locomotive was engaged at 545 a.m. bringing up the navvies, and on reaching Statham meadows, on her way to flollin's Green, the fog was so dense that the driver did not see the locomotive "waste" which was standing on the line until close upon it. The impact caused the waggons to tip up, bundling the navvies in a motley heap, but for- tunately no one Was hurt. They gathered themselves into the waggons again, and by extra caution on the part of the engine-driver:they were deposited safely at Hollin's Green. Some, however, proceeded on foot to- wards their destination, but on reaching Rixton Ley islands they found the locomotive "St. Andrew" setting out for the goal at which they wished to be landed, and they cast in their lot with it. The fog did not seem to clear away much, and before this locomotive got far on its way it collided with the "Mersey," and as the latter was running a waggon before it, meeting the "St.
