div.head: _LOSS OF EIGIITY-SEVEN LIVES.
div.p: _LOSS OF EIGIITY-SEVEN LIVES.

A cablegram received in Liverpool on Thursday afternoon reports a frightful collision between two large steamers off the Canary Islands, and the loss of about 100 lives. The colliding steamers are re- ported to be both foreign vessels—viz„ the French steamer La France and the Italian steamer Sud America. The particulars at present to hand are very brief, but it seems that the collision, which was of a terrific nature, resulted in the Sad America sinking in a very short time. She appears to have had a large number of people on board, and as she belonged to an Italian line which traded with South America, it is surmised that many of the people who have lost their lives are emigrants. La France also belongs to a line of steamers running to South America. The message did not Aate if all the un- fortunate people who perished belonged to the one boat, but it is believed that, as the Sud America went down very soon after the collision, most, if not all, of the drowned belonged to her. It is also un- derstood from the serious nature of the impact that the French steamer was badly damaged, though she remained afloat up to the latest accounts. The Sud America was a four-masted steamer of 2.217 tons gross register, built by Messrs. Wigham, Richard- son, and Co., on the Tyne. in 187 P. She was under the command of Captain Bertova, and belonged to La Valoce Nay. Italians., of Genoa. La France was a much larger vessel,.being 3,572 tons gross register. She was built in 1871. and was own-NI by the Societe Generale des Transports, of Marseilles. A Reuter's telegram, dated Madrid, Thursday says :—A telegram received here states that the steamer La France, from Marseilles, while entering ' Port Luz, in the Canary Islands, at six o'clock last evening, came into collision with the Italian steamer Sud America, from Monte Video, and that the latter, which was lying at anchor, sank in ten minutes in ten fathoms of water. The Sud America carried 261 passengers and a crew of 69 men. One hundred and eighty of the former and 63 of the latter are stated to have reathed the shore. Nine dead bodies have been recovered.

A Lloyd's telegram states that six of the 'crew and eighty-one passengers of the steamer Sud America have been drowned through collision with the steamer La France. RECOVERY OF BODIES. There is hope of raising the Italian liner Sud Ameiica, which sank off Port Luz, on Thursday, after colliding with the French steamer La France. Many bodies have been recovered. _

MIDRID, FRIDAY.—A despatch from the Canary Islands states that 20 bodies have been recovered from the wreck of the Sud. Many of those rescued are in the hospital suffering from injuries Of exhaus- tion.

FRODSHAM. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—On Sunday anniversary ser- vices were held at the Union Church, the preacher being the Rev. Thomas Hartley, of Burslem. The sum of £l7 13s 9d was collected. Appropriate hymns werg given by the members of the choir, who were assistdd by the scholars of the Sunday school.

Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's. which for strength is utiequalled.—Advt. The Marchioness of Ripon has subscribed £2O towards the Parnell Expenses Fund. The Bank rate of discount was raised on Thursday from 3 per cent. to 4 per cent. Earl Granville will be entertained at dinner on October 20 by the Liverpool Reform Club. _ . . _

Tlie ancient custom of ringing the curfew bell has been resumed at Stratford-on-Avon, the same bell being used as was tolled at Shakespeare's funeral. ' MURDER IN IRELAND.—James Curtin, who was ar- rested on Tuesday night on a charge of complicity in the murder of John Forhan at Mountcole, county Kerry, on July 20, was taken before a magistrate at Listowel on Wednesday and remanded. On the day referred to For- ham was returning from Tralee , with, Some labourers whom he had hired, when a man , approached the car in the roadway and fired several shots from a revolver. Forhan was killed, and the persons with him, with the exception of his young son, made off back to Tralee. Curtin was in custody three weeks ago, but was dis- charged, as there was no evidence offered against him. The lad Forhan on Wednesday gave a graphic accour* Of the outrage, and positively identified the prisoner as the guilty man, stating that he abstained from giving evidence before because he was afraid. ' A WESTMORELAND TRAGEDY.—WeStMOreIand has tor many years been almost free from heinous crime ; but flithas been startled this week by a tragedy that has kOtsed the most intense excitement through the coun- tryside. On Tuesday Mr. William Atkinson and his fe arrived from their home in London at Lupton Tower, near Kirkby Lonsdale, and quarrelled with their To , ther-in-law, John Vernon, a'gamekeeper. There had I been a family feud for some time, and Vernon, becoming enraged at this new development of it, threatened to shoot his visitors. It is said he endeavoured to do so, but that they succeeded in wresting a revolver from his grasp. Nothing daunted, he seized a gun, and shot At- kinson dead, and then went to his room and blew out his own brains. The inquest on Atkinson concluded late On Wednesday night. The evidence showed that the crime was most deliberate, and that Vernon, the gamekeeper, who afterwards committed suicide, fired on Atkinson without any provocation. Mrs Atkinson was standing at the side of her husband, and had a miraculous escape. The two bodies presented a shocking spectacle. The jury found that Atkinson was murdered by Vernon, and that the latter committed suicide whilst temporarily in- sane. ,

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The funeral of Annie Chapman took place on Friday morning with the utmost secrecy. On Friday morning a marker was shotthrough the body at the Government Range, Middlewich, Colchester. He is in a critical condition.

An alarming fire broke out in the business portion of Guildford on Thursdaynight. Some shops were destroyed, but the ancient Town Hall escaped. A Downpatrick telegram states that William Allen, one of the men injured in the explosion at the quarry near Holywood, co. Down, died on Friday. The Duke of Cambridge arrived at Glasgow from Edinburgh, on Friday, and was received by the city magistrates. He made a circuit of the city, and visited the Exhibition.

SENTENca ON Mn. Ranntoxri.—On Friday, at Wexford, before Mr. M‘Leod, R.M. and Mr.' Bodkin, R.M., Mr. William Redmond, M.P., for inciting persons to resist the sheriff on the occasion of the evictions at Coolroe, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment without hard labour.

ATTExPrsa MURDER BY. A Womvi.—A Skibbereen telegram states that a woman attacked another woman named Doolan with a knife, with intent to murder her, at four o'clock on Friday morning. Doolan escaped by jumping through a window, and sustairted severe injur- ies. She lies m a precarious condition. The assailant was arrested with difficulty.

EVICTIONS ON CLARE ISLAND.--A Westport correspon- dent states that at six o'clock on Friday morning. the Deputy Sheriff and a party of bailiffs, accompanied by about 50 police, embarked on the gunboat Britomast at Rossmina, and proceeded to Clare Island to execute a number of decrees for possession on the property of the Misses O'Connell, of Ashleagh. Two SISTERS DROWNED.—A melancholy drowning case was reported 'cm Friday from Galway. Two little girls named Stewart were blackberrying on a cliff, when one fell over into the river, 24 feet below. Her sister tried to save her and also fell over, striking a pro- jecting boulder in her descent. Both were swept off by the rapid current, but the bodies were afterwards recovered. Tos SWIMMING CHAMPIONSHIP.—The challenge match for the mile championship in sea water. £5O a-side, be- tween Tames Finney, of London, champion of the world, and George Kistler, of Penzance, came off in Mount's Bay, on Friday morning, and resulted in an easy victory for Finney. At the finish he was at least 100 yards ahead of Kistler. Finney's time was 29mins. 28secs. ; Kistler's time, 30mins. 43secs.

The detectives have not yet inquired at Heath-st. respecting the infor- mation published by the Press Association, but the des- cription of the man with the long knife who was pursued into a bye street corresponds with one who was seen in Flower and Dean-streets on Sunday afternoon, and with whom a woman named Lyons went into a public-house. THE REVOLT IN AFGHANISTAN. The Ameer Abdurrahman reports to the Indian Govern- ment that his troops have captured the Kamard fort held by the rebels, and have taken many prisoners, among whom is the father-in-law of Ishak Khan.
THE STANLEY EXPEDITION.-MAJOR ilAwrrnoT ASSASSINATED.

The followiniteleir-am- has been -i:Q;;;a from Sir F. De Winton: It is with the atest regret I send you the following telegtam just received from the Congo : " Barttelott assassinated by his carriers. Jameson back at the falls reorganising, with probable success, new expedition. Tippoo absent at Nyangwe.--PAn- MINTER.

In the absence of dekail it is impossible to arrive at any conclusion which would account for this most sad event—l am, sir, your obedient servant, F. Du WINTON. 24, Tavistock-road, Westbourne Park, September 13th. Major Edmund Musgrave Barttelot was the second son of Walter Barttelot, M.P., and was a Major in the Ist Battalion of the Royal Fusiliers. He served in the Af- ghan Campaign, for which he received the medal and clasp, and the Egyptian Campaign winning a similar decoration. He was born in March, 1859. . . . . .

The murder of Major Barttelot in Central Africa while' advancing to the succour of Stanley, has caused in Lon- don a gloomy view to be taken of the position of the other explorers. It is believed that the natives compri- sing the expedition, finding the difficulties in the way al- most insurmountable, clamoured to ,return, and finding that Major Barttelot persisted in advancing, murdered him. The disaster crushes any reasonable hope of ano- ther Stanley search expedition being raised and equipped in time to render aid to the gallant explorer, and- unless Stanley himself can hold his own unaided in the face of the, turbulent tribes ,inhabiting his line of advance, there can be little donbt as to what his fate must be. The greatest sympathy is felt in London for the deceased's father (Sir Walter Barttelot), who is now on the Conti- nent. LATEST. BRUSSELS, FRIDAY,—SOVeraI Belgian officers recently arrived from the Congo have expressed the belief that Major Barttolet's murder was due to personal vengeance. They are confident in Stanley's ultimate success. No further news has been received from the Congo. Sir Walter Barttolet has received no direct information respecting ' his son's death. The Government have no inforrnation on the subject. There are some who think Tippoo Tib has had a hand in the murder, and that Stanley, too, may have been a victim of his treachery.
